0.title: That You May Know: The Epistle of Assurance
0.overview:
There is a letter in the New Testament that reads like the heartbeat of an old man who has seen everything and lost nothing. John — the apostle whom Jesus loved, the one who leaned against the Lord at the Last Supper, the one who stood at the foot of the cross when the others had fled (John 13:23; 19:26) — writes at the end of a long life with the urgency of a man who knows that what he carries is the most important thing in the world. He has handled the Word of Life with his own hands. He has seen the glory. And he cannot be silent.

The First Epistle of John was written to a community under assault — not from Rome, but from within. Teachers had arisen who denied the full humanity of Christ, claiming that the eternal Son had not truly come in the flesh, that the spiritual and the material could not really meet. They were sophisticated, confident, and wrong. When they left the fellowship, John writes to those who remain, not to condemn the departed but to assure the faithful: you are not the ones who have missed it. The letter is saturated with the word "know" — used over thirty times. John wants his readers to know that they have eternal life, that they are in fellowship with the Father and the Son, that the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

But assurance in John is never cheap. It is tested by three great evidences that run through the letter like interwoven cords: the moral test (do you walk in the light, keeping his commandments?), the social test (do you love your brothers and sisters?), and the doctrinal test (do you confess that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh?). These are not conditions for salvation but symptoms of it — the fingerprints of new birth on a redeemed life. The person who has truly been born of God will love, will obey, and will confess. Not perfectly — John is the one who tells us that if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves — but genuinely and persistently.

At the theological centre of the letter stands the cross. "The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin" (1:7). "He is the propitiation for our sins" (2:2). "He laid down his life for us" (3:16). "God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (4:10). John circles back to the atoning death of Christ again and again, because the cross is the ground of everything — fellowship, forgiveness, assurance, love. The love of God is not an abstraction in 1 John; it is a specific act: the sending of the Son into the world to bear the wrath that our sins deserved so that we might live through him.

1 John was written to produce settled, humble, joyful assurance in the hearts of those who have truly come to Christ — and such assurance, far from producing complacency, is the very fire that fuels a life of love.

1.title: The Word of Life and the God of Light
1.text: <sup>1</sup>That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—<sup>2</sup>the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—<sup>3</sup>that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.<sup>4</sup>And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.<sup>5</sup>This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.<sup>6</sup>If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.<sup>7</sup>But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.<sup>8</sup>If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.<sup>9</sup>If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.<sup>10</sup>If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
1.overview:
The letter opens with a declaration, not a greeting. John insists four times on the physical reality of what he witnessed: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The eternal Word became someone John could hold. Against teachers who claimed a higher spiritual knowledge and despised the body, John’s answer is the incarnation.

The purpose is fellowship with the Father, the Son and one another. Then comes the first test: God is light, with no darkness at all. Any claim to know him that is comfortable with sin is self-deception. But the answer to sin is not despair. The blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin, and God forgives all who confess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before any command or warning, John rests the whole letter on one fact: the eternal Word became audible, visible and touchable. John is writing as a man who was there, who ate with him and touched him after he rose. And the purpose of his witness is not just correct information, but that his readers would share the fellowship he has with the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Incarnation as the Ground of Fellowship

The eternal life was heard, seen and touched. A Christ who did not truly come in the flesh could not truly atone, and fellowship with God rests on that fact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Teachers were spiritualising Christ out of his humanity.

Now: The gospel is not a philosophy but a report of what was heard and seen.

verseByVerse.quote: That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—
verseByVerse.commentary:
That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life—the life was made manifest, and we have seen it, and testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and was made manifest to us—

Meaning first. 1 John 1 lays the foundation of the letter: the reality of Christ and the reality of fellowship with God. The eternal Word of life, who was with the Father from the beginning, became visible; the apostles heard him, saw him and touched him (vv. 1–2). They proclaim him so that the readers may share their fellowship, which is fellowship with the Father and the Son, and so that their joy may be complete (vv. 3–4). The message they heard from him is that God is light, with no darkness at all (v. 5), and it exposes three false claims: to have fellowship with God while walking in darkness (v. 6), to have no sin (v. 8), and never to have sinned (v. 10). Against each John sets grace: walking in the light, where Jesus’ blood cleanses us from all sin (v. 7), and confession, which God is faithful and just to forgive (v. 9). The chapter that begins with God’s Son touched by human hands ends with sinners touched by his blood.

The setting. The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that the church has always received it as the work of the apostle John, son of Zebedee, the beloved disciple. He probably wrote from Ephesus near the end of the first century, as an old man (he calls his readers little children, 2:1), to churches in Asia. A group had left the church (2:19) teaching a false Christ: perhaps an early Docetism, which held that matter is evil and that the divine Christ only seemed to have a body, or the view of Cerinthus (according to Irenaeus) that the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left before his death. They claimed special knowledge of God while living carelessly and without love. Irenaeus, passing on a story from Polycarp, John’s own disciple, tells how John once ran out of the public baths at Ephesus on seeing Cerinthus inside, saying the building might fall because the enemy of the truth was in it. The apostle who wrote more about love than any other could not bear to share a roof with a man who unmade Christ. John writes to assure true believers (5:13) and to give them tests of genuine faith: truth about Christ, obedience, and love.

A sentence that cannot wait for its verb. The Greek sentence that opens the letter is one long, breathless accumulation before the main verb arrives. You do not reach “we proclaim” until verse 3. John piles up the evidence first, clause on clause, like a witness who has been waiting sixty years to be asked and cannot get it out in order. It has no greeting, no name, no thanksgiving. It is the most abrupt opening of any letter in the New Testament, and the abruptness is the point: the thing he has to say is too large for pleasantries.

That which was from the beginning. “From the beginning” (ap’ archēs) echoes John 1:1, “In the beginning was the Word”, and behind that Genesis 1:1. John is speaking of the eternal Son, who existed before creation. The Gospel begins before time and moves forward into flesh; the letter begins with the same eternity and moves straight to fingertips. And John uses the neuter, “that which”, not “he who”, to embrace the whole message about Christ, his person and his work: everything that came with him, everything he said and did and was.

Which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands. Three senses, rising in intensity, as though John were walking closer. Heard (akēkoamen) is what you can do from the edge of a crowd. Seen (heōrakamen) needs line of sight, and both are perfect tenses: a completed act whose effect is still with him. Then the tense changes. “Looked upon” (etheasametha) is not a glance but a long, careful gaze; it is the word of the Gospel’s great sentence, we have seen his glory (John 1:14), the word from which we get theatre, watching something until you have taken it in. And “touched” (epsēlaphēsan) is the most physical word available, used of groping with the hands, feeling for something in the dark. It is the word the risen Lord used when he said, “See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see” (Luke 24:39). John is answering those who denied that Jesus had a real body. He and the other apostles touched him, before and after the resurrection (John 20:27). The eternal Son became truly, physically human.

The head on his chest. Remember who is writing. This is the disciple who reclined next to Jesus at the last supper and leaned back against his chest to ask a question (John 13:23–25). He had felt the Lord breathe. Now an old man, he hears clever teachers saying the divine Christ only seemed to have a body, and he does not argue from philosophy. He says, in effect: I put my head on him. The word Docetism comes from the Greek dokein, to seem. John’s reply is that a man does not lean his weight on an appearance.

Concerning the word of life. “Word of life” (tou logou tēs zōēs) is Christ himself, the Word (John 1:1, 14), who is life and gives life (John 1:4; 11:25; 14:6). It is also the message about him, and John will not let the two be separated. The message is not a set of ideas a man once taught; the message is the man.

The life was made manifest, and we have seen it. “Made manifest” (ephanerōthē): was revealed, made visible, brought out into the open. This is the incarnation. Eternal life was invisible, as invisible as the God who has it; in Jesus it walked into Galilee. Notice that John does not say a teaching about life was published. He says the life itself appeared, in the way a person appears in a doorway. Life was not a theory to John. It had a face and a voice and calloused hands.

And testify to it and proclaim to you the eternal life. “Testify” (martyroumen) is to bear witness, the word of the courtroom, from which our word martyr comes, because so many who gave this testimony were killed for it. “Proclaim” (apangellomen) is to announce, to bring news. The apostles are witnesses in a court, giving firsthand evidence, and heralds in a street, giving news. Of the twelve, tradition says John alone died old. Every one of the others sealed this testimony with his life, and men do not die for what they know they invented.

Which was with the Father and was made manifest to us. “With the Father” (pros ton patera) means face to face with the Father, the same phrase as John 1:1, “the Word was with God”. The Son eternally existed in personal relationship with the Father. He is distinct from the Father, yet eternal and divine. The life that appeared to fishermen had not come from nowhere; it had come from the Father’s side, where it had been for ever. When John saw Jesus, he was looking at what had always been in the presence of God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christianity rests only on the apostles’ experience. It rests on Christ himself; the apostles were eyewitnesses who testified to him. Their testimony is preserved in Scripture.

How can I know the apostles were not mistaken or lying? Look at what their testimony cost them and what it claimed. They were not describing private visions that no one could check; they spoke of things done in public, within living memory, among hostile witnesses who could have produced a body and never did (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). They gained nothing from it in this world but beatings, prison and death. Their accounts have the untidiness of real testimony: the disciples look slow and frightened, women are the first witnesses, which no inventor in that culture would choose. And the Spirit who inspired them still bears witness through their words to those who read them (John 15:26–27; 1 John 5:6). Faith is not a leap in the dark. It is trust in reliable witnesses about a real man.

I never saw or touched him. Is my faith second-hand? It is not second-class. John writes these very words so that people who never saw can share exactly what he had (v. 3), and the Lord himself pronounced a blessing over you in the room where Thomas touched him: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). You know him through the same Word and the same Spirit. The apostles’ eyes were the window God built once, so that everyone afterwards could see through it.

In a sentence. We proclaim to you what was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked at and our hands have touched: this we proclaim concerning the Word of life. The life appeared; we have seen it and testify to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life, which was with the Father and has appeared to us.

On a Tuesday. Your faith is not a feeling to be protected from bad days; it is anchored in a man who could be touched. When doubt comes, do not first take your own pulse. Go back to the evidence: read a Gospel account of the resurrection slowly, as testimony given in court. And remember that the same flesh-and-blood Lord means your flesh and blood matter. Washing up, mending, working with your hands are not beneath a faith whose God had hands.

For worship. The hands that flung the stars into place were held out to be touched. He who was with the Father before anything was made let fishermen jostle him in a boat, let a tired disciple rest against his chest, let Thomas put a finger in the wound. The eternal life of God did not stay where it was safe. It came near enough to be handled, near enough to be nailed, and it is in that flesh, risen and glorified, that he sits now at the Father’s right hand. The Word of life has a human face, and he has not put it away.
verseByVerse.note: The letter does not name its author, but its language is so close to John’s Gospel that it has long been received as the apostle John’s, written late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. Some had left the church denying that Jesus the Christ truly came in the flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us; and indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.

That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you. The main verb of the long sentence (vv. 1–3) arrives at last: we proclaim. Everything John has heard and seen presses toward this act. And notice that he repeats himself, seen and heard, as though he wants to be sure you know he is not passing on rumour. The apostles pass on what they witnessed, no more and no less. And “also to you”: what began in a small circle on a lake shore is not to stay there.

So that you too may have fellowship with us. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, partnership, communion, having something in common. Luke uses a related word for James and John as business partners with Simon in the fishing (Luke 5:10): men who owned the boat together, shared the nets, split the catch. The purpose of proclamation is not information transfer but inclusion. John does not write so that you will know about something he has; he writes so that you will have it too. Christian fellowship is not merely friendship or a pleasant hour after the service. It is sharing a common life in Christ, being co-owners in the same inheritance.

And indeed our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ. “Indeed” (kai de): and truly, and what is more. The apostolic fellowship is not merely human; it is fellowship with God himself, the Father and the Son. The Father and the Son are named together as equal partners in this fellowship, which no mere man could be. And fellowship with God and fellowship with other believers go together; you cannot have one without the other (v. 7).

A circle that was turning before the world began. Before there was a world, the Father loved the Son and the Son delighted in the Father, in the Spirit (John 17:24). That love was not lonely and needed nothing. To enter the gospel is to be drawn into a circle of love that has been running from eternity. Jesus prayed for exactly this the night before he died: that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us (John 17:21). Fellowship is not God allowing us to stand outside and watch. It is God opening his own life and bringing us in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fellowship with God depends on the apostles personally. It means the way into fellowship with God is through receiving the apostolic message about Christ. Those who reject the apostolic gospel, as the false teachers did, have no fellowship with God (2:22–23).

What does fellowship with God actually look like on an ordinary day? It is quieter than people expect. It is speaking to him in prayer and hearing him speak in Scripture, as friends talk. It is bringing him the day’s worries rather than carrying them alone (1 Peter 5:7). It is confessing sin quickly rather than hiding it (v. 9). It is sharing his interests: loving what he loves, grieving what grieves him. And it is enjoyed with his people, at his table, in his house. Fellowship with God does not depend on a feeling of closeness; it is a shared life. The feelings come and go; the sharing does not stop.

Can I have fellowship with God without a church? Not in the way John means. The sentence runs: fellowship with us, and our fellowship is with the Father. The road into the Father’s company goes through the apostles’ message, and that message gathers people. A Christian alone is like a coal taken out of the fire: it does not stop being coal, but it goes cold. Some cannot attend for illness or persecution, and God meets them where they are. But choosing to stay away cuts you off from the very means God uses to keep you warm (Hebrews 10:24–25).

In a sentence. We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with his Son, Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of one believer you know only by a handshake at the door. You are co-owners of the same inheritance, partners in the same boat. Ask him to lunch, and find out what God has been doing in his life. Fellowship is learnt at tables, not only in rows.

For worship. The Father did not need us. He had the Son, and the Son had the Father, and the Spirit was the bond of their joy. Yet he determined to open the door of his own life and set places at his own table for rebels. The Son came out from the Father’s side to fetch them, and went to the cross to make them clean enough to sit down. Now men and women who were strangers to God call him Father, and call the eternal Son their brother. There is no higher company in the universe, and he has made room in it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we are writing these things so that our joy may be complete.

And we are writing these things. “Writing” (graphomen): the letter is itself part of the proclamation. What the apostles once said aloud they now commit to a page, so that people who never heard their voices can have their testimony. Every time you open this letter, the eyewitness is still speaking.

So that our joy may be complete. The stated purpose of the letter is joy. Not doctrinal correction for its own sake, not institutional self-preservation, not even the safety of the community, though all of those are in it, but joy. Some manuscripts read “your joy”; “our” is better supported, and it includes both writer and readers. The apostle’s joy is bound up with the reader’s flourishing. “Complete” (peplērōmenē) means filled up, made full, like a jar filled to the brim. John writes because he cannot be fully glad until those he loves are fully in the fellowship of verses 1–3. A father is not at peace while one of his children is missing from the table.

The joy of the upper room. Jesus spoke of the same full joy, in the same Greek, on his last night: “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full” (John 15:11; see also 16:24; 17:13). John was in the room. Sixty years later he is still trying to pass on what he heard there. And the joy is not located in favourable circumstances but in the shared life of the Son communicated to his people. It is the joy of the psalmist: in your presence there is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian joy depends on circumstances. It depends on fellowship with God, which nothing can take away.

What if I do not feel joyful? Then you are not unusual, and you are not disqualified. Christian joy is deeper than mood. It can sit alongside grief, as Paul was sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10), and it can be buried for a season under illness, depression or loss. Joy is not something to manufacture by trying to feel happy. It grows from its sources: being near God in his word, being honest with him about sin, being with his people. Keep going back to the spring, even when the cup feels empty. The Lord who wants your joy full knows how to fill it, and he knows how to wait.

In a sentence. We write this to make our joy complete.

On a Tuesday. Ask what fills your joy most this week: a result at work, a purchase, a team’s win, a compliment? None of those is wrong, but none can bear the weight. Tell another believer one thing God has shown you or done for you lately. Joy shared is how John says it becomes full.

For worship. God is not a reluctant giver of gladness. The Father’s purpose in sending his Son, the Son’s purpose in his last discourse, the apostle’s purpose in this letter all run to the same place: that your joy should be full. The joy he gives is his own joy, the joy the Son has had in the Father’s presence from eternity, and nothing in the world can take it away (John 16:22). He is the happy God, and he means to make us happy in him for ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — God Is Light: Walking in the Truth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing John says about God is not a comfort but a blinding claim: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” Then he exposes three things people say to live comfortably without facing that light: that they have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, that they have no sin, and that they have not sinned. But the light that exposes also heals. The blood of Jesus cleanses, and God forgives those who confess.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Light

Three claims keep people from the light: fellowship while walking in darkness, having no sin, never having sinned. The remedy is confession to a God who is faithful and just to forgive.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers claimed an enlightenment that placed them above sin.

Now: Honest confession, not self-defence, keeps a believer in fellowship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.

This is the message we have heard from him and proclaim to you. “Message” (angelia) is an announcement, news brought by a messenger. “From him” is from Jesus. This claim did not originate with John. He heard it from Christ, who called himself the light of the world (John 8:12) and whose life made the claim visible. And this is the governing premise of the entire letter compressed into one sentence. Everything John teaches about sin, love and fellowship is grounded here, in the moral character of the God with whom we seek communion.

That God is light. “Light” (phōs). In Scripture, light represents God’s holiness, purity, truth and glory (Psalm 27:1; 36:9; Isaiah 60:19–20; 1 Timothy 6:16). Light reveals, exposes, purifies, gives life. God is not merely a source of light, not a god who uses light as a symbol; he is light in his very nature. The first words he spoke into the dark of creation were “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and the last page of the Bible shows a city that needs no sun, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). Between those two pages he shone in a pillar of fire over Israel and on the face of Moses, and then, fully, in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

What light does. Think about what light actually does in a room. It shows what is there: the dust, the crumbs, the stain you did not know about. It warms. It makes growth possible; nothing green lives without it. And it is pure: you can shine a light into a sewer and the light does not become dirty. All of that is God. He sees everything exactly as it is. He gives life. And he enters our filth without being stained by it, which is why the Son could touch lepers and remain clean, and the leper did not.

And in him is no darkness at all. “No darkness at all” (skotia en autō ouk estin oudemia) is a strong double negative in Greek: darkness is not in him, none, not any. Darkness represents sin, falsehood, evil and ignorance. God is absolutely holy: no shadow of sin, no mixture of good and evil, no hidden corners, no moods in which he is less than himself (James 1:17). Every human being has a dark room somewhere. God has none. You will never discover something about him that makes you trust him less. This was aimed at the false teachers, who apparently treated sin as unimportant or claimed that knowledge of God was compatible with sinful living.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is an impersonal force or physical light. It is a metaphor for his moral and spiritual perfection. God is personal.

If God is light, why does my life sometimes feel so dark? Because the darkness John means is moral, not circumstantial. A believer can walk through a very dark valley of grief, illness or confusion and still be walking in the light, in John’s sense, because he is walking honestly with God. Scripture expects such seasons and speaks to them: let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isaiah 50:10). When you cannot see his face, you can still lean on his name. The darkness around you is not a darkness in him, and it will not have the last word.

Does this make God frightening rather than loving? It makes him trustworthy. A love with dark corners would be a love you could never be sure of; you would always wonder what was hidden. Because God is light, his love is exactly what it appears to be, with no hidden terms. And John will say just as plainly that God is love (4:8). The two are not rivals. At the cross the light did not dim and the love did not hold back: sin was exposed and judged, and sinners were embraced, in the same act.

In a sentence. This is the message we have heard from him and declare to you: God is light; in him there is no darkness at all.

On a Tuesday. Pick one thing you would not want God to see: a browser history, a resentment, a conversation you have rehearsed, the way you spoke about someone. He has already seen it. Say so to him today, out loud if you can. And when you are tempted to suspect God of hidden unkindness in your circumstances, answer the suspicion with this verse: in him is no darkness at all.

For worship. There is no shadow in God. In the whole of his being there is nothing to hide, nothing to regret, nothing that would shame him if it were seen. The burning purity before which the seraphim cover their faces is the same light that came down into a stable and walked our roads, and in that light we see what God is: holy and never compromised, yet stooping to the darkest places to bring his people out. He did not shine on us from a safe distance. He entered our night, and at noon on the day he died darkness covered the land while he bore the judgement our sins deserved (Mark 15:33), so that people of the dark might stand in his light and not be consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.

If we say we have fellowship with him. The first of three false claims, each beginning “If we say” (vv. 6, 8, 10). John is perhaps quoting the slogans of the false teachers, and each slogan names a lie that protects the ego at the cost of reality. “Say” (eipōmen) marks a claim, not necessarily a reality. And John says we, not they. He does not stand outside the danger and point at it. He knows that the habit of saying the right words over a wrong life is not a sect’s peculiarity but a temptation in every human heart, including an apostle’s.

While we walk in darkness. “Walk” (peripatōmen) means to live, to conduct oneself habitually: not an occasional stumble but a sustained orientation. “In darkness” is living in sin, falsehood and moral evil, as a settled way of life. The picture is of a man who has chosen the unlit side of the street and keeps to it, because he does not want to be seen. Jesus named the motive exactly: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil (John 3:19).

We lie and do not practice the truth. “Lie” (pseudometha) is the blunt word. To claim intimacy with the God who is light while the pattern of life runs toward darkness is not a theological error; it is a lie. And “practice the truth” (poioumen tēn alētheian, do the truth) is one of John’s most striking phrases: truth in John is not merely believed but done, lived out, embodied (John 3:21). A professed relationship with God that does not produce a truthful, light-oriented life is self-refuting.

The lie we tell with our lives. Most people who live this verse have never said anything false aloud. They sing the hymns, pray the prayers, and believe every word of the creed. The lie is not in their mouths but in the distance between their mouths and their days: the husband who leads family devotions and is cruel when the door is shut; the businesswoman who tithes on money she obtained by deceit. Nobody would call such a person a liar at the time. John does, because God hears the whole sentence, and the sentence is what the life says.

Whoever follows me. John learnt the language of this verse from Jesus, who stood in the temple and said, I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life (John 8:12). So walking in the light is not first a moral standard to reach; it is walking behind a person. Fellowship with God is fellowship with the Son who is the light, and no one can follow someone while walking the other way down the street. That is why the claim in this verse is a lie and not merely a weakness: it says I am with him while the feet go elsewhere. And it is why the remedy is not trying harder in the dark but turning round to follow him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any sin in a believer proves he is not a Christian. Verses 8–10 show that believers do sin. It means a settled pattern of living in darkness contradicts a claim to know God.

How do I tell the difference between stumbling and walking in darkness? Ask what you do with your sin. A believer stumbles, sometimes badly and often, but he hates the sin, confesses it, and turns back toward God; it troubles him, and he does not want to be left in it. The person walking in darkness has made peace with it: he hides it, excuses it, renames it, and has no intention of changing. Another test is whether you want God to see. A stumbling Christian, ashamed, still runs toward the light. A man in darkness avoids it. If your sin grieves you and drives you to Christ, that grief is itself a sign of light.

In a sentence. If we claim to have fellowship with him and yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not live out the truth.

On a Tuesday. Is there an area of your life you keep in the dark? Bring it into God’s light this week. Name it to him plainly, and if it is the kind of thing that grows in secret, tell one trusted believer as well. Darkness loses most of its power the moment it is spoken.

For worship. The God who is light does not merely forbid the dark; he came into it to fetch us. The Son of God walked into a world that loved the darkness, and the darkness put him out, for three days. But it could not hold him, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5). Every true walk in the light today is the fruit of that Easter morning, when the light came back out of the tomb and has never gone out since.

verseByVerse.quote: But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.

But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light. The positive counterpart to verse 6, and it contains two gifts that the person walking in darkness cannot reach: genuine fellowship with other believers, and ongoing cleansing by Christ’s blood. “Walk in the light” is living openly before God, honestly, in truth and obedience, hiding nothing, letting his light expose and correct us. Not sinlessness, but transparency and obedience: no zone of the life sealed off from his gaze. And the standard is arresting: as he is in the light. God dwells in light (1 Timothy 6:16), and we walk where he is. The light is not a standard we must reach before we may come; it is the place where he lives, and we are invited to live there with him.

We have fellowship with one another. Surprising: we might expect fellowship with him, but John says with one another. Walking in God’s light produces genuine fellowship among believers, because darkness, which is pretence, hidden sin and hypocrisy, destroys relationships. Two people who are both hiding cannot be close; they can only be polite. Fellowship with God and with one another go together (v. 3). When each is honest with God, they can be honest with each other, and the masks come off.

And the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin. “Blood” is Christ’s sacrificial death, his life poured out (Hebrews 9:14, 22; 1 Peter 1:18–19). “Jesus his Son”: the human Jesus is the divine Son, against the false teachers who separated them. His real blood was shed, the blood of a real man who was God’s eternal Son. “Cleanses” (katharizei, purifies) is present tense: it keeps on cleansing. Not that we are re-justified, but that the ongoing sins of believers are continually covered by Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice. “All sin” (pasēs hamartias): every kind, no exceptions. Walking in the light does not mean we never sin; it means our sins are brought into the light, where Christ’s blood deals with them.

A spring, not a bucket. Picture a stream running over stones. The water is not poured once and then gone; it runs continuously, and anything dropped into it is washed. That is the present tense of this verse. Even those living honestly before God remain sinners who need cleansing, and the provision never runs dry. The hymn speaks of a fountain filled with blood, and the image is right: what Christ did once at Calvary flows on, and it flows on because it was finished.

Why the light is not to be feared. Here is the great surprise of the verse. You might expect that walking in the light, where everything shows, would be the most terrifying thing a sinner could do. John says it is the place of cleansing. The darkness is where sin stays and festers; the light is where it is washed. We hide because we think exposure means condemnation. In the presence of the blood of Jesus, exposure means cleansing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s blood must be re-applied through repeated sacrifices or rituals. His sacrifice was once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). Its cleansing power is ongoing.

Do I have to tell other people my sins to walk in the light? Not everyone, and not everything. Walking in the light is first honesty with God. But it includes being willing to be known by fellow believers rather than keeping up a performance. Confess to those you have wronged, and ask their forgiveness. Have one or two trusted, mature believers to whom you can admit your struggles and who will pray for you (James 5:16). Wisdom is needed: some things would harm others if broadcast, and public confession is for public sins. The aim is not display but freedom from pretence.

In a sentence. But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son, keeps purifying us from all sin.

On a Tuesday. Think of the believer you are most guarded with. What would it take to be honest with him about one real struggle? Begin there. And the next time you sin today, do not wait until evening to deal with it; walk straight into the light with it and let the blood do its work.

For worship. The blood that was shed once outside Jerusalem has never lost its power. It was the blood of Jesus, a man who bled like any man, and it was the blood of God’s Son, which is why it can cleanse not some sin but all sin. The Lamb of God has borne it all, and his sacrifice goes on availing for his people every hour of every day until the last of them is home. We walk in the light, not because we are clean enough to stand in it, but because he keeps us clean while we are there.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

If we say we have no sin. The second false claim. Not “I have never sinned” (past, v. 10) but “I have no sin”: present, ongoing, indwelling sinfulness denied. “Have no sin” (hamartian ouk echomen) may be a claim to a sinless nature, that sin is no longer in us, or a claim that sin does not matter, does not count, or is not really sin for the enlightened. The false teachers may have claimed that their special knowledge put them beyond sin, or that what the body does does not affect the spirit.

We deceive ourselves. “Deceive” (planōmen) means lead astray, mislead, make to wander, the word from which planet comes, the wandering star. We fool ourselves, though we may not fool others; the deceit begins within. It is a terrible kind of blindness, because the man who has deceived himself has no one left to tell him. Everyone else can see the thing in his life; he alone has stopped seeing it, and he is the one most confident.

And the truth is not in us. To deny our sin is to have no grasp of the truth about God or ourselves. The word of God, which plainly diagnoses every human being as a sinner (Psalm 143:2; Romans 3:23), has not taken up residence in such a person. The gospel begins with acknowledging our sin. Claimed superiority to sin is actually evidence of the most basic spiritual failure.

The holiest people feel it most. Notice who in Scripture has the sharpest sense of his own sin. Not the beginners. Isaiah, the prophet of the holy, cried out that he was lost, a man of unclean lips, when he saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:5). Paul, near the end of his life, called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The nearer you come to the light, the more of the dust you can see. A Christian who thinks he has little sin left has usually wandered further from the light, not closer.

The one man of whom it is true. There is one person of whom the words I have no sin are simply true, and John names him in this same letter: in him there is no sin (3:5). Jesus could ask his enemies which of them could convict him of sin (John 8:46), and none could. The claim the false teachers made for themselves belongs to him alone, and he did not keep it as a boast: the sinless one appeared to take sins away (3:5), carrying ours to the cross. So the Christian who says I have no sin is not only deceiving himself. He is taking for himself the one title that belongs to the Saviour, and leaving himself no need of him.

Where Christians differ: can a believer become free of all sin before glory? Some Wesleyan and holiness traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state in which they no longer sin knowingly. Verdict: John says plainly that anyone who claims to have no sin deceives himself. He includes himself, and every believer, in the we. He writes to Christians, and in the same breath he promises forgiveness to those who keep confessing (1:9). When he later says that no one born of God makes a practice of sinning (3:9), he means the settled direction of a life, not sinlessness; the believer still sins, but he no longer lives in it at peace. Believers are freed from sin’s dominion (3:9; Romans 6:14), and they grow in holiness, but sin remains in them until glory (Romans 7:14–25; James 3:2; Philippians 3:12). We should strive for holiness while daily confessing sin and trusting Christ’s blood.

What it does not mean. It does not excuse sin or make it inevitable in every moment. John writes so that we may not sin (2:1). But when we do, we must not deny it.

If I still have sin, am I really a new creation? Yes. The Christian is a new creation in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), with a new heart that loves God, and sin no longer rules him. But sin still lives in him as an unwelcome tenant, and he fights it until he dies (Galatians 5:17). Both are true at once: you are a saint, set apart and loved, and you are a sinner who still needs cleansing. Admitting your sin does not deny your new identity. It is how the new man behaves. Only the new heart hates the old sin enough to confess it.

In a sentence. If we claim to be without sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

On a Tuesday. Self-deception keeps you from grace; honesty opens the door. Ask someone who lives with you, or works closely with you, what one fault of yours they notice most. Do not defend yourself. Thank them, take it to God, and ask him to show you what you have stopped seeing.

For worship. The Holy One does not shame the honest. He who alone had no sin sits at the Father’s right hand, and he is not embarrassed by the people who come to him admitting everything; he was numbered with transgressors so that transgressors could be numbered with him. And he has promised more than pardon. When he appears we shall be like him (3:2), and the day is coming when his people will say they have no sin and it will be true, not because they have deceived themselves but because he has finished his work in them. Until then we can afford to tell the whole truth about ourselves, because the truth about him is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

If we confess our sins. This is the most generous verse in the chapter. Over against self-deception (v. 8) John sets the promise of honest confession. “Confess” (homologōmen) is literally to say the same thing: to agree, to acknowledge. To confess is to agree with God about our sin, to call it what he calls it, without excuse or minimising. The present tense means keep confessing: it is a habit of life, not a single event. And it is specific, honest admission, as the psalmist found: when he kept silent his bones wasted away, and when he acknowledged his sin and did not cover his iniquity, God forgave (Psalm 32:3–5; 51:3–4). Proverbs puts the same choice before every sinner in a single line: hidden sin does not prosper, but sin confessed and forsaken finds mercy (Proverbs 28:13).

He is faithful. “Faithful” (pistos) means reliable, trustworthy. God keeps his promises. He has promised to forgive those who confess (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:12), and he has staked his name on it. Your forgiveness does not depend on how sorry you managed to feel, or on how well you worded it, but on whether God keeps his word. And he has never once broken it.

And just. Surprising: we might expect merciful. “Just” (dikaios) means righteous. But forgiveness is just because Christ has paid for sin (2:2; Romans 3:25–26). Because the penalty has been fully paid at the cross, forgiving the one who confesses is not a waiving of justice but its satisfaction: the justice has already been executed on the Son. God would be unjust to punish twice for the same sin. So the very attribute that once stood against us now stands for us. A sinner who comes in Christ’s name can appeal not only to God’s kindness but to his fairness.

To forgive us our sins. “Forgive” (aphē) means release, send away, cancel the debt. It is the word for letting a prisoner go and for cancelling what is owed. The sins are not filed for future use. He casts all our sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19); as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12).

And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. “Cleanse” (katharisē, purify), as in verse 7. Forgiveness removes guilt; cleansing removes defilement. A forgiven debt is cancelled; a cleansed garment is washed. God does both, and both are complete: all unrighteousness, the deeper contamination beneath the surface acts, including the sins we have not yet noticed.

Where Christians differ: must we confess to a priest to be forgiven? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest. Verdict: John directs confession to God: he is faithful and just to forgive. Christ is our only mediator and advocate (2:1; 1 Timothy 2:5). Confessing sins to one another is good and healing (James 5:16), but forgiveness comes directly from God through Christ, not through priestly absolution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers lose their justification when they sin and regain it when they confess. Justification is once for all (Romans 8:1). Confession restores the enjoyment of fellowship with God, like a child confessing to a father, not a criminal before a judge. Nor does it mean unconfessed sins are unforgiven in the judicial sense; it means confession is how believers continually live in the experience of forgiveness.

Must every sin be specifically confessed before it is forgiven? No. The believer’s standing before God was settled once for all when he believed: the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (v. 7), and there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Confession is the way a child of God keeps short accounts with his Father, restoring fellowship, not a ledger in which any sin forgotten remains unpaid. Confess specifically the sins you know, and trust him with the ones you do not; David prayed, declare me innocent from hidden faults (Psalm 19:12).

And what of sins unconfessed at death? A believer is not lost because he dies with a sin he did not name. This verse describes the pattern of a Christian’s life, walking in the light and confessing as God shows us our sin, not an exam we must pass at the end. Our advocate is Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1), and his propitiation covers all our sins.

What if I keep confessing the same sin? Keep confessing it, and keep fighting it. God’s promise has no limit on the number of times; Jesus told Peter to forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22), and he is not less patient than he asks us to be. But confession is agreeing with God, and God hates the sin, so true confession includes turning from it: removing what feeds it, asking for help, taking practical steps. Repeated failure is not proof that you are not a Christian. Giving up the fight would be the danger. Each return to him is a sign that grace has not let you go.

I have confessed, but I do not feel forgiven. Then believe the promise rather than the feeling. John does not say that if we confess we will feel forgiven; he says God is faithful and just to forgive. Your feelings may lag behind for weeks, especially after a serious sin, and the accuser will happily remind you of it. Answer him with the cross: the debt was paid there, and God does not collect twice. If something can still be put right with the person you wronged, put it right. Then thank God for his forgiveness, even before you feel it. The feeling usually follows the faith, not the other way round.

In a sentence. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness.

On a Tuesday. Before you sleep tonight, look back over the day with God. Name to him specifically where you sinned: the sharp word, the lie, the lust, the prayerlessness. Do not argue for yourself. Then read this verse aloud and believe it: he has forgiven and cleansed you. And if your sin wronged someone, put it right with them tomorrow.

For worship. Here is a God whose justice and mercy kiss each other. He does not forgive by looking away from sin but by having looked straight at it on the cross, where he poured out on his Son what we deserved. So now his faithfulness is pledged to us and his justice is on our side, and every honest sinner who comes finds the door already open and the Father already running. Not one sin brought to him has ever been held back. He is faithful, because he cannot lie; he is just, because Christ has paid; and he is glad to forgive.

verseByVerse.quote: If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we say we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.

If we say we have not sinned. The third false claim, and the most extreme. Not merely denying present sinfulness (v. 8) but denying any personal history of sin. “Have not sinned” (ouch hēmartēkamen) is perfect tense: we have not sinned and are in a sinless state. It is a denial of ever having sinned, or of having sinned since conversion.

We make him a liar. God has declared that all have sinned (Romans 3:23; Psalm 14:3; Isaiah 53:6). He sent his Son to die for sin. To deny our sin is to call God a liar and to make the cross unnecessary. John does not soften this: refusing the universal diagnosis of sin is not an honest difference of opinion but an accusation against the truthfulness of God. If I have not sinned, then God’s whole account of the world is false and the death of his Son was a mistake. Pride always, in the end, accuses God.

And his word is not in us. “His word” is his revealed truth: Scripture, the gospel. Its message has not penetrated our hearts. Someone who claims never to have sinned has never really heard God’s word. The good news has not yet reached him because the bad news has not yet landed.

Two men in the temple. Jesus told of them. One stood and thanked God that he was not like other men, and listed his virtues. The other stood far off, would not lift up his eyes, beat his breast and said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus said the second went home justified. The first had made God a liar without realising it; the second agreed with God and was forgiven. Every one of us goes into the temple as one of those two men.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should dwell morbidly on our sins. John writes to bring assurance and joy (v. 4; 5:13). Honest confession leads to forgiveness and freedom.

How do I take sin seriously without being crushed by it? Look at your sin only long enough to confess it, and look at Christ for much longer. John never mentions sin in this chapter without mentioning the remedy in the same breath: the blood that cleanses (v. 7), the God who forgives (v. 9), and, as the letter runs straight on, the Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1). A Christian who only examines himself will despair; one who never does will become proud. The healthy pattern is honest about sin and glad about grace, with the gladness the larger of the two. For every look at yourself, take ten looks at Christ.

In a sentence. If we claim we have not sinned, we make him out to be a liar and his word is not in us.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you have been calling something else: a mistake, a weakness, a personality trait, just the way I am? Call it sin, confess it, and receive forgiveness. Notice too how quickly you defend yourself when someone points out a fault. The speed of the defence is often the measure of the pride.

For worship. God’s word about us is severe, and it is true, and it is the beginning of every mercy. He tells us we have sinned because he has come to forgive sinners, and he will not let us hide from the diagnosis because he is holding out the cure. The Physician did not come for the healthy. He came for the man who will say, in agreement with God, I have sinned; and to that man he gives his own righteousness, his Father’s welcome, and a word that lives in him for ever.

1.theology:
The Incarnation as Foundation. Everything in 1 John rests on the physical, historical, tangible reality of the incarnation. John's stacked verbs in verses 1–2 — heard, seen, looked upon, touched — are a theological rampart against every form of docetism (the heresy that Christ only appeared to be human). If Christ did not truly come in flesh, the blood shed on Calvary has no atoning value, the resurrection is a spirit's trick, and there is no real fellowship between God and humanity. The incarnation is not incidental to Christianity; it is its structural foundation. God became graspable so that we could grasp him — and through him, life.

The God Who is Light. John's declaration that "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all" has massive ethical implications. Fellowship with a God of absolute moral purity cannot coexist with a comfortable relationship with sin. The light of God is not a comfortable mood but a searching, penetrating, all-revealing reality. It is also a liberating one: in the light, where our sin is exposed, the blood of Jesus cleanses. Reformed theology has always insisted on the holiness of God as the backdrop against which the grace of God becomes luminous. You cannot appreciate the gospel without first standing in the light of who God is.
1.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had just experienced a painful split. People they had worshipped with, broken bread with, called brothers and sisters, had walked out. The departure of the false teachers left wounds and questions. Were the ones who stayed the ones who had missed the deeper truth? John's answer in chapter 1 is the apostolic testimony: we were there. We heard him, saw him, touched him. This is not speculation; it is witness. The assurance of the community rests not on their spiritual experiences but on the testimony of those who were eyewitnesses of the Word of Life.

Now: We live in a culture that treats the interior life as the truest life — feelings, impressions, spiritual experiences. The incarnation is John's counter-word: Christianity is tethered to history, to flesh, to blood, to an empty tomb. Our fellowship with God is not a feeling; it is a fact grounded in the historical reality of the Son of God made flesh. And the practice of confession — agreeing with God about what we are — is the daily discipline that keeps that fellowship living and real. Every day we come back to the same place: not to earn forgiveness, but to receive what has already been purchased.

2.title: Our Advocate, Our Obedience, Our Love
2.text: <sup>1</sup>My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.<sup>2</sup>He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.<sup>3</sup>And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.<sup>4</sup>Whoever says “I know him” but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him,<sup>5</sup>but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:<sup>6</sup>whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.<sup>8</sup>At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.<sup>9</sup>Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.<sup>10</sup>Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.<sup>11</sup>But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.<sup>12</sup>I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.<sup>13</sup>I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.<sup>14</sup>I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.<sup>15</sup>Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.<sup>16</sup>For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.<sup>17</sup>And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.<sup>18</sup>Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.<sup>19</sup>They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.<sup>20</sup>But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.<sup>21</sup>I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.<sup>22</sup>Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.<sup>23</sup>No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.<sup>24</sup>Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.<sup>25</sup>And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.<sup>26</sup>I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.<sup>27</sup>But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.<sup>28</sup>And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.<sup>29</sup>If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
2.overview: Chapter 2 moves in three steps. First, John wants his readers not to sin, but knows they will, and points them to their advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins. Second, he gives the first test of real faith: obedience. Not sinless perfection, but a life that keeps God’s commands and walks as Jesus walked, and that loves the brothers. Third, he warns against loving the world, which is passing away, and against the antichrists who have left the church, and he urges his readers to abide in what they heard from the beginning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Advocate and the Test of Knowing God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John aims at holiness: he writes so that his people will not sin. But he knows they will, so the provision comes with the command. We have an advocate with the Father, who pleads not our innocence but his own righteousness, and who is himself the propitiation that turned away God’s wrath. On that ground of grace, John gives the first test: those who know him keep his commandments and walk as he walked.
verseByVerse.theology:
Advocate and Propitiation

John writes so that believers will not sin, and provides for when they do: Jesus Christ the righteous pleads for us, and he is the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Separating the divine Christ from the suffering Jesus emptied the cross.

Now: Knowing God shows itself in keeping his commandments and walking as Jesus walked.

verseByVerse.quote: My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

Meaning first. 1 John 2 gives tests by which believers may know that they truly know God. If they sin, they have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, the propitiation for their sins and for the whole world (vv. 1–2). Those who know God keep his commands and walk as Jesus walked (vv. 3–6), and they love their brother, for whoever hates him is still in darkness (vv. 7–11). John assures them that they are forgiven, know the Father and have overcome the evil one (vv. 12–14), and warns them not to love the world, which is passing away (vv. 15–17). It is the last hour: many antichrists, who left the church because they never belonged, deny that Jesus is the Christ and so deny both the Father and the Son (vv. 18–23). But the readers have the Spirit’s anointing; they must remain in the original message and in Christ, so as to be confident when he appears (vv. 24–29). The chapter opens with Christ pleading for us in heaven and closes with Christ appearing from heaven, and everything between is how to live in the meantime.

My little children. “Little children” (teknia, dear children) is a tender term, used seven times in the letter, and it sets the pastoral tone at once. He is not a lecturer correcting students but a grandfather with his hand on a child’s head. Whatever hard things follow, and there are many, they are said by someone who loves the people he is saying them to.

I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. “May not sin” (hina mē hamartēte) is an aorist: may not commit an act of sin. Chapter 1 might be misused: if everyone sins and God forgives, why worry? John answers: the goal is not to sin. Forgiveness is not a licence. The verse holds two truths that must never be collapsed into each other: holiness is the aim, and the provision for failure is already in place. Lose the first and grace becomes an excuse; lose the second and holiness becomes despair.

But if anyone does sin. “If” (ean): John knows believers will sin (1:8, 10). He does not say when, because he does not want to sound resigned, and he does not say never, because he will not lie. He says if, with the remedy already in the next breath.

We have an advocate with the Father. “Advocate” (paraklētos) is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7): one called alongside to help, especially a defence lawyer in court. The Spirit is our advocate within us; Christ is our advocate before the Father. When Satan accuses (Revelation 12:10), Christ speaks for us. “With the Father” (pros ton patera) is face to face with the Father, as in 1:2. Our advocate is in the Judge’s presence and is the Judge’s Son. And the tense is present: we have. The advocate is not an emergency measure summoned after the crisis; he is already standing before the Father on behalf of the imperfect.

The scene in Zechariah. The prophet saw it centuries before. Joshua the high priest stood before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan at his right hand to accuse him. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. But the LORD rebuked the accuser: is not this a brand plucked from the fire? And the filthy garments were taken off, and he was clothed in clean ones (Zechariah 3:1–5). That is what happens in heaven when a Christian sins. The charge is not disputed. It is answered.

Jesus Christ the righteous. “The righteous” (dikaion): Christ is perfectly righteous, and that is the ground of his advocacy. His plea is not that we are innocent, but that he has paid for our sins (v. 2). An ordinary lawyer must argue that his client did not do it, or that there were circumstances. This advocate admits everything, and wins, because he pleads not our righteousness but his own.

What it does not mean. Christ’s advocacy does not mean the Father is reluctant and must be persuaded. The Father sent the Son in love (4:9–10). Christ’s advocacy is his continual presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice covers our sins (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34).

Does having an advocate make sin less serious? It makes it more serious. Look at what it costs: the eternal Son must stand in the Father’s presence with the marks of the nails in his hands, and his plea is his own death. No one who understands that can treat sin lightly. But it changes what sin does to a believer. It no longer threatens his standing, so he is free to stop hiding it. A child who knows his father will not disown him is not more careless; he is more honest. And honesty is where holiness begins.

What does this mean in the moment after I have sinned? It means you go straight to him, not away from him. You do not need to wait until you feel sorry enough, or until you have done a week of better behaviour to earn the right. Your advocate is already speaking for you. Name the sin to the Father, plainly, and thank him that Jesus has answered for it. Jesus told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift him like wheat, and then said, “but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:31–32). He prays for you before you fall and while you are down.

In a sentence. My dear children, I write this to you so that you will not sin. But if anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the Righteous One.

On a Tuesday. The next time you sin, notice your first instinct. Is it to hide, to excuse, to sulk, to promise God you will make it up to him? Replace it with this: Father, I did that; Jesus has paid for it; thank you. Then get up and walk on. And aim, today, at not sinning at all. The advocate is not a reason to aim lower.

For worship. There is a man in heaven. At the right hand of the Majesty on high sits one who knows what it is to be tired and tempted and wept over, and he is there for us. He never needs to be reminded of our names. He has never lost a case. He does not plead our tears or our resolutions but his own blood, and the Father who sent him delights to hear him. When the accuser speaks, the Righteous One answers, and heaven is silent, because there is nothing more to be said.
verseByVerse.note: “Advocate” is the word Jesus used of the Holy Spirit (“Helper”) in John’s Gospel; here it is Jesus himself pleading for us.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.

He is the propitiation for our sins. The advocate of verse 1 is also the propitiation. He does not merely plead; he has already paid, and the advocacy in heaven rests on an atonement finished on earth. “He is” (autos estin, he himself is): not merely he provided a propitiation, but he himself is the propitiation. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The word is hilasmos, atoning sacrifice, the means of appeasing wrath, and it matters which English word carries it. To expiate is to deal with the sin; to propitiate is to deal with the wrath. Scripture does both, and this word is the stronger one: the holy anger of God against sin has been absorbed, not overlooked. The word is related to the mercy seat in the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:5), the lid of the ark where, once a year, the blood was sprinkled between God’s presence and the broken law. Christ’s death satisfied God’s just wrath against sin by bearing it in our place (Romans 3:25; Hebrews 2:17; 1 John 4:10). This is why the Father can be both just and forgiving (1:9). This is penal substitution.

Not a pagan bribe. People sometimes recoil from the word because pagan propitiation meant men trying to calm a moody god with gifts. The biblical propitiation is the reverse at every point. It is not man appeasing God but God providing the sacrifice himself: in this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (4:10). The wrath is not a tantrum but the settled, just opposition of holiness to evil. And the one who bears it is not a victim dragged in but the Son who came willingly, and is himself God.

And not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world. “Ours” means John and his readers, Jewish and Gentile believers. “The whole world” (holou tou kosmou). This is a key verse in debates about the extent of the atonement, a clause argued over for four centuries. But before the argument, notice what the verse is for. John is not opening a debate about the scope of the cross. He is writing to Christians who have just been told not to sin and who know perfectly well that they will, and he is telling them what is true when they do. Whatever else this verse settles, it was written to keep a failing believer from despair, and on every reading of it the person reading who trusts Christ is covered.

Where Christians differ: did Christ propitiate the sins of every person? Arminians and others read the whole world as every individual without exception, so that Christ’s death was a propitiation for the sins of all people, including those who are finally lost. Universalists conclude that all will be saved. Among those who hold to grace, the strength of the wider reading is the plain force of sentences like this one, and of others: he gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Timothy 2:6); he tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9); one has died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14). Read without a system, this verse does look as though it is widening something, and honesty requires saying so. Godly, careful men have stood on both sides, and neither side holds its view in order to shrink the cross. Verdict: Propitiation means God’s wrath is actually turned away. If Christ propitiated God’s wrath for every individual, then no one would face God’s wrath, which Scripture denies (John 3:36; Revelation 14:10). So the whole world must mean something other than every individual. In John’s writings, world often means people of every kind and nation, not just Jews. In John 11:51–52 Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad: the same shape of sentence, from the same author, with the same widening. John’s point is that Christ’s sacrifice is not limited to one group, John’s churches, or Jewish believers; it is for people throughout the whole world, of every nation (Revelation 5:9). It is also the only propitiation there is: there is no other sacrifice available anywhere in the world. This is definite atonement: Christ’s death actually and effectively propitiated God for all his people, from every nation. Scripture’s language about the cross points this way throughout: he will save his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21); the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11, 15); Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25); God obtained the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28). Its value is infinite and sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to all.

What both sides agree on. It is more than the disagreement, and it is the part that changes how you live. The death of Christ is of infinite worth: there is no shortage in it, no ceiling, nobody for whom it would have been insufficient. The offer is genuine and it goes to everyone without exception. No one who comes is turned away, ever, for any reason. And nobody at all is saved by any other means.

What it does not mean. It does not mean John is restricting the gospel invitation. The gospel is to be preached to every person, and anyone who believes will be saved (John 3:16). It means the propitiation is effective, not merely potential.

Then can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? Tell him what the apostles told people. They did not open with the extent of the atonement; they proclaimed that Christ died for sinners, that he is a perfect and sufficient Saviour, and that everyone who repents and believes will be forgiven (Acts 2:38; 13:38–39). You can say with complete sincerity: Christ is offered to you; there is room for you; if you come to him he will never cast you out (John 6:37). That is a real offer from a real Saviour, and it is the most generous sentence a human being can hear.

How do I know he died for me? Not by searching the secret decrees of God, but by coming to Christ. Everyone who comes finds that he was expected. The question is not first whether your name is on a list but whether you will take what is held out. If you trust him, rest on him and want him, you have every right to say with Paul that the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20). The doctrine was given to comfort believers that their salvation was actually accomplished, not to keep seekers at the door.

In a sentence. He is the atoning sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath from our sins, and not only from ours but from the sins of people throughout the whole world.

On a Tuesday. If your own failure is the thing on your mind today, the sentence is doing exactly what it was written to do: there is an advocate with the Father, the case he pleads is his own blood, and there is no sin of yours that outruns it. Then think of a nation, a people, or a neighbour far from the gospel. The propitiation is not a local provision. Pray for them by name, give toward their hearing, and speak of it to someone this week.

For worship. The wrath that should have fallen on us fell, and it fell on him. God did not lower his justice to save us; he satisfied it himself, at his own cost, in his own Son. The cup that was ours he drank to the bottom, and when he cried that it was finished, it was. So the mercy seat is no longer a box hidden in a curtained room but a cross lifted up before the nations, and from every tribe and language and people a multitude is being gathered whom he bought. He saves completely, and his blood has never failed for one of those for whom it was shed.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath.

verseByVerse.quote: And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And by this we know that we have come to know him, if we keep his commandments.

And by this we know that we have come to know him. “Know” (ginōskomen) is a keyword of 1 John, used about forty times. “Have come to know” (egnōkamen) is perfect tense: have known and continue to know, a knowledge acquired and still possessed. The false teachers claimed special knowledge of God; John gives tests by which true knowledge can be recognised. And knowing, in John, is never a matter of information alone. It is the knowledge of a husband for his wife, of a friend for a friend: relational, life-sharing, the knowing of which Jesus said, this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God (John 17:3).

If we keep his commandments. “Keep” (tērōmen) means observe, guard, obey; it is present tense: habitually keep. It is the word for keeping watch over something precious. “His commandments” are God’s moral will, summed up in love for God and neighbour (3:23; John 13:34; 15:12). This is the first test: obedience. Knowing God is not merely intellectual; it shows itself in a changed life (John 14:15, 21). John is not setting up salvation by works; he is describing what a genuine relationship produces. You cannot live for years with someone you love and not begin to care about what he cares about.

The Son who kept his Father’s commandments. John did not invent this test; he watched it lived. Jesus said, I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love (John 15:10), and his whole life, from the carpenter’s bench to the cross, was knowledge of the Father worked out in obedience.
