The commandments a Christian keeps are not a ladder he climbs alone but a path the Son has already walked, and those who know the Father through him find their feet beginning to follow his. Obedience is the family likeness of the obedient Son.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn knowledge of God by obedience, or that perfect obedience is required. John has said we all sin (1:8). It means a settled pattern of obedience is evidence that we truly know God.

How much obedience is enough to be sure? John does not give a percentage, because he is not grading a performance. He is looking for a direction. The question is not whether you ever fail, since you do, but whether obedience is the settled direction of your desire and effort. Do you want to do what God says? When you see that something is his will, does it matter to you? When you disobey, does it trouble you and send you back to him? A real but weak obedience is evidence of real life. What contradicts the claim to know God is not stumbling but a life that has stopped caring what he commands.

In a sentence. We know that we have come to know him if we keep his commands.

On a Tuesday. Look at your life this week: where is there clear evidence of obedience to Christ? A temptation refused, an unpleasant duty done, a hard word not spoken, a truth told when a lie was easier. Thank God for it, because he did it in you. And ask for growth where there is little.

For worship. It is astonishing that God can be known at all. The Maker of galaxies is not a theory to be argued about but a person to be met, and he has made himself known in his Son, so that fishermen and housewives and children can say, I know him. And the knowledge changes us, because he is the kind of God whom to know is to begin to resemble. His commands are not the price of his friendship. They are the shape of his own goodness, given to those he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says ‘I know him’ but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may know that we are in him:

Whoever says I know him. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10, and perhaps the false teachers’ slogan. The words are the right words. The question is what stands behind them.

But does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him. “Liar” (pseustēs) is strong language, and John has no interest in diplomatic softening. A claim to know God without obedience is false; the claim and the life are irreconcilable. The truth has not taken hold of him. He has the vocabulary of faith without its substance, like a man who can describe a country in detail from the guidebook and has never set foot in it.

Words first spoken by Jesus. To men who claimed God as their Father while plotting to kill him, Jesus said: you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you, but I do know him and I keep his word (John 8:55). All of John’s terms are there: knowing, lying, keeping his word. The true knower of God is Jesus himself, in whom knowing the Father and obeying him never parted by a hair.

But whoever keeps his word. “His word” (autou ton logon) is broader than commandments: the whole of God’s revealed will. The man in view does not merely obey a list; he treasures everything God has said and lets it rule him.

In him truly the love of God is perfected. “Love of God” (hē agapē tou theou) can mean God’s love for us, our love for God, or the love that comes from God. Probably our love for God, which shows itself in obedience (5:3; John 14:15). “Perfected” (teteleiōtai) means brought to completion, reached its goal, its telos. Love for God reaches its full expression in obedience. Love that never reaches the hands has not finished its journey.

By this we may know that we are in him. “In him” (en autō) is union with Christ. This final clause is easily missed, and it is crucial. Kept commands are not merely moral evidence; they are assurance of union. Obedience tells us we are in him, not just that we agree with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for God is only a matter of obedience, with no feeling. It means genuine love always shows itself in obedience.

What if I obey out of duty, not love? Then keep obeying, and ask God for the love. Duty is not the enemy of love; it is often the scaffolding inside which love is built. A husband who keeps his vows on the days he feels nothing is not a hypocrite but faithful, and the feelings usually return. Jesus himself said, if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15), and the road also runs the other way: those who obey come to know him better, and knowing him they love him more (John 14:21). Tell God honestly that your heart is cold, and do the next right thing.

In a sentence. Whoever says, “I know him,” but does not do what he commands is a liar, and the truth is not in that person. But if anyone obeys his word, love for God is truly made complete in them. This is how we know we are in him.

On a Tuesday. Do your words about knowing God match your life? Ask God to make your obedience as real as your profession. Think of the sentence you would most hate a colleague to hear you say about your faith, because he has seen how you actually behave. Then go and close the gap, starting with the smallest thing.

For worship. God’s love is not a sentiment that stays in heaven. It came down in a Son who kept every word of his Father, and was obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. In him love was perfected, brought all the way to its goal, and now that same love is at work in us, finishing what it started. He who began it does not leave it half done.

verseByVerse.quote: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he walked.

Whoever says he abides in him. “Abides” (menein) means remains, stays, dwells, continues. It is a favourite word of John, at the heart of the vine and the branches (John 15:4–10). To abide in Christ is to live in continuing union and fellowship with him, the way a branch lives in a vine: not visiting, not attending, but drawing its life from him all the time.

Ought to walk in the same way in which he walked. “Ought” (opheilei) means is obligated, owes it, a debt. “Walk” (peripatein) is to live. “He” (ekeinos, that one) is Jesus, emphatically: that man, the one we saw. The test is Christlikeness: living as Jesus lived, in love, obedience, humility and holiness (John 13:15; 1 Peter 2:21). Jesus’ earthly life is the pattern. And it is not self-improvement by willpower, but the natural consequence of genuine union with him: those who truly abide in the vine begin to bear the vine’s fruit.

The man John watched walk. John is not recommending an abstract virtue. He had walked behind Jesus on the roads of Galilee for three years. He had watched him stop for a blind beggar the crowd wanted silenced, eat with tax collectors, rise before dawn to pray, weep at a friend’s tomb, wash twelve pairs of dirty feet, and set his face to go to Jerusalem knowing what waited there. When John writes the way in which he walked, he is seeing it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must imitate every detail of Jesus’ life (being a carpenter, staying unmarried, walking on water). It means we must follow his character and pattern of obedience to the Father and love for others.

Is this not an impossible standard? As a ladder to climb into God’s favour, yes, completely. But John is not writing to people trying to get in; he is writing to people who abide in him. The standard is the direction of the life, not the measure of its success. A child learning to write copies the teacher’s letters and makes a mess of them, and the teacher is delighted, because the child is copying the right letters. Christ does not merely set the pattern; he lives in those who follow it, by his Spirit. Where the walk diverges radically and permanently from his, the claim to abide deserves scrutiny. Where it is stumbling after him, it is the real thing.

In a sentence. Whoever claims to live in him must live as Jesus did.

On a Tuesday. Pick one encounter in Jesus’ life from the Gospels: the woman at the well, the washing of feet, the healing of a leper he touched first. How can you walk as he walked in a situation this week? Look for the person in your path whom everyone else is stepping round.

For worship. There has been one perfect human life. For thirty-three years a man walked this earth who never once took a wrong step, who loved God with all his heart and his neighbour as himself, every hour. He walked that road for us, to the cross, and now he walks beside us and in us, so that the life he lived becomes, slowly and surely, the life we live. We follow footprints made by the Son of God in the dust of our world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The Old-New Commandment: Love and Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command to love is both old and new. Old, because it was there from the beginning (Leviticus 19:18). New, because Christ has given it a new measure, “as I have loved you” (John 13:34), and because the new age has begun: the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining. The test of whether we are in the light is concrete: do we love our brother?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Old-New Commandment

The command to love is old, and new in Christ, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The split in the church showed where the darkness was.

Now: Nursed grudges blind; love keeps the path clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you have heard.

Beloved, I am writing you no new commandment. “Beloved” (agapētoi) is John’s word of choice when he is about to make a major point, and it is the first time he uses it in the letter. He is about to talk about love, and he begins by calling them loved. Unlike the false teachers, with their new knowledge and advanced insight, John keeps returning to the original.

But an old commandment that you had from the beginning. “Old” (palaian): worn, long-established, familiar. “From the beginning”: from when they first heard the gospel. This is the command to love, taught by Jesus and passed on by the apostles. Its roots go back to the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 6:5; Leviticus 19:18), to Moses, centuries before Bethlehem.

The old commandment is the word that you have heard. It is part of the original apostolic message. The antidote to spiritual novelty is not more sophistication but deeper rootedness in the apostolic foundation already received.

The oldest command in the mouth of Christ. Asked which commandment was the greatest, Jesus did not produce a new one. He reached back to Moses for the two oldest, love the Lord your God with all your heart, and love your neighbour as yourself, and said that all the Law and the Prophets hang on them (Matthew 22:37–40). Then he did what no one before him had done: he kept them, all the way to the cross. So the old command reached John’s readers inside the news of Christ, and they learnt what love is by hearing about him.

The old man’s one sermon. Jerome tells a story about John in extreme old age at Ephesus. He was too frail to walk to the church meetings, so his disciples carried him in, and he could manage only one sentence: little children, love one another. He said it every time. At last someone asked him, wearily, why he always said the same thing. He answered that it was the Lord’s command, and if this alone were done, it would be enough. Whether every detail is exact or not, the story fits the man who wrote this verse. He was not bored by the old commandment. He had spent seventy years discovering that he had not finished obeying it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean John’s teaching was merely traditional. It was apostolic, and in Christ it is also new, because he has given it a new measure: love one another as I have loved you (John 13:34).

Does this mean Christians should not learn anything new? No. We should grow in knowledge all our lives (2 Peter 3:18), and every generation discovers more of what is in Scripture. What John warns against is new content: a gospel beyond the gospel, a secret level of truth that the apostles did not teach. Growth digs deeper into what was given; error builds somewhere else. A good test of any teaching that excites you: does it send you back to the Christ of the apostles with fresh wonder, or does it make the plain gospel seem elementary and leave it behind?

In a sentence. Dear friends, I am not writing you a new command but an old one, which you have had since the beginning. This old command is the message you have heard.

On a Tuesday. You do not need something new; you need to live the old. Take the oldest command you know, love your neighbour as yourself, and apply it to one person you will see today, as though you had never heard it before.

For worship. God does not change his mind about what is good. The love he commanded at Sinai is the love he showed at Calvary and the love he will crown in glory. His word is old because he is eternal, and it is never stale because he is never tired. The command that sounds familiar is the voice of a Father who has been saying the same loving thing to his children since the beginning, and will go on saying it until we have learnt it perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you, which is true in him and in you, because the darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining.

At the same time, it is a new commandment that I am writing to you. “New” (kainēn) means new in quality, fresh, not merely recent. Jesus called it a new commandment (John 13:34): love one another as I have loved you. It is old in its source, from the beginning, but new in its standard, which is Christ’s love, and in its power, which is the new age. Moses said love your neighbour as yourself. Jesus said love one another as I have loved you, and then went out and was crucified. The cross is now the measure and the pattern of love.

Which is true in him and in you. “True” (alēthes) means real, realised. The command is fulfilled in Christ’s life, because he embodied it perfectly, and it is being fulfilled in believers, because the Spirit is now producing it in them. The command was a description waiting for a person; now it has one, and the person is reproducing it in his people.

Because the darkness is passing away. “Passing away” (paragetai) means is going by, disappearing; the present tense pictures it in progress. The old age of sin and darkness is ending.

And the true light is already shining. “True light” (to phōs to alēthinon) is Christ (John 1:9; 8:12). “Already” (ēdē). The new age has dawned with Christ’s coming. Light and darkness overlap now, but the darkness is fading. And this gives love its context. To love is not moral effort against the grain of reality but participation in the age that has already, in Christ, arrived. Hatred belongs to the night that is ending; love belongs to the day that is coming. When you love, you are living in tomorrow.

The grey before dawn. Anyone who has been up before sunrise knows the moment. It is still dark, the street lights are on, and nothing has visibly changed; and yet the darkness is not what it was an hour ago. The sky in the east has thinned. You cannot point to the sun, but you know it is coming, and nothing can stop it. That is where the church lives: in the grey before dawn, with the first light on the hills.

What it does not mean. It does not mean darkness has vanished completely. The world still lies in the evil one’s power (5:19). But the dawn has come, and the day is certain.

The world seems to be getting darker. How is the darkness passing? John is not measuring the evening news. He is reading history by its centre. Christ has risen, the decisive battle is won, and the light has entered the world and cannot be put out. Darkness can still be thick in places and seasons; in some ways it rages more as its time runs short (Revelation 12:12). But every person brought out of darkness into his light (1 Peter 2:9) is the dawn spreading, and since the resurrection it has spread to every continent. The darkness is losing, even when it is loud.

In a sentence. Yet I am writing you a new command; its truth is seen in him and in you, because the darkness is passing and the true light is already shining.

On a Tuesday. Measure your love this week by the new standard, not the old one: not as you love yourself, but as he loved you. Ask what love would cost you today if it looked like his: time, pride, money, the right to be proved right. Then pay it somewhere specific.

For worship. The true light is already shining. He came into a world that had been dark since Eden, and the darkness has been retreating before him ever since. Every act of Christlike love in the most obscure place on earth is a ray from that rising Sun of righteousness, who rose with healing in his wings. The night is far gone; the day is at hand, and the day is him.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever says he is in the light and hates his brother is still in darkness.

Whoever says he is in the light. Another claim, as in verses 4 and 6. The claim to spiritual light is now tested by the most concrete and most uncomfortable measure: the treatment of a fellow believer.

And hates his brother. “Hates” (misōn) is present tense: keeps on hating. It indicates not a passing offence but a settled, habitual disposition. Hatred includes contempt, resentment, ill will, refusing to love. “His brother” is a fellow member of the church. The false teachers apparently despised ordinary believers. And it is the brother, the one in the same family, the person on the next chair on Sunday. It is easy to love humanity at large. John points at someone with a name.

Is still in darkness. “Still” (heōs arti): until now. Whatever he claims, he has never left the darkness. This is the second test: love. Hatred of a brother while claiming illumination is not inconsistency in the ordinary sense; it is evidence that the claimed light has never arrived. John does not allow the vertical to be separated from the horizontal.

The brother Christ has made. Why does hatred of a brother prove that a man is still in the dark? Because the light John means is Christ, the true light already shining (v. 8), and the brother is someone that light has claimed: born of God (5:1), cleansed by the blood of Jesus (1:7), and called brother by the Son himself (Hebrews 2:11). To stand in the light is to stand beside Christ and see this person as he sees him. No one can be near the Lord and keep his back turned on the Lord’s family.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer can never feel anger or have conflict with another believer. It describes a settled attitude of hatred and contempt.

Who is my brother, and may I hate those outside the church? Your brother here is your fellow believer, because John is giving a test of genuine membership in God’s family. But it does not follow that you may hate anyone else. Jesus commands love for enemies and persecutors (Matthew 5:44), and the neighbour of Leviticus 19:18 is whoever is in front of you (Luke 10:29–37). John narrows the focus because love inside the family is the first proof that you belong to it. If you cannot love a Christian who shares your Lord, your claim to love the unbeliever down the road is unlikely to be real.

In a sentence. Anyone who claims to be in the light but hates a brother or sister is still in the darkness.

On a Tuesday. Is there a believer you resent or despise? Ask God to replace that with love, and take one step toward reconciliation: pray for his good by name, speak well of him to someone else, or write the message you have been putting off.

For worship. When we were enemies, God did not wait for us to become likeable. Christ died for the ungodly, for people who had nothing to offer him but resentment, and he made them his brothers. The love that refuses to hate a brother is only the overflow of a love that refused to give up on us.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves his brother abides in the light, and in him there is no cause for stumbling.

Whoever loves his brother abides in the light. “Loves” (agapōn) is present tense: keeps on loving. Love shows that one is in the light.

And in him there is no cause for stumbling. “Cause for stumbling” (skandalon) is a trap, a snare, a stumbling block; originally the stick in a trap that springs it. Either the loving person does not stumble himself, because he can see where he is going, or he does not cause others to stumble. Probably both. Love keeps us from tripping and from tripping others (Romans 14:13; Psalm 119:165).

Twelve hours in the day. John had heard this picture from Jesus. When the disciples begged him not to go back to Judea, where men had just tried to stone him, he answered: if anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world (John 11:9). He was going to Bethany because Lazarus, whom he loved, had died (John 11:5), and that walk of love led in the end to the cross. Love made his road plain, though not safe, and the loving believer walks the same road behind the same Lord.

How hatred trips us. Think about how resentment actually works in a life. It distorts judgement: you misread the other person’s every move. It makes you say what you regret. It makes you avoid church, or a meeting, or a family gathering, and so cuts you off from grace. It hands the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Most spiritual falls have a grudge somewhere upstream. The loving person is not cleverer; he simply has nothing on the path for his feet to catch on.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the loving person never sins. It means love keeps him on the path.

What does love for a brother look like when he is difficult? Love is not mainly a warm feeling but a settled will for his good, shown in action (3:18). With a difficult brother that means praying for him honestly, refusing to gossip about him, speaking to him rather than about him, giving him the benefit of the doubt, and forgiving when he wrongs you. It may mean telling him a hard truth gently. It does not mean pretending wrongs did not happen or putting yourself in danger. You can love someone you do not naturally like, because the love comes from God, not from your temperament.

In a sentence. Anyone who loves their brother and sister lives in the light, and there is nothing in them to make them stumble.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for those who love you and keep you from stumbling. Ask him to make you that kind of person for others. Think of one younger or weaker believer who watches you. What in your life could trip him? Remove it.

For worship. The one who never stumbled holds the hands of those who do. He walked every step of his Father’s will without a slip, through every trap his enemies laid, and now he walks with his people as the shepherd who goes before them and knows every stone on the path. He does not merely show the way and wait to see whether we reach the end of it. He is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24), and he will not loosen his grip on one of us between here and there.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.

But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. “Is in” and “walks in”: his position and his practice. He lives in darkness. The grammar is relentless: is in the darkness (present state), walks in the darkness (habitual movement), does not know where he is going (lost orientation), the darkness has blinded his eyes (a past act whose result now stands).

And does not know where he is going. Like someone stumbling in the dark, without direction (John 12:35). He thinks he knows; he has strong opinions about everybody. But he is walking in circles.

While you have the light. Jesus spoke these words first, in the last days before the cross: the one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going (John 12:35). And he gave the remedy with them: while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light (John 12:36). A blind man cannot cure his eyes by staring harder into the dark. The cure for hatred’s blindness is faith in the Light himself, while he is near.

Because the darkness has blinded his eyes. “Blinded” (etyphlōsen). Hatred is not only a sin; it blinds. A person full of hatred cannot see clearly about God, himself, or others (2 Corinthians 4:4). Think of a man who stays in a dark cellar for years: when he finally comes up, the daylight he needs is the very thing he cannot bear, and he turns back to the dark. Hatred does that to the soul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean such a person cannot be rescued. Christ came to open blind eyes (John 9:39). But hatred must be repented of.

Can I hate someone and not know it? Yes, and that is the frightening part of this verse: blindness does not feel like blindness. Hatred rarely calls itself by name. It calls itself justice, discernment, honesty, or just being realistic about him. Some signs that it is present: you feel pleasure when he fails; you replay his offences; you cannot pray for his blessing; you find yourself telling others about him; you cannot bear to hear him praised. If any of these are true, do not argue with the diagnosis. Ask God to open your eyes, and begin by praying for that person’s good.

In a sentence. But anyone who hates a brother or sister is in the darkness and walks around in the darkness. They do not know where they are going, because the darkness has blinded them.

On a Tuesday. Has resentment been blinding you to the truth about someone? Ask God to open your eyes and help you see him as he does. Write down three good things God has done in or through that person. It will be harder than it should be, and that is the point.

For worship. Christ is the light of the world, and he is the one who opens the eyes of the blind. He spat on the ground, made mud, and gave a beggar his sight; he can do the same for a heart blinded by bitterness. No darkness is too long-standing for him, and no grudge too old. He who said, let light shine out of darkness, shines in our hearts, and where he shines we see our brother as one for whom Christ died.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — Assurance for Every Stage of Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the tests, John pauses to reassure. He addresses little children, fathers and young men, and tells each what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of the eternal Christ, and victory over the evil one through the word abiding in them. Assurance comes before further commands.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance for Every Stage

Before further commands, John tells children, fathers and young men what is already theirs: forgiveness, knowledge of God, and victory over the evil one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were being told they needed something more.

Now: The newest believer needs first to hear that his sins are forgiven for Christ’s name’s sake.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven for his name’s sake.

I am writing to you, little children. After hard tests, John pauses to reassure. Verses 12–14 address three groups: little children, fathers, and young men. Either these are three stages of spiritual maturity, or little children addresses all believers (as in v. 1), and fathers and young men are two groups within the church, older and younger. John uses teknia here, his most affectionate term, for all believers regardless of spiritual age.

Because your sins are forgiven. “Because” (hoti) can mean because, the reason for writing, or that, the content. Probably because: John writes to them because they are genuine believers. “Are forgiven” (apheōntai) is perfect tense: have been forgiven and remain forgiven. Every believer, from the youngest, is fully forgiven. Forgiveness is the first word to every believer because it is the ground of every other word.

For his name’s sake. “His name” is Christ’s name, his person and work (Acts 4:12; 10:43). Forgiveness is on account of who Christ is and what he has done, not on account of anything in us. A name in Scripture stands for the whole person and reputation, and God forgives in order to honour his Son. Your forgiveness rests on the honour of Christ, which is the most secure foundation in the universe.

Why the reassurance comes here. It is pastorally brilliant. John has just put his readers through a series of searching tests: do you obey, do you love, do you walk as he walked? A sensitive believer reads them and begins to tremble. So John stops and says: I am not writing because I doubt you. I am writing because you are forgiven. The tests are not meant to make the children of God unsure, but to show the counterfeit for what it is, and to let the real children see the family likeness in themselves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean forgiveness is conditional on passing all the tests. The tests show who is forgiven; they do not earn forgiveness.

What if I am not sure my sins are forgiven? Then look away from yourself to the ground of forgiveness: his name’s sake. If forgiveness rested on the depth of your sorrow or the quality of your faith, you could never be sure. It rests on Christ. Ask yourself: am I trusting him, and him alone, to be my righteousness? If the answer is yes, however weakly, then God’s word says you are forgiven (Acts 10:43), and it is not humility but unbelief to doubt it. Assurance grows by looking at Christ more than at yourself.

In a sentence. I am writing to you, dear children, because your sins have been forgiven on account of his name.

On a Tuesday. Rest in this today: your sins are forgiven, completely and permanently, for Christ’s sake. When an old sin comes back to accuse you, do not reopen the case. Say aloud: forgiven, for his name’s sake.

For worship. The God who keeps the stars in their places has staked the honour of his own Son’s name on the pardon of sinners. He does not forgive grudgingly or provisionally, keeping a file in case we disappoint him. He forgives like a king who has cancelled the whole debt and burned the record, for his name’s sake, and his name will never be dishonoured.

verseByVerse.quote: I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, children, because you know the Father.

I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. “Fathers” are mature believers, perhaps older in years. “Him who is from the beginning” is Christ, the eternal Word (1:1), the one John introduced in the prologue. The mark of maturity is a deep, long-tested knowledge of Christ. Long years in the faith have not produced familiarity that breeds contempt; they have produced rootedness in the person of Christ. What John praises in his fathers is not their achievements or their offices but that they know him.

I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. “Young men” are believers in the vigour of spiritual life, perhaps younger in years. “Overcome” (nenikēkate) is perfect tense: have conquered and remain victorious. It is from nikē, victory. “The evil one” is Satan (5:18–19). Young believers are in the thick of battle, and they have won by Christ’s victory (4:4; 5:4–5; John 16:33).

I write to you, children, because you know the Father. “Children” (paidia, little ones, young children) is a different word from verse 12, suggesting those newer in faith. The simplest and most precious knowledge is this: knowing God as Father (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6), the Abba relationship granted in adoption. The newest believer, who could not explain a single doctrine, knows the one thing the false teachers with all their learning did not: that the God of the universe is his Father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean each group has only one quality. All believers are forgiven, know the Father, overcome the evil one, and grow in knowing Christ. Each is highlighted in its characteristic stage.

Which group am I in? Probably more than one, and it does not matter much. If you are new, you are not second-class: you know the Father, which is the heart of everything. If you are in the thick of the fight, you have overcome, even on days when it does not feel like it. If you have walked with Christ for decades, the goal is not to retire but to know him more deeply still. And every church needs all three. Older believers should seek out younger ones to encourage, and the young should seek out the fathers to learn from.

In a sentence. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one. I write to you, dear children, because you know the Father.

On a Tuesday. If you are older in the faith, find one younger believer this month and ask how you can pray for him. If you are younger, ask an older believer what he has learnt about knowing Christ over the years. Then listen.

For worship. The God who is from the beginning welcomes the newest child and the oldest saint into the same embrace. The one who has walked with him fifty years has not exhausted him, and the one who met him last week is not kept at a distance. Every stage stands on what the Son has done: the child knows the Father because the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18); the young man overcomes because the Son has overcome the world (John 16:33); and the father’s long knowledge is knowledge of the Son himself, the one who was from the beginning. One Father, one victorious Son, one family, and for all of them an eternity in which to know him more.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. This is repeated from verse 13 for emphasis, as though the blessing must be said twice to be fully received. The tense changes from I am writing to I write (egrapsa, aorist), perhaps referring to the whole letter, or to an earlier writing, or simply for variety and emphasis. To the fathers, John adds nothing new. What could be added to knowing the eternal Son?

I write to you, young men, because you are strong. “Strong” (ischyroi): spiritual strength. The young men receive an expanded description.

And the word of God abides in you. This is the source of their strength: God’s word dwelling in them (John 15:7; Colossians 3:16; Psalm 119:11). The order is illuminating: strength is not the cause of the word abiding, but its result. The word of God dwelling in the young man is what makes him strong for the fight. Jesus overcame Satan in the wilderness by quoting Scripture (Matthew 4:1–11), three times, all from Deuteronomy. The eternal Word defended himself with the written word.

And you have overcome the evil one. Strength through the word leads to victory over Satan (Ephesians 6:17). Scripture is not information about spiritual warfare; it is the weapon itself, the sword of the Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean young believers never struggle with temptation. They are in the fight. But they fight from victory, with the word as their weapon.

How does the word actually make me strong? Not by magic, but by changing what you believe in the moment of temptation. Every temptation is a lie: this will satisfy you, God is holding out on you, no one will know, you cannot help it. The word that abides in you answers the lie with the truth, as Jesus answered with written words. That only works if the word is already inside you, read, remembered and believed, before the moment comes. And if reading is hard for you, listen to Scripture read aloud, sing it, and learn a few verses well. A small sword in the hand is better than a large one left in the cupboard.

In a sentence. I write to you, fathers, because you know him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God lives in you, and you have overcome the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Memorise one verse of Scripture this week, chosen for the temptation you face most often. Let God’s word abide in you as your weapon against the evil one. Say it aloud the next time the temptation comes.

For worship. The Word of God has made his home in his people. He who was the Word in the beginning, by whom all things were made, now dwells in the hearts of ordinary young men and women through the words he has given, so that a schoolboy with a verse in his memory stands on ground the devil cannot take. The strength is not theirs. It is his word abiding, and behind the word the living Lord who spoke it, who has bound the strong man and plundered his house (Matthew 12:29). Every Christian who answers a lie with Scripture is a trophy of that victory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–17 — Do Not Love the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not love the world.” John does not mean God’s creation, which God loves, or a call to withdraw from culture. He means the world system organised against God, with its own values and desires. He names its three roots: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life. And he gives the decisive reason: the world is passing away, but whoever does God’s will abides for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
Do Not Love the World

The desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life are not from the Father. The world is passing away; whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Wealth and religion were on public display in the cities of Asia.

Now: Receive created things as gifts, but enthrone none of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.

Do not love the world. “Love” (agapate) is present tense: keep on loving, make it your settled affection. The command is absolute. “The world” (ton kosmon) is not the created earth, which is good (Genesis 1:31), or the people of the world, whom God loves (John 3:16), but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values, desires and priorities (James 4:4; 1 John 5:19).

The same word, two loves. John uses the same word in the same Gospel for something God does and something we must not do. God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16). Do not love the world. The difference is not the word but the direction. God loves the world as a rescuer loves a drowning man: to save it. We are forbidden to love it as the drowning man loves the current: to be carried by it.

Or the things in the world. The things it values and offers: possessions, pleasures, status, power, when sought as ends in themselves, in place of God.

If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. “Love of the Father” is love for the Father. Love for the world and love for God are mutually exclusive as ultimate loyalties (Matthew 6:24; James 4:4). Where the world’s system holds the heart’s primary allegiance, the Father has no room. Everything in the world may be received and enjoyed as God’s gift, but nothing in it may be enthroned as the heart’s supreme good.

What the world did with the Son. The plainest way to see what the world is, in John’s sense, is to watch what it did when the Father sent his Son into it. It did not know him (John 1:10), it hated him without a cause (John 15:25), and it nailed him to a cross. To love the world is to take the side of those who crucified the Son. And the cross is also the cure: by it, Paul said, the world had been crucified to him, and he to the world (Galatians 6:14). A heart that has seen the Son of God die for it finds the world’s prizes losing their shine.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society, despise beauty, or refuse to enjoy God’s good gifts (1 Timothy 4:4; 6:17). It means they must not give their hearts to the world’s rebellious system or let its values rule them.

How do I know if I love the world? Is it wrong to enjoy films, sport or nice things? Enjoying good things is not worldliness; God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). The question is what rules the heart. Some tests: what do you think about when your mind is free? What could you not bear to lose? What makes you envious? What do you spend on most gladly? Would you give it up at once if God asked? Do you laugh at what dishonours him? Does it make you want God less? Worldliness is not a list of activities but a direction of love. Anything, even good things, becomes worldly when it replaces the Father.

In a sentence. Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, love for the Father is not in them.

On a Tuesday. What does the world offer that most tempts your heart? Name it, and give your heart to the Father instead. One practical way: the next time you want the thing badly, stop and thank God for something you already have in him. Love is retrained by gratitude.

For worship. The Father is the better love. Nothing the world dangles can compare with him: no pleasure as deep, no treasure as lasting, no honour as high as being his child. He did not ask us to give up the world and get nothing; he gave us himself. And he loved the world in the right way, sending his Son into it to die for it, so that people who had been in love with the current could be pulled out of it onto the rock.

verseByVerse.quote: For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world.

For all that is in the world. Three things sum up the world’s system. John anatomises it into three streams, as a doctor might name the three branches of a disease.

The desires of the flesh. “Desires” (epithymia) are cravings, lusts. “Flesh” (sarkos) is sinful human nature. These are cravings for physical gratification: sexual immorality, gluttony, drunkenness, laziness, comfort above all. Appetite is treated as sovereign, the body’s cravings as moral authorities.

And the desires of the eyes. These are cravings aroused by what we see: covetousness, greed, envy, materialism, pornography. The eyes lead the heart (Genesis 3:6; Joshua 7:21; 2 Samuel 11:2). Achan saw, coveted and took; David saw from the roof and sent. And we live in the most visually saturated culture in history, with screens built by brilliant people to make the eyes want.

And pride of life. “Pride” (alazoneia) is arrogance, boastful pretension, showing off, as in James 4:16. It was used of the travelling salesman who promised more than he could deliver. “Life” (biou) is livelihood, possessions, means of living. This is arrogance about what one has or does: status, wealth, achievements, appearance. It is the boasting of self-sufficiency, the person who needs no God because he has his own resources.

The oldest temptation. Commentators since Augustine have seen the same three in Eden. The fruit was good for food (the flesh), a delight to the eyes (the eyes), and desirable to make one wise (pride) (Genesis 3:6). And in Jesus’ temptation: bread (the flesh), the kingdoms of the world shown in a moment (the eyes), and throwing himself from the temple (pride) (Luke 4:1–13). The world’s system is very old, and so is its remedy. The first Adam fell at all three points in a garden. The last Adam met all three in a wilderness and did not fall.

Is not from the Father but is from the world. These desires do not come from God. They come from the fallen world system. They are the distortions that sin introduced into capacities that were originally oriented toward God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean physical desires, beauty or achievements are sinful in themselves. God made our bodies, our eyes and our abilities. The problem is desire that is disordered, ruling us in place of God.

Are sexual desire and ambition the desires of the flesh and pride of life? Not in themselves. Sexual desire is God’s good gift for marriage (Genesis 2:24; Proverbs 5:18–19), and wanting to work hard and do well can be obedience (Colossians 3:23). They become the desires of the flesh and the pride of life when they rule: when desire demands satisfaction outside God’s design, or ambition wants glory for self rather than for God. The test is the master. Hunger is good; gluttony is hunger on the throne. Excellence is good; pride is excellence worshipped.

In a sentence. For everything in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, comes not from the Father but from the world.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to show you which of these three has the strongest grip on you, and pray for freedom. Then take one practical step against it: a filter on a device, a fast from something, a purchase not made, a compliment given to someone else instead of the boast you were about to make.

For worship. The one who refused the devil’s offer of the kingdoms of the world has received them from his Father’s hand. He would not take a crown without a cross, and now the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever (Revelation 11:15). And he gives his people better desires than the three that ruined Adam: a hunger for righteousness that he fills, eyes that will see the King in his beauty (Isaiah 33:17), and a boast in nothing but his cross. What the world offers on loan, he gives for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.

And the world is passing away along with its desires. “Passing away” (paragetai) means going by, disappearing, and the present tense pictures it already in motion, as in verse 8. The world’s system, with all its attractions, is temporary and already fading (1 Corinthians 7:31). To love the world is to invest in a structure that is in the process of collapse. Why love what you will lose? And notice: along with its desires. Not only the things pass, but the wanting of them. The appetite that seemed so urgent at twenty is gone at eighty, and what it sacrificed for is gone with it.

Every empire passes. When John wrote, the Roman Empire looked eternal. Its roads ran from Scotland to Syria; its emperors were worshipped as gods. Today tourists photograph its ruins. Every great city, every fashion, every fortune, every name in lights will be the same. A man who builds his life on any of them is building a house on a tide.

But whoever does the will of God abides forever. Doing the will of God is living in obedience (Matthew 7:21; 12:50). “Abides forever” (menei eis ton aiōna) means remains to the age, endures eternally. Not that obedience earns eternal life, but that those who do God’s will share in his eternal life and will last when the world is gone. The universe is ageing; the believer who does God’s will is being renewed.

The one who did the will of God. There has been one man of whom this sentence is perfectly true. Jesus came saying, behold, I have come to do your will, O God (Hebrews 10:7), and he did it all the way to the cross; by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The believer who does God’s will abides for ever, not because his obedience can outlast the world, but because he is joined to the Son who did the Father’s will perfectly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the world will be annihilated. The present order will be renewed (2 Peter 3:13). What passes away is the world as a rebellious system.

How do I know what the will of God is? Mostly, by reading it. God’s will in John’s sense is not a hidden plan for your career that you must decode, but his revealed will in Scripture: to believe in his Son and love one another (3:23), to be holy (1 Thessalonians 4:3), to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). For decisions Scripture does not settle, such as which job or which house, obey what is clear, pray for wisdom (James 1:5), seek counsel, and then choose freely within his commands. A believer who is doing the revealed will of God is in the will of God, whichever good option he picks.

In a sentence. The world and its desires pass away, but whoever does the will of God lives for ever.

On a Tuesday. Invest this week in what lasts: God’s will, God’s word, God’s people. Look at your calendar and your bank statement for the last month and ask how much of each went into things that will outlast the world. Then make one change.

For worship. Everything else is passing, and he remains. The heavens will wear out like a garment, and he will change them like a robe, but he is the same, and his years have no end: words of the psalm that Hebrews sings to the Son (Hebrews 1:10–12). And because he abides, those who belong to him abide with him. The one who does his will will outlive the stars, not because of his own strength, but because he has been joined to the eternal life of God, which cannot die.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — Antichrists, Apostasy, and the Anointing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Antichrists have appeared and left the church, denying the Father and the Son. John turns this crisis into confidence. Their departure revealed that they never truly belonged. And ordinary believers have what the false teachers claimed and lacked: the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who teaches them the truth and keeps them in it. The answer to deception is to abide in what was heard from the beginning, and so in the Son and the Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointing

Those who left showed that they were never of the church. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit, who keeps him in the truth he heard from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teachers offered superior knowledge.

Now: Beware any teaching that says Scripture, the Spirit and the church are not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, it is the last hour, and as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come. Therefore we know that it is the last hour.

Children, it is the last hour. “Children” (paidia), as in verse 14. “Last hour” (eschatē hōra) is the final period of history before Christ’s return, which began with his first coming (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Peter 1:20). The whole church age is the last hour, the final stage of God’s plan. And he says it twice, opening and closing the verse, as rhetorical insistence. The clock of history has struck the last hour, and every hour since has been part of it.

And as you have heard that antichrist is coming. “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters (2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7); the word appears nowhere before them. The prefix anti carries two senses at once: against, an opponent, and in place of, a counterfeit substitute. The antichrist is both: an adversary of Christ and a false usurper who offers himself as an alternative Christ. The readers had been taught that a great opponent of Christ would come at the end, as Jesus and Paul foretold (Mark 13:22; 2 Thessalonians 2:3–12, the man of lawlessness; compare Revelation 13, the beast). John never uses those passages’ terms, and his word is a category of his own: the spirit of opposition to, and substitution for, the true Christ.

So now many antichrists have come. “Many” (polloi). Before the final antichrist, many smaller antichrists appear: all who deny Christ, especially false teachers within the church (vv. 19, 22). The spirit of antichrist is already at work (4:3). And here is the shock: the anticipated singular antichrist has been preceded by many antichrists in the community, not pagan outsiders but former insiders. The enemy had sung in their meetings and eaten at their tables.

Therefore we know that it is the last hour. Their presence is evidence that the final period has begun. The very thing that frightened the church is turned into a sign that God’s timetable is running exactly as foretold. Nothing has slipped out of his hands.

Where Christians differ: who is the antichrist? Some identify the antichrist with a specific future world ruler who will appear during a seven-year tribulation after a secret rapture; the Reformers often identified the papacy as the antichrist; others see the antichrist as a principle only, not a person. Verdict: John teaches both: the spirit of antichrist is present throughout the church age in the many who deny Christ, and Scripture also foretells a final, personal climax of opposition before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3–8). This fits the amillennial view: throughout the age between Christ’s comings, antichrists arise, culminating in a final great deceiver whom Christ will destroy at his single, visible return. Believers should not speculate about identities but test every spirit by its confession of Christ (4:1–3).

What it does not mean. “Last hour” does not mean John expected the end within months. It describes the character of the age. Nor should believers be fearful; antichrists cannot snatch Christ’s sheep (John 10:28).

Is it right to call a false teacher antichrist today? John did, so the category is real, and it is defined by the denial of Christ’s true identity (v. 22; 4:3), not by politics, personality or how much we dislike someone. Any teaching that denies that Jesus is the eternal Son of God who came in the flesh, died and rose, is of the spirit of antichrist, however warm its tone. But the label is not for throwing at fellow Christians with whom we disagree about secondary matters, nor at every leader we fear. Use it seldom, carefully, and with sorrow, and always more concerned to protect the sheep than to win the argument.

In a sentence. Dear children, this is the last hour; and as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, even now many antichrists have come. This is how we know it is the last hour.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus this week: does it confess him truly as the Christ, God come in the flesh? Apply it to the book, the podcast, the video, the friend’s new spiritual idea. Ask not first whether it is helpful or inspiring, but who it says Jesus is.

For worship. The last hour belongs to Christ. Every antichrist, from the first false teacher in Ephesus to the final man of lawlessness, rises only within the limits God has set and falls when he says. The Lord Jesus will kill the last of them with the breath of his mouth and bring him to nothing by the appearance of his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:8). The true Christ is not anxious about the counterfeits. He has already won, and the last hour is simply the time he is taking to gather his own.
verseByVerse.note: “Antichrist” appears in the Bible only in John’s letters.

verseByVerse.quote: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us.

They went out from us. The false teachers had left the church, perhaps forming a rival group. “From us” (ex hēmōn): they had been members, part of the fellowship. John does not pretend this was not painful or destabilising. People they had prayed with were gone, and some were now teaching against what they had once confessed.

But they were not of us. “Of us” (ex hēmōn) here means truly belonging, sharing the same life. They were among us, but not of us. Their membership was outward only. John interprets the departure: it was not caused by superior argument; it revealed an internal reality.

For if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. “Continued” (memenēkeisan) is would have remained, abided. True believers persevere. Those who are genuinely born of God continue in the faith and the fellowship.

But they went out, that it might become plain that they all are not of us. “Become plain” (phanerōthōsin) means be revealed, be made manifest. Their departure exposed what was always true: they never truly belonged. God used their leaving to reveal their real condition. Even apostasy serves the purpose of God, separating what only appeared united. This is not comfortable, but it is clarifying.

John had seen it happen at the table. The first man to go out from the apostolic circle went out from the Last Supper. Judas had walked with Jesus for three years and been sent out to preach with the rest; then he took the morsel from Jesus’ hand and went out, and it was night (John 13:30). Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64). Peter fell the same night, more loudly, and came back weeping, because he was one of them; Judas went out, and showed that he never had been. The difference lay not in the size of the sin but in the keeping of the Lord, who had prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail (Luke 22:32).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer fall away and be lost? Arminian Christians hold that true believers can fall away, pointing to the warnings of Hebrews (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). Verdict: This verse is one of the clearest statements of the perseverance of the saints. Those who finally depart from Christ and his people show that they were never truly of us, never genuinely regenerated. If they had been, they would have continued. True believers may stumble, backslide and need restoring, but they will not finally fall away, because God keeps them (John 6:37–40; 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The warnings of Hebrews are real, and they are one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. This is not a cause for complacency, but for assurance, and for testing ourselves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone who leaves a particular church is an unbeliever. People move, churches err, and believers sometimes leave for good reasons. John speaks of those who left the apostolic faith and fellowship, denying Christ (v. 22).

Someone I love professed faith and has now walked away. What do I make of it? First, grieve; John did not pretend it was nothing. Then remember that you cannot see the end of the story. Some who wander are true believers in a terrible backslidden season, like Peter after his denial, and they come back. Others, if they never return, will show that they did not truly belong, and that is the sorrow of this verse. You do not have to decide which today. Your part is to pray, to keep loving them, to keep the door open, and to speak the truth when it can be heard. God is able to bring back the lost, and he often does it years later.

Could I be one of those who leave? The people who ask this anxiously are rarely the people in danger of it. The warning is real, and it is meant to keep you close. But the promise is just as real: no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). Your perseverance rests on his keeping, not on the strength of your grip. Stay where his grace is given: in his word, at prayer, among his people, at his table. Those are the very means by which he keeps you.

In a sentence. They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us; but their going showed that none of them belonged to us.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for one person who has drifted from Christ and his church. Then send him a message that has no agenda but kindness. And ask yourself honestly whether there is any slow drift in your own life, a habit dropped, a coldness tolerated, and turn back now, while it is small.

For worship. The Shepherd does not lose his sheep. All that the Father gives him will come to him, and of all that he has been given he will lose nothing, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:37–39). He keeps them through storms, through backsliding, through their own weakness and the devil’s rage, and he will bring every one of them home. The church on earth is mixed, but the Lord knows those who are his, and not one of them will be missing when he counts them in.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you all have knowledge.

But you have been anointed by the Holy One. “But you”: in contrast with those who left. “Anointed” (chrisma echete, you have an anointing). Chrisma is related to Christ (Christos, Anointed One) and to antichrist. The wordplay is unmistakable: the anti-anointed ones have gone; you are the anointed ones of the Anointed One. The anointing is the Holy Spirit, given to all believers (2 Corinthians 1:21–22; Acts 10:38). “The Holy One” is Christ (John 6:69; Acts 3:14), who gives the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7), or God the Father.

And you all have knowledge. “You all” (pantes). Some manuscripts read “you know all things” (panta). “You all” is better supported. Against the false teachers who claimed knowledge only for an elite, John says every believer has the Spirit and knows the truth (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11). The elitism of the false teachers, superior knowledge for the spiritually advanced, is quietly devastated: the ordinary believer, anointed by the Spirit, already has what the elite cannot provide.

In the Old Testament, oil was poured on few heads. Prophets, priests and kings were anointed, a handful in each generation, and the oil marked them as set apart for God. Moses longed for the day when all the LORD’s people would be prophets, and the LORD would put his Spirit on them (Numbers 11:29). Joel promised it (Joel 2:28). Now John says to an ordinary congregation of slaves, tradesmen and widows: you have the anointing, all of you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer knows everything. It means every believer has the Spirit, who enables them to recognise the truth of the gospel and to discern error.

Do I need a special experience to have this anointing? No. John says all his readers have it, and he is writing to ordinary believers, not to a spiritual elite. The anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every Christian at conversion (Romans 8:9; Ephesians 1:13). You may not have felt anything dramatic when you came to faith, but if you trust Christ, love him, and find the gospel true and precious, the Spirit is at work in you, for no one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). Some believers have vivid experiences and some quiet ones; the anointing is the same.

In a sentence. But you have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth.

On a Tuesday. Do not be intimidated by people who sound more spiritual or more learned than you. You have the same Spirit. Open your Bible today, ask him to teach you, and trust that he will.

For worship. The Christ, the Anointed One, received the Spirit without measure, and he has poured that Spirit out on his people. What was once reserved for kings and priests is now given to every believer. The Holy One has not left us to find our way to the truth alone; he has taken up residence in us, as teacher and guide and seal. Every Christian is an anointed one because he belongs to the Anointed One.

verseByVerse.quote: I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because no lie is of the truth.

I write to you, not because you do not know the truth. John is not adding new knowledge. He writes not to inform the ignorant but to confirm what his readers already know: this is a letter of assurance, not a course in basic Christianity.

But because you know it. What they need is to be reminded of it firmly enough to resist the deception circulating among them. Most of the Christian life is not learning new things but remembering old ones at the right moment.

And because no lie is of the truth. “Of the truth” (ek tēs alētheias) means comes from the truth. Truth and lies have different sources. Because they know the truth, they can recognise lies (John 8:44; 14:6). Truth is not relative; there is a clear line between truth and falsehood. The false teaching is not a partial truth or a different angle on the same reality; it is simply incompatible with the truth. Bank clerks are said to learn counterfeit notes not by studying every forgery but by handling the real thing until anything else feels wrong in the hand.

The truth has a face. In John’s writings truth is not first a list of correct statements but a person: Jesus said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6), and the false teachers’ lie was a lie about him (v. 22). To know the truth was to know the real Jesus of the apostles, the Son of God come in the flesh, crucified and risen. A believer who has spent years with the Christ of the Gospels may not answer every clever argument, but he knows when the Jesus he is being offered is not the one he loves.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are immune to deception. John warns them (v. 26). It means they have what they need to resist it.

How can I tell truth from a lie when both sides quote the Bible? Ask several questions. Does this teaching agree with the plain meaning of Scripture read in context, or does it depend on one verse twisted away from the rest? Does it exalt Christ as fully God and fully man, the only Saviour, or does it shrink him? Does it agree with what the church has confessed across the centuries, or does it claim that everyone was wrong until now? Does it produce humility, holiness and love, or pride and division? And take it to mature believers and faithful pastors. A lie usually fails at least one of these.

In a sentence. I do not write to you because you do not know the truth, but because you do know it and because no lie comes from the truth.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen what you already know: review the core truths of the gospel this week, so you can recognise lies. Read the Apostles’ Creed slowly, and ask of each line where Scripture teaches it.

For worship. The Truth once stood on trial. Pilate looked at him and asked what truth is, while the Truth stood in front of him, bound, and was handed over to be crucified on the word of liars (John 18:38). But no lie could keep him in the grave. He rose, and the world’s verdict was overturned by the verdict of God. Every lie told about him since has the same future as that first one. He is the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14), the Spirit he sends is the Spirit of truth, and the God who gave us his Son will not let his children be finally deceived.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son.

Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? “The liar” (ho pseustēs) is the liar par excellence, the definite article marking the lie of lies. “Denies that Jesus is the Christ”: the false teachers apparently separated the human Jesus from the divine Christ, claiming the Christ spirit came on Jesus at his baptism and left before his death (the view associated with Cerinthus). That would leave only a man to die on the cross, and a death that saves no one. To deny that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah, the eternal Son come in the flesh (4:2), is the ultimate lie. The confession about Christ is not optional theology; it is the load-bearing wall of the gospel.

This is the antichrist, he who denies the Father and the Son. “The antichrist” is the embodiment of the antichrist spirit (v. 18). “Denies the Father and the Son”: you cannot deny the Son without denying the Father, because the Father is known only through the Son (John 14:6–9). Claims to know God while rejecting Jesus as the Christ are false.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone with a confused view of Jesus is the antichrist. John speaks of a deliberate denial of the apostolic truth about Christ, by those who once knew it.

Who denies that Jesus is the Christ today? Anyone who denies who Jesus really is, whatever words he keeps. Some deny his full deity, making him a created being, a great prophet or a good teacher. Some deny his real humanity or his bodily resurrection. Some keep the name Jesus but empty it of the Christ of Scripture, so that he becomes a symbol of their own values. The test is not whether someone speaks warmly of Jesus but whether he confesses the Jesus of the apostles: the eternal Son of God, truly man, crucified for sin and risen bodily, the only Saviour.

In a sentence. Who is the liar? It is whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ. Such a person is the antichrist, denying the Father and the Son.

On a Tuesday. Practise saying clearly, in your own words, who Jesus is: the eternal Son of God, who became truly man, died for our sins and rose bodily. If someone asked you at lunch, could you say it in two sentences? Try it today.

For worship. Jesus is the Christ. The carpenter of Nazareth is the Anointed One promised from Eden, the Son of the Father, God from God. The man who hung on the cross was not a husk abandoned by the divine; he was the Lord of glory, crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8). Because he is both, his death is our life, and in his face the Father himself has come near to be known.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also.

No one who denies the Son has the Father. “Has” (echei) means possesses, is in relationship with. There is no access to the Father apart from the Son. All other religions, however sincere, which deny the Son, do not have the Father (John 5:23; 14:6; Acts 4:12). This is Christian exclusivism. The Son is not a pointer to the Father or a useful mediating concept that can be adjusted while the Father relationship is kept intact; he is the only way the Father is known, loved and reached.

Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also. “Confesses” (homologōn) means acknowledges publicly. Confessing the Son brings the Father with him. Father and Son are inseparable. Whoever has the Son has not part of God but all of him: Father and Son together, in the Spirit.

Where Christians differ: can people be saved through other religions? Inclusivists hold that people of other faiths may be saved through Christ without knowing him; pluralists that all religions lead to God. Verdict: John’s statement is absolute: no one who denies the Son has the Father. Salvation is found in Christ alone, received through faith in him (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–17). This is why the church must take the gospel to every nation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be arrogant toward people of other religions. It means they must lovingly point them to the only Saviour.

What about those who never hear of Christ? Scripture does not give us another way, and we must not invent one. People are not condemned for failing to believe in a Christ they never heard of, but for their sin against the light God has given them in creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–16), and the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Infants who die in infancy, who are elect, are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. But for everyone who can hear, Paul’s logic stands: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? (Romans 10:14). That is why we send missionaries, not why we stop.

In a sentence. No one who denies the Son has the Father; whoever acknowledges the Son has the Father also.

On a Tuesday. Pray for a friend of another faith or no faith, that he will come to know the Father through the Son. Ask God for an opening this month to tell him, kindly and plainly, why you believe Jesus is the only way.

For worship. To have the Son is to have everything. The Father does not keep back part of himself from those who come through his Son; he gives himself wholly. The only way is not a narrow gate grudgingly opened, but a door flung wide by a Father who sent his only Son to fetch the lost from every nation. There is one name under heaven by which we must be saved, and it is the sweetest name on earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father.

Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. “What you heard from the beginning” is the original apostolic gospel, not new teaching (v. 7). “Abide” (menetō): remain, stay. Hold onto the original message; do not drift to novelties.

If what you heard from the beginning abides in you, then you too will abide in the Son and in the Father. The condition is structured as a promise. Holding the apostolic truth keeps us in union with God. Truth and fellowship with God go together (John 8:31; 15:7). Holding fast to right doctrine is not merely intellectual hygiene; it is the means of holding fast to the persons of the Trinity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep ourselves saved by holding onto doctrine through our own strength. God keeps us (5:18), through his word abiding in us.

What if what I heard at the beginning was wrong? From the beginning in John means the apostolic gospel, not whatever you happened to be taught first. Some people were raised on a distorted message: a gospel of works, of prosperity, of fear, or of a Jesus who was merely an example. Abiding in what was heard from the beginning means going back past your own beginning to the apostles’ beginning, the gospel written in the New Testament. If your first teachers were wrong, let Scripture correct them, and you will find yourself not drifting from the faith but arriving at it.

In a sentence. As for you, see that what you have heard from the beginning remains in you. If it does, you also will remain in the Son and in the Father.

On a Tuesday. Go back to the gospel this week. Read 1 Corinthians 15:1–8, the gospel Paul received and passed on, and let it settle in you again. Notice anything in your thinking that has drifted from it.

For worship. God has not hidden his truth or kept changing it. He gave it once for all to the saints through the apostles, and it is as fresh today as on the day of Pentecost. In that word the Father and the Son make their home with us, and we with them. The gospel we first believed is not the shallow end of the faith; it is the whole ocean.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the promise that he made to us—eternal life.

And this is the promise that he made to us. “Promise” (epangelia). “He” is Christ. The content of the apostolic message is reduced to its essential promise, and the promise is secured not by the believer’s faithfulness in holding it but by the faithfulness of the one who made it.

Eternal life. “Eternal life” (tēn zōēn tēn aiōnion) is not merely endless existence, which the lost also have, in a tragic sense, but the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, knowing the Father and the Son (John 17:3), now and for ever (5:11–13; John 10:28). The reward of abiding in the Son is eternal life. The eternal life is in the Son (5:11–12), so abiding in the Son is the way of possessing the promise. What the false teachers offer is a detour away from the one in whom the promise resides.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is only future. Believers have it now (5:12–13). It will be fully experienced at Christ’s return.

If I have eternal life now, why does it not feel like it? Because eternal life is first a relationship, not a sensation. It is knowing God (John 17:3), and that knowing is real on dull days as well as bright ones. It is like a seed in winter ground: alive, growing roots you cannot see. It shows itself in small ways: a love for God’s word, a hatred of sin, a care for his people, a hope that will not quite die. And the full flowering is still to come.
