Jesus said whoever believes has eternal life and has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Trust his word over your mood.

In a sentence. And this is what he promised us: eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Thank Christ for his promise of eternal life, which you already possess and will enjoy for ever. Then let it reshape one fear today: the fear of loss, of illness, of death. What can these take from someone who has the life of God?

For worship. He promised, and he cannot lie. The Son who is himself the life has given himself to us, and that life will never be taken back. Death will touch our bodies but not our life, because our life is hidden with Christ in God. When everything we have known has passed away, we will still be just beginning, and the life that started the day we believed will open out into an eternity of knowing him.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you.

I write these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you. “Trying to deceive” (planōntōn) means leading astray, and the present tense says they are actively trying. The false teachers were still at work, trying to win over those who remained. The word shares its root with we deceive ourselves (1:8): self-deception and active deception are two faces of the same spiritual disorder. Naming the threat clearly is an act of pastoral love; it equips the community to resist rather than absorb the false teaching out of misplaced charity.

Words John heard on the Mount of Olives. John was one of the four who asked Jesus privately about the end (Mark 13:3), and the Lord’s first words were a warning: see that no one leads you astray; many will come in my name and lead many astray (Mark 13:5–6). John uses the same verb here. Sixty years later the old disciple is doing what his Lord did, naming the danger before it strikes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the readers had been deceived. John writes to protect them before they are.

How do I recognise a deceiver if he seems sincere and kind? Remember that most deceivers are sincere; they have been deceived first (2 Timothy 3:13). Sincerity is not truth, and kindness is not orthodoxy. The most dangerous deceptions in the church are usually the ones not identified as deceptions, because they arrive wrapped in spiritual language and appealing sincerity. Watch what is said about Christ, about sin, and about Scripture. Notice whether the teaching draws you to Christ and his people, or to the teacher and his group. Be wary when you are told the church has missed something only this teacher sees. And do not judge alone; take it to faithful pastors.

In a sentence. I am writing these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray.

On a Tuesday. Be alert to anyone trying to lead you away from the truth about Christ, whether in person, in books or online. Look at what you have listened to or watched this week, and ask whether it made Christ larger or smaller to you.

For worship. The Good Shepherd knows the wolves by name and is not deceived by their clothing. He has given us his word and his Spirit, and he has given us shepherds to warn us. More than that, he himself holds us. No deceiver can lead astray one whom the Father has given to the Son, because the Shepherd goes after his sheep and brings them home on his shoulders, rejoicing.

verseByVerse.quote: But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the anointing that you received from him abides in you, and you have no need that anyone should teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about everything, and is true, and is no lie—just as it has taught you, abide in him.

But the anointing that you received from him abides in you. “Anointing” (chrisma) is the Holy Spirit, as in verse 20. “Abides”: the Spirit remains permanently (John 14:16–17). He is not a visitor who comes for good meetings and leaves on bad days.

And you have no need that anyone should teach you. In context, John means: you do not need the false teachers, with their claims to new, higher knowledge. You already have the Spirit and the apostolic truth.

But as his anointing teaches you about everything. “Teaches” (didaskei). The Spirit teaches believers, guiding them into the truth (John 14:26; 16:13), not by giving new revelation, but by illuminating the apostolic word, confirming it in their hearts, and enabling them to discern error. He teaches about everything that pertains to salvation and godliness.

And is true, and is no lie. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). His teaching is the opposite of the deceivers’.

Just as it has taught you, abide in him. “Abide in him” means in Christ. The Spirit’s teaching always leads to Christ. The remedy for every form of false teaching is not intellectual victory but sustained union with the Son, kept by the Spirit, anchored in the word received from the beginning.

Where Christians differ: does this verse mean believers do not need teachers? Some have used this verse to reject all church teaching, or to claim private revelations from the Spirit. Verdict: John himself is teaching them in this very letter. Christ gave teachers to the church (Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 2:2). John means they do not need the false teachers’ new knowledge, because the Spirit has given them the true knowledge through the apostolic gospel. The Spirit does not give new revelation that contradicts or adds to Scripture; he illuminates Scripture and confirms its truth to the heart. Every claim to Spirit-given teaching must be tested by the apostolic word (4:1–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be independent of the church or of faithful teachers. It means they are not dependent on human teachers in the way the false teachers claimed, as if the Spirit were not enough.

What about when I feel the Spirit has told me something? Test it by Scripture, humbly. The Spirit who inspired the Bible does not contradict it, and he no longer adds to it, since the canon is closed. He does give believers conviction of sin, assurance, comfort, and wisdom to apply his word, and he guides through his word and through providence. But an inner impression is not a revelation with authority over anyone else, and it can come from our own desires. If a feeling leads you toward something Scripture forbids, it is not the Spirit. If it leads you to obey what Scripture says, follow it gladly, and say I believe God wants this, not God told me.

In a sentence. As for you, the anointing you received from him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things, and as that anointing is real, not counterfeit, just as it has taught you, remain in him.

On a Tuesday. Before you read Scripture today, pray a short prayer for the Spirit to open your eyes (Psalm 119:18). Then read slowly, expecting him to teach you, and write down one thing he shows you about Christ.

For worship. The Spirit of truth lives in the weakest believer. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation, who overshadowed Mary, who raised Jesus from the dead, has made his home in us to teach us Christ. He is the anointing that never runs dry and never lies, and he will never stop pointing us to the Son until we see him face to face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–29 — Abide in Him: The Returning King and the Family Likeness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by looking to Christ’s return. John urges his dear children to remain in Christ now, so that when he appears they will meet him with confidence instead of shrinking from him in shame at his coming. Then he introduces a theme that will run through the rest of the letter: because God is righteous, everyone who practises righteousness shows the family likeness of one who has been born of him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Abide in him

Abide in Christ so as to have confidence at his coming. Those born of the righteous God practise righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Christ’s appearing was still ahead.

Now: Live now as someone who will meet him face to face.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, little children, abide in him, so that when he appears we may have confidence and not shrink from him in shame at his coming.

And now, little children, abide in him. “Abide” (menete): keep remaining. The command that sums up the chapter. The exhortation to abide has gathered force through the chapter (vv. 6, 10, 24, 27) and now reaches its grounding in the end of history.

So that when he appears. “Appears” (phanerōthē) means is revealed, made visible. It is the same word as 1:2, where the life appeared in the incarnation. He appeared once in humility; he will appear again in glory. This is Christ’s second coming, visible and public, the event toward which the whole Christian life is oriented.

We may have confidence. “Confidence” (parrēsian) means boldness, freedom of speech, openness: in the ancient city, the right of a citizen to speak freely in the assembly, with nothing to fear. Like a child running to greet a returning father, not hiding. John includes himself: we may have confidence.

And not shrink from him in shame at his coming. “Shrink in shame” (aischynthōmen) means be put to shame, shrink back ashamed. Those who have not abided in him will be ashamed. “Coming” (parousia) is arrival, presence, the word used of a king’s official visit to a city, and this is the only use of the word in John’s writings. The shame is not punishment imposed from outside alone but the inevitable horror of meeting the one whose commands you spent your life ignoring.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be condemned if they are not perfect. It means those who abide in Christ will meet him with joyful confidence, not guilty fear.

Will I be ashamed when he comes because of my sins? Not if you are in him. Your sins were judged at the cross, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The confidence John speaks of is not earned by perfection but rests on abiding: trusting him, staying near him, walking in the light with your sins confessed. There may be things in your life you will wish you had done differently, and some work may be lost (1 Corinthians 3:15). But the believer will meet his Lord as a child meets a father coming home, not as a criminal meets a judge. Live now in the way you will be glad of then.

In a sentence. And now, dear children, continue in him, so that when he appears we may be confident and unashamed before him at his coming.

On a Tuesday. Ask: if Christ appeared this evening, what would I wish I had done today? Do it. Is there a sin you would want to have confessed, a person you would want to have forgiven, a word you would want to have spoken? Do not leave it until tomorrow.

For worship. He is coming. The one who appeared in a manger will appear in the sky, and every eye will see him. For his enemies that day will be terror. For his own it will be the homecoming they have waited for all their lives, when the bridegroom comes for the bride and the king enters his city. Those who have stayed close to him will run to meet him unashamed, because the one they meet is the one who covered all their shame.

verseByVerse.quote: If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you know that he is righteous, you may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him.

If you know that he is righteous. “He” is Christ (v. 1) or God the Father, since born of him refers to the Father. “Righteous” (dikaios). This verse is a hinge connecting chapter 2 to chapter 3.

You may be sure that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of him. “Practices righteousness” (poiōn tēn dikaiosynēn) is does righteousness, present tense: habitually. “Has been born of him” (ex autou gegennētai) is perfect tense: has been begotten and remains so. This is the first mention of new birth in 1 John. Note the order: being born of God comes first; practising righteousness follows as the evidence. The new birth is not merely a change of legal status but a change of nature: the divine life implanted in the believer tends toward the character of the one who gave it. Children resemble their Father.

The likeness of the Son. John has just called Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1), and now he speaks of being born of the righteous one without stopping to say whether he means the Father or the Son, because their righteousness is one. The family likeness God is producing in his children is the likeness of his Son, whom he has made the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). When a child of God does what is right, it is the life of the Firstborn showing in a younger brother.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the perfectly righteous are born again. It means a settled pattern of righteous living shows that one is God’s child.

Must I have had a dramatic born-again experience? No. New birth is God’s work, done once, often silently: the wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes (John 3:8). Some can name the day; many raised in Christian homes cannot remember a time when they did not trust Christ. What matters is not the memory of the birth but the evidence of the life. A man does not prove he was born by remembering his birthday but by being alive. If you trust Christ and are growing, however slowly, in doing what is right, you have been born of him.

In a sentence. If you know that he is righteous, you know that everyone who does what is right has been born of him.

On a Tuesday. Look for the family likeness this week. Where do you see your Father’s righteousness showing in you, in honesty, in kindness, in faithfulness? Thank him for it. And look for it in another believer and tell him so.

For worship. God has children. The Righteous One has begotten sons and daughters out of the dead and the unrighteous, and he has put his own life in them. They do not yet look much like him, but they will. He has never yet failed to raise a child to his likeness, and he will finish what he started, until the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13:43).

2.theology:
Advocacy and Propitiation. The paired terms of 2:1–2 give us the two aspects of Christ's saving work seen from different angles. As advocate, he represents us before the Father — our case is in his hands, and he is qualified to plead it because he is righteous. As propitiation, he has already dealt with the ground of the accusation — the wrath of God against our sin has been absorbed at the cross. These are not two separate acts but two perspectives on the one act of the cross. The same sacrifice that satisfied divine justice now grounds our ongoing access to divine mercy. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is both objective (propitiation — something accomplished outside us, in history, on a cross) and applied (advocacy — an ongoing ministry of Christ on our behalf). Both are necessary; together they produce the settled assurance John wants his readers to have.

The Three Tests. John's three tests — obedience (2:3–6), love (2:9–11), and belief (2:22–23) — are not a checklist for earning assurance but symptoms of new birth. Just as a doctor looks for signs of life, John looks for the signs that genuine regeneration has occurred. These tests are not meant to produce anxiety but clarity: not "have I been good enough?" but "is there genuine fruit of the Spirit in my life?" The tests are cumulative and mutually reinforcing — genuine obedience produces love; genuine love flows from right belief; genuine belief manifests in how we treat the brothers and sisters.
2.examples:
Then: The antichrists who had left the community had claimed a superior knowledge of God. Their departure seemed, to some, like the enlightened ones leaving the unenlightened behind. John's response is pastoral and pointed: the ones who left proved by their leaving that they were never truly of the community (2:19). This is not cruelty but theology — genuine new birth produces perseverance. The ones who remained, confused and perhaps diminished, were the ones who had "the anointing from the Holy One" and knew the truth (2:20). The test of authenticity is not sophistication but faithfulness to the beginning.

Now: We live in a world of novelty — new spiritualities, new therapies, new paths to self-actualization. The church is perpetually tempted to trade the apostolic gospel for something more culturally current, more psychologically satisfying, more intellectually respectable. John's word is the same: let what you heard from the beginning abide in you. The gospel does not need to be updated; it needs to be inhabited. The depth we seek is not found by moving beyond the cross — it is found by going deeper into it.

3.title: Children of God, Love in Deed
3.text: <sup>1</sup>See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.<sup>2</sup>Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.<sup>3</sup>And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.<sup>4</sup>Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.<sup>5</sup>You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.<sup>6</sup>No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.<sup>7</sup>Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.<sup>8</sup>Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.<sup>9</sup>No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.<sup>10</sup>By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.<sup>11</sup>For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.<sup>12</sup>We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.<sup>13</sup>Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.<sup>14</sup>We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.<sup>15</sup>Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.<sup>16</sup>By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.<sup>17</sup>But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?<sup>18</sup>Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.<sup>19</sup>By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him;<sup>20</sup>for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.<sup>21</sup>Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;<sup>22</sup>and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.<sup>23</sup>And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.<sup>24</sup>Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 opens in wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” We are God’s children now, and when Christ appears we shall be like him. That hope makes us pure.

Then John shows what God’s children look like. They do not live in sin, because God’s seed abides in them and the Son came to destroy the devil’s works. And they love one another, not in words only, but in deeds, as Christ laid down his life for us. When the heart condemns, God is greater than our heart. His command is to believe in his Son and love one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Children of God: Now and Not Yet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John commands us to look: “See what kind of love”. The phrase suggests something foreign and astonishing. God calls us his children, “and so we are”. The world does not recognise us, because it did not recognise him. We are children now; what we will be is not yet seen. But when Christ appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone with that hope purifies himself now.
verseByVerse.theology:
Children Now, Like Him Then

We are God’s children now; when Christ appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. That hope purifies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Some claimed they had already arrived.

Now: We become what we behold; set your hope on his appearing.

verseByVerse.quote: See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are. The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him.

Meaning first. 1 John 3 is about the children of God: who they are, how they live, and how they can be sure. The Father’s love makes us his children now, and when Christ appears we will be like him, a hope that purifies (vv. 1–3). Sin is lawlessness; Christ appeared to take away sins and destroy the works of the devil, so no one born of God keeps on sinning as a settled practice, because God’s seed remains in him (vv. 4–10). Love for the brothers, unlike Cain’s murderous hatred, shows that we have passed from death to life (vv. 11–15). Love is defined by Christ laying down his life for us, and it acts, in deed and truth, toward a brother in need (vv. 16–18). So we can reassure our hearts before God, who is greater than our hearts, pray with confidence as we believe in his Son and love one another, and know that he abides in us by the Spirit he has given (vv. 19–24). It is a chapter that begins with the Father’s love and ends with the Father’s Spirit living in us, and everything between is the family likeness.

See what kind of love the Father has given to us. “See” (idete) is behold, look!: an imperative demanding attention, an exclamation of wonder. John is not filing a doctrine; he is stopping in the road and pointing. “What kind of” (potapēn) originally meant from what country: how foreign, how astonishing. It is used in the New Testament of things extraordinary; the disciples used it of the man whom winds and sea obeyed, what sort of man is this? (Matthew 8:27). This love does not come from the world; it comes from outside it. It is a love from another country, utterly unlike human love. “Given” (dedōken) is perfect tense: has given, and the gift remains. Love here is not a mood in God but a gift that has been handed over and not taken back.

That we should be called children of God. “Called” (klēthōmen): named, given the title. “Children” (tekna) means born ones. Not merely adopted (though that is true, Romans 8:15), but born of God (2:29), sharing his nature. Both pictures are needed. Adoption says we have the legal standing of sons; birth says we have the life of sons. A king might adopt an orphan and give him his name, but he cannot give him his blood. God does both.

And so we are. “And so we are” (kai esmen): and we are! John adds the two most important words in the verse, as though he cannot help interrupting himself. Not just a title, but a reality. Some later manuscripts omit it; the earliest include it. The calling is not a courtesy title but a declaration of fact. We are truly God’s children, now, on the day we read this, with all our failures in plain view.

The reason why the world does not know us is that it did not know him. “The world” is unbelieving humanity. “Does not know” means does not recognise, understand or accept. The world did not recognise Jesus as the Son of God (John 1:10–11); so it does not recognise his children. Our true identity is hidden from the world, as his was. Having rejected the Father, it cannot recognise his family likeness in us.

The prince in the rags. Think of the old stories of a king’s son who travels his father’s kingdom in disguise. The innkeepers are rude to him, the soldiers push him aside, and no one guesses. He is no less the prince for being unrecognised. The day will come when he rides back through the same towns with his father’s banners, and everyone who pushed him aside will know. That is the believer in the world. The Son himself came like that: born in a borrowed stable, a carpenter in a despised town, crucified as a criminal, and the world did not know him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people are God’s children by nature. All are his creatures, but only those born of him by faith in Christ are his children (John 1:12–13; 8:42–44).

What if I do not feel like a child of God? Then look again at what John says. He does not say, see how you feel. He says, see what love the Father has given. Your sonship rests on his gift, not on your feelings, and the gift was given to those who received his Son and believed in his name (John 1:12). If you trust Christ, you are God’s child on the bad days as fully as on the good. Children do not stop being children when they are sulking, ill or ashamed. Say to yourself what John says: and so we are. Then speak to God as Father, even if the word feels strange. The Spirit teaches us to say it (Romans 8:15).

Should I want the world to like me? Wanting to be at peace with people is good (Romans 12:18), and Christians should be the kindest neighbours on the street. But you cannot make being understood by the world your aim, because the world did not understand your Lord. If people misread you because you will not join in their sin, or because you love a Christ they do not know, do not take it as a sign that you have failed. It is the family likeness showing. Be gentle, be honest, and be content to be known by your Father.

In a sentence. See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know him.

On a Tuesday. Stop and marvel at this before you open your inbox: you are God’s child. When you pray today, begin with the word Father and stay with it for a moment. And when someone treats you as unimportant, remember whose child you are, and let it make you humble rather than proud. A child of a king has nothing to prove.

For worship. The God who needs nothing has chosen to have children. He looked at rebels who had run from his house and wasted his gifts, and he did not merely pardon them and send them on their way; he brought them into his family, gave them his name, put his life in them, and seated them at his table. It cost him his only Son, who became a child of man so that the children of men might become children of God. Behold what manner of love: the Son left his Father’s house for our far country, so that runaways might be brought home as sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.

Beloved, we are God’s children now. “Now” (nyn) is present reality, not merely future hope. John holds the now and the not yet of Christian existence in perfect tension.

And what we will be has not yet appeared. “Not yet appeared” (oupō ephanerōthē) means not yet been revealed. Our final state is not yet visible. We are children now, but the full glory of what that means is hidden (Romans 8:18–19; Colossians 3:3–4). An acorn is a real oak in the making, but nobody looking at it would guess the tree.

But we know that when he appears we shall be like him. “When he appears” (ean phanerōthē) is Christ’s return (2:28). “Like him” (homoioi autō) means like Christ in his glorified humanity: holy, immortal, with resurrection bodies (Philippians 3:21; 1 Corinthians 15:49; Romans 8:29). Not divine in essence, but conformed to his image. And notice the word we know. John does not know what we will look like, but he knows whom we will look like.

Because we shall see him as he is. “See him as he is” (opsometha auton kathōs estin). This is what the church has called the beatific vision, the sight of God that makes us blessed. Now we see dimly (1 Corinthians 13:12); then face to face (Revelation 22:4; Matthew 5:8). Seeing him will transform us. As Moses’ face shone after seeing God’s glory (Exodus 34:29), so seeing Christ fully will make us fully like him. The direction of cause is crucial: the vision of Christ produces the likeness, not the other way round. We do not become like him and then qualify to see him. We see him, and are changed. The glorified Christ, seen face to face without the distortion of our present fallen sight, will accomplish in an instant what a lifetime of sanctification has been working toward.

Becoming what we behold. It happens already in a small way. People grow like what they gaze at: married couples come to share expressions; children pick up a parent’s laugh; a man who watches cruelty becomes cruel. Paul says that even now, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The final sight will finish the work. The psalmist saw it from far off: when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness (Psalm 17:15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become God or lose our individual identity. It means we will be perfected in his likeness.

Will I still be me? Yes, more than you have ever been. The risen Jesus was recognisably himself: he ate fish, showed his wounds, called Mary by name. Moses and Elijah were recognisable on the mountain. Being made like Christ does not erase your personality any more than the sun erases the colours of a stained-glass window; it makes them shine. Everything sin has bent will be straightened, and everything God made you to be will be completed. You will be like him, and fully yourself, and you will know and be known.

In a sentence. Dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. But we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is.

On a Tuesday. When you look in the mirror and see age, weakness, or the marks of sin, say: this is not yet what I will be. And when you are discouraged by how slowly you are changing, remember who will finish it. Spend five minutes today simply looking at Christ in a Gospel passage. It is how the likeness grows.

For worship. We shall see him. The eyes that have wept at gravesides and strained to read the promises in the dark will look on the face of the Son of God, with nothing between. No mirror, no dimness, no faith struggling to hold on, but sight. And in that seeing we will be made like him, all at once and for ever. There is no greater thing a creature can receive than this: to see the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, and to be changed into his likeness by the sight.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.

And everyone who thus hopes in him. “Hopes” (echōn tēn elpida) is literally has this hope. “In him” (ep’ autō) means set on him: hope fixed on Christ. Biblical hope is not wishful thinking but certainty not yet seen: an anchor, not a guess.

Purifies himself as he is pure. “Purifies” (hagnizei) means makes holy, cleanses, and the present tense means keeps purifying. It is the word used of ritual purification before a festival (John 11:55), when pilgrims went up to Jerusalem early to make themselves ready for the Passover. Hope of seeing Christ leads to preparing for that meeting. “As he is pure” (hagnos): Christ is the standard, not “as pure as humanly possible” but with Christ’s own purity as the target. Eschatology produces ethics: true hope in Christ’s return always leads to holy living (2 Peter 3:11–14; Titus 2:12–13). Hope is not passive; it pulls the future into the present.

The bride before the wedding. Think of a bride in the week before her wedding. Nobody needs to tell her to get ready. She is not anxious that the groom will reject her; he has already chosen her. She gets ready because she is going to see him, and she wants to be lovely for him. That is the purifying of this verse: not fear of rejection, but the joy of an approaching meeting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we purify ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1:7), and the Spirit sanctifies. But we actively cooperate, turning from sin and pursuing holiness (2 Corinthians 7:1). Nor is it perfectionism in the sense of achieved sinlessness (1:8 has ruled that out), but orientation: the hope of seeing Christ trains the moral eye on his character as the goal.

How does hoping in Christ’s return actually make me purer? By changing what you want and what you fear. If you truly believe you will see him, soon and face to face, the things that compete with him start to look small, and the sins you cherish start to look like stains on a wedding dress. Hope also gives you staying power: you can say no to a pleasure now because you know a greater joy is coming. Practically, think about his return on purpose. Read the passages about it (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; Revelation 21–22), sing about it, and ask of each choice whether you would be glad of it when he appears.

In a sentence. All who have this hope in him keep purifying themselves, just as he is pure.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would you want to have dealt with? Deal with it now, as one preparing to see him. A message to send, a habit to break, a thing to give back. Then go about your day as a pilgrim on the way to the feast.

For worship. He is pure. In the whole of his life there was not one unclean thought, one false motive, one stain, and the Father looked on him and was well pleased. That pure one is coming back for a people he has washed, and he will present them to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle. Our hope is not that we will make ourselves fit to meet him, but that he who is pure has promised to make us like him, and he has already begun.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Sin, the Devil, and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This passage must be read carefully, or it will either terrify the true believer or comfort the false one. John speaks of two families, known by how they live. The devil has sinned from the beginning; the Son of God appeared to destroy his works. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives. John is not teaching sinless perfection (1:8–10), but that the new birth changes the direction of a life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The New Birth

The Son appeared to take away sins and to destroy the works of the devil. God’s seed abides in those born of him, so that sin is no longer the settled pattern of their lives.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Claimed spiritual knowledge was being used to excuse sin.

Now: Avoid both errors: tolerating sin as normal, and thinking that any sin proves you are not born again.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who makes a practice of sinning also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness.

Everyone who makes a practice of sinning. “Makes a practice of sinning” (ho poiōn tēn hamartian) is literally the one doing sin, present tense: habitually, as a way of life. It is the contrast with practises righteousness (2:29). John is describing the person whose life is oriented toward self-government rather than God’s government.

Also practices lawlessness; sin is lawlessness. “Lawlessness” (anomia) is rebellion against God’s law, defiance. John defines sin theologically before he defines it morally. Sin is not a mere mistake or weakness, nor primarily a social infraction or a psychological disorder; it is the assertion of self-rule against the claim of God. The false teachers may have treated sin as trivial; John defines it as defiance of God. And lawlessness has end-time overtones: the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Persistent sin aligns a person with the antichrist. Every act of sin, however small it may appear, shares in the spirit of rebellion that is the deepest nature of the fallen age.

The small rebellion. We usually measure sin by its damage: a lie that hurt no one seems minor, a theft that was never noticed seems trivial. John measures it by its direction. A child who is told not to touch the fire and touches it has not done much harm if he was not burnt, but he has done something serious: he has decided that his will outranks his father’s. That is every sin. The size of the act may vary; the shape is always the same. It says to God, I will decide.

Not my will. Sin says to God, I will decide. The whole life of the Son of God said the opposite, and nowhere more plainly than in Gethsemane, with the cup of wrath before him: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). The first Adam reached for the fruit to have his own way; the last Adam bowed to the cross to do his Father’s. Lawlessness is answered not by a better rule but by a perfectly obedient Son, who then took the place of the lawless.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sin a believer commits is deliberate rebellion. But all sin, at root, is a departure from God’s will.

If all sin is lawlessness, are all sins equally bad? All sins are rebellion, and any one of them is enough to condemn us apart from Christ (James 2:10). But Scripture also teaches that some sins are more serious than others: in their effects, in the light sinned against, and in the hardness of heart they show (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48; the Westminster Larger Catechism, question 150). A flash of impatience and a lifetime of cruelty are both sin, but they are not the same. Both truths keep us healthy: we never call any sin small, and we never treat a struggling brother’s weakness as if it were a monster’s crime.

In a sentence. Everyone who sins breaks the law; in fact, sin is lawlessness.

On a Tuesday. Pick a sin you tend to call minor: a white lie, an unkind joke, a spending habit, a lazy hour. Ask what it says to God. Then confess it under its true name, and thank him for forgiveness.

For worship. God’s law is not a cage but the shape of his own goodness, and to rebel against it is to rebel against the most beautiful being there is. Yet the Lawgiver himself came under his own law for the lawless. He was born under the law, kept it perfectly, and was numbered with the transgressors. The only one who never rebelled bore the punishment of rebels, so that rebels might become sons.

verseByVerse.quote: You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know that he appeared in order to take away sins, and in him there is no sin.

You know that he appeared in order to take away sins. “Appeared” (ephanerōthē) means was revealed: his incarnation. The clause is purposive: this is why he came. The atonement is not an afterthought or a divine improvisation; it is the mission. “Take away” (arē) means lift up, carry away, remove, as in John 1:29: “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” Not merely to cover but to remove: the guilt lifted from the sinner and placed on the Son. Christ came to remove sin: its guilt by his death, its power by his Spirit. To continue in sin contradicts the very purpose of his coming.

The goat into the wilderness. Israel had seen it every year. On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid both hands on the head of a live goat, confessed over it all the sins of the people, and sent it away into the wilderness, carrying their iniquities to a solitary land (Leviticus 16:21–22). The people watched it go until it was out of sight. John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, there is the one who carries it away. He took our sins out of sight, and they are not coming back.

And in him there is no sin. Christ is sinless (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). The sinless one came to remove sin. The sinless one can bear the sins of others without being destroyed by them; the pure one can absorb the impurity without becoming impure. The sinlessness of Christ is not a theological curiosity; it is the load-bearing foundation of the atonement. A drowning man cannot rescue another drowning man. Those united to him cannot be at home in sin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ removed all sin from believers instantly. He removed its guilt completely and is removing its presence progressively, and will remove it entirely at his return (v. 2).

How could Jesus be truly tempted if he had no sin? Temptation is not sin; yielding is. Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). He felt hunger, weariness, the pull of escape from suffering, and the devil’s offers were real. In fact he felt the force of temptation more than we do, because he never gave way. A man who gives in after a minute never learns how heavy the pressure can become; Jesus held out to the end. That is why he can sympathise with us. He knows the full weight, and he can help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18).

In a sentence. But you know that he appeared so that he might take away our sins. And in him is no sin.

On a Tuesday. When a sin from your past comes back to mind, picture it carried away out of sight, as the goat went into the wilderness. Then refuse to go out into the desert to fetch it back. What Christ has taken away, do not pick up again.

For worship. The Lamb of God came. The holy one, in whom there was no sin, came into a world thick with it, and walked through it untouched, and then took it all on himself. He who knew no sin was made sin for us. He carried it away, out of sight, out of mind, out of God’s record, and he did it because this was why he had come. Not one sin laid on him has ever been laid on his people again.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one who abides in him keeps on sinning; no one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him.

No one who abides in him keeps on sinning. The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse. “Keeps on sinning” (hamartanei) is present tense: continually sins, sins as a pattern of life. Those living in union with Christ do not live in persistent, unrepented sin. This verse must be read in the light of 1:8–10, or it will produce either false assurance in the person who sins at peace and claims to abide, or false despair in the struggling believer who concludes he cannot be born again. John is speaking of habitual orientation, not occasional failure.

No one who keeps on sinning has either seen him or known him. “Has seen” (heōraken) and “known” (egnōken) are both perfect tense. Spiritual seeing and knowing. Someone who lives a life of habitual sin has never truly encountered Christ. Nobody meets the Lord and goes on exactly as before. Zacchaeus met him at lunch and gave away half his goods by the afternoon.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer never sins. John has said that would be self-deception (1:8–10), and he has provided for believers who sin (2:1–2). The present tense indicates ongoing, characteristic practice. A believer may fall into sin, even serious sin, but will not remain comfortable in it as a way of life.

I have fought the same sin for years. Am I keeping on sinning? The key word is comfortable. John is describing a person who sins and does not mind, who has made peace with it and stopped fighting. If you hate this sin, confess it, grieve over it and keep fighting it, even after many defeats, you are not the person in this verse. The fight itself is evidence that you have seen him. Paul describes exactly that war in Romans 7, and he was an apostle. Keep fighting with every means God gives: Scripture, prayer, accountability, removing occasions. And keep running to Christ each time you fall. The person who has given up the fight is the one in danger.

In a sentence. No one who lives in him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has either seen him or known him.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you have settled into as a habit? Union with Christ calls you out of it. Confess it and ask for his power to change. Then take one concrete step today that makes the sin harder: tell someone, change a route, delete an app, move the bottle.

For worship. To see Christ is to be changed. He has never yet been truly met by a sinner who went away unmoved. The woman at the well ran into town; Matthew rose from his tax booth and never went back; the persecutor fell on the road and rose an apostle. His beauty breaks the grip of sin, and his presence makes the old life taste of ashes. Those who abide in him are being changed by the one in whom they abide.
verseByVerse.note: The verbs point to a settled habit of sin, not a single lapse (compare 1:8–2:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous.

Little children, let no one deceive you. “Deceive” (planatō) is lead astray. The warning is pointed. The false teachers taught that one could be righteous without living righteously, offering a spirituality that could be claimed without an ethical pattern to match. John will not allow the separation.

Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, as he is righteous. “Practices righteousness” (ho poiōn tēn dikaiosynēn) is habitually does what is right. “Is righteous” (dikaios estin). The one who habitually does right shows that he is righteous, like Christ. Not that doing right makes him righteous (justification is by faith alone), but that doing right reveals the reality of a righteous standing and a renewed nature (2:29). The practice is the evidence of the status, not its cause, and the declaration always produces its evidence. And the standard, as he is righteous, is Christ himself: the direction of the life is toward his righteousness, because his righteousness is what has been given and is now being reproduced.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our righteous deeds are the basis of our righteousness before God. Christ’s righteousness credited to us is the basis (Philippians 3:9). Our deeds are the evidence.

How can I be righteous and still sin? Because righteous means two things in the Christian life, and both are true of you. Before God’s court you are counted righteous, completely and for ever, because Christ’s righteousness is credited to you (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). That never grows or shrinks. And in your life you are being made righteous, gradually, by the Spirit, and that does grow, unevenly. Luther summed it up in a phrase: at the same time righteous and a sinner. The first is the root; the second is the fruit. Rest on the first, and pursue the second.

In a sentence. Dear children, do not let anyone lead you astray. The one who does what is right is righteous, just as he is righteous.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone, including the voice in your own head, who says it does not matter how you live as long as you believe. Ask where in your life faith and practice have drifted apart, and bring the practice back into line, starting today.

For worship. Christ is righteous, wholly and without remainder, and he has not kept his righteousness to himself. He has wrapped his people in it as a robe, so that God sees them in his Son. And then he has done more: he has begun to make them what he has declared them to be. The one who clothed us will also fit us to the clothes, until his righteousness is not only on us but in us, and shines out of us for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil, for the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil.

Whoever makes a practice of sinning is of the devil. “Of the devil” (ek tou diabolou) means from the devil, belonging to him. Not that he is literally born of the devil, but that he shares the devil’s character and belongs to his family (John 8:44). The family of the devil is defined by pattern.

For the devil has been sinning from the beginning. “From the beginning” (ap’ archēs): from the beginning of his rebellion, or from the beginning of human history (Genesis 3). Sin is the devil’s nature. He has been sinning continuously, unrelentingly, unrepentantly, and those whose lives share that pattern bear his family mark.

The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil. “Destroy” (lysē) means loose, undo, dismantle, break up, take apart at the joints. It is the word for untying a knot, breaking up a building, releasing a prisoner. “Works of the devil”: sin, deception, death, bondage. Christ came to undo all of it (Hebrews 2:14; Colossians 2:15; Genesis 3:15). The Son of God entered the domain the devil thought he owned and began dismantling everything the devil had built: sin’s power, death’s reign, accusation’s hold, bondage’s chains. He has already won the decisive victory at the cross, and will complete it at his return. The incarnation is cosmic warfare, and its outcome is already determined.

The demolition in the Gospels. Watch the Son of God at work and you see the devil’s works coming apart. A man in the synagogue cried out and the unclean spirit left him. A woman bent for eighteen years, whom Satan had bound, was loosed and stood up straight (Luke 13:16), and the word Jesus uses is the same family of words as John’s. A widow’s son on his bier sat up and spoke. Lepers were cleansed and the dead raised. Every miracle was a brick pulled out of the devil’s wall. Then at the cross the foundations went.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers who sin belong to the devil. Habitual, unrepentant sin as a way of life reveals the devil’s family. Believers who sin and repent belong to God.

If Christ has destroyed the devil’s works, why is there still so much evil? Because the victory is decisive but not yet complete. A war can be won in one battle while fighting goes on for months afterwards; the enemy is beaten but has not yet laid down his arms. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15), and he is now dismantling the devil’s works in every life he saves. At his return the demolition will be finished, and the devil will be thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10). So do not fear the devil as though he were Christ’s equal. Resist him, firm in your faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

In a sentence. The one who keeps on sinning is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the devil’s work.

On a Tuesday. Name one work of the devil still standing in your life: a lie you believe, a fear that rules you, a habit that binds you, a bitterness that will not let go. Bring it to the Son of God by name and ask him to take it apart. He came for exactly that.

For worship. The Son of God came to tear down. Every chain the devil forged, every lie he told, every grave he dug, Christ has come to undo. He walked into the strong man’s house, bound him, and plundered it. He went down into death and broke it open from the inside. Every work of the devil is under demolition, and the Son who is doing it has never yet lost a single one of his people or left a single job unfinished.

verseByVerse.quote: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God's seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him; and he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God.

No one born of God makes a practice of sinning. “Born of God” (ho gegennēmenos ek tou theou) is perfect tense: has been born and remains so. “Makes a practice of sinning” (hamartian ou poiei) is does not do sin habitually. The new birth is not a past transaction now complete and finished with; it is an ongoing reality, the divine life continuing to work in the one it has entered.

For God’s seed abides in him. “Seed” (sperma) is God’s life implanted in the believer at the new birth: his nature (2 Peter 1:4), the Holy Spirit, or the word of God (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). Probably the divine life itself, given through the word by the Spirit. “Abides” (menei) means remains permanently. It does not die or leave. The image of seed conveys both origin, born of God, and an ongoing principle of life. A seed planted does not stay a seed; it grows, pushes through soil, and in the end it bears the likeness of the plant it came from.

And he cannot keep on sinning, because he has been born of God. “Cannot” (ou dynatai) is is not able. “Keep on sinning” (hamartanein) is a present infinitive: continue sinning as a lifestyle. The new nature makes persistent, comfortable sin impossible. A child of God cannot settle down in sin, because God’s life in him resists it. Sin in the believer’s life is always an anomaly, always resisted, never domesticated. This is also a promise of perseverance: the seed remains.

Kept by the one born of God. Why does the seed remain? John answers near the end of the letter: everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him (5:18). The one who protects there is most naturally the Son, born of God in a unique and eternal sense. The seed does not survive because the soil is good; it survives because the Son of God stands guard over it. The perseverance of the child rests on the faithfulness of the eternal Son.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach sinless perfection? Some read cannot sin as teaching that a born-again person is incapable of sinning at all, or that sinless perfection is possible. Verdict: John has already said that anyone who claims to be sinless is deceived (1:8, 10), and he provides for believers who sin (2:1). The present tense verbs in chapter 3 indicate habitual practice. A child of God cannot continue in a settled lifestyle of unrepented sin, because God’s seed in him makes it impossible. He may fall, but he will not stay down. He will be grieved, convicted and restored. This is the Reformed doctrine of perseverance and progressive sanctification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin, or that a single sin proves one is not born of God. It means sin is no longer the believer’s master or his comfortable habitat (Romans 6:14).

What about a believer who falls into serious sin, like David? David committed adultery and arranged a murder, and for months he seems to have covered it up. Scripture does not soften it. But God did not leave him there: he sent Nathan, and David was broken, confessed, and wrote Psalm 51. That is what the seed does. It does not stop a believer from falling, sometimes terribly, but it will not let him stay at peace in the mud. If you have fallen badly, the misery you feel is not proof that you are lost; it may be the seed at work. Come back the way David came: honestly, quickly, to the God of steadfast love.

In a sentence. No one who is born of God will continue to sin, because God’s seed remains in them; they cannot go on sinning, because they have been born of God.

On a Tuesday. When you sin today, notice the discomfort that follows: the unease, the loss of joy in prayer, the desire to put it right. Do not drown it out. Thank God for it, because it is the seed refusing to let you settle, and follow where it leads, back to him.

For worship. God does not plant and then walk away. The life he has put into his children is his own life, and it cannot die. It grows through droughts and storms; it pushes up through the hardest ground; it outlasts every fall. He who began a good work will bring it to completion. The seed of God in the weakest believer is stronger than all the sin that remains in him, and on the last day it will flower into the full likeness of his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil: whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother.

By this it is evident who are the children of God, and who are the children of the devil. “Evident” (phanera) means visible, manifest, plain. There are only two families. Every person belongs to one or the other (John 8:42–47). The difference shows in how they live. John allows no neutral ground, no third category, no comfortable middle of decent irreligion.

Whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother. Here the two tests meet: righteousness (vv. 4–10) and love, which John develops next (vv. 11–18). Righteousness and love go together. They are not two separate criteria but two aspects of the same life. Love is the heart of righteousness (Romans 13:8–10).

The Son who remains in the house. It was Jesus who first spoke of the devil as a father, to religious men who were trying to kill him (John 8:44). In the same conversation he told them how anyone moves from one family to the other: the slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:35–36). No one changes families by trying harder. The Son, who belongs in the Father’s house by right, brings slaves in with him and makes them sons.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can always tell with certainty who is a child of God by outward observation. God alone knows the heart. But the general pattern of a life reveals its family.

Are there really only two families? What about decent people who are not Christians? Scripture recognises that unbelievers can be kind, honest and brave; God restrains evil and gives common gifts to all (Matthew 5:45; Romans 2:14–15). We should honour such goodness and thank God for it. But John is asking a deeper question: not whether a person does good things, but to whom he belongs. Jesus said the same to very religious men (John 8:44). Outward decency does not make anyone a child of God; only new birth does (John 3:3). That is not an insult to our neighbours but the reason we must tell them about Christ.

In a sentence. This is how we know who the children of God are and who the children of the devil are: anyone who does not do what is right is not God’s child, nor is anyone who does not love their brother and sister.

On a Tuesday. Which family does your life resemble this week? Ask God to make your righteousness and love unmistakable. Ask one honest friend what in your life most clearly shows that you belong to Christ, and what most obscures it.

For worship. God has a family, and he knows every member of it by name. He has drawn them out of the devil’s household, where they were born, and adopted and begotten them into his own. The line between the two families is not drawn by birth or race or effort but by the grace of God in Christ, and it runs straight through the cross. On that line every child of the devil who comes is welcomed and made a child of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — Love One Another: The Cain Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John brings love down to earth: the brother in front of you. He starts with Cain, who hated and murdered his brother because Abel was righteous. That is why the world hates believers. Then comes the clearest definition of love in the New Testament: “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us.” The cross defines love, and obliges us to love the same way, starting with an open hand to a brother in need.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love Defined by the Cross

Cain hated his brother; Christ laid down his life for us. By this we know love, and we ought to lay down our lives for one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The world’s hatred was not to surprise the church.

Now: Love in deed and truth: an open hand to a brother in need.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.

For this is the message that you have heard from the beginning. “Message” (angelia), as in 1:5. The first message was that God is light; the second, that we love one another. “From the beginning” is from the first preaching of the gospel (2:7), John’s recurring marker that he is proclaiming not novelty but foundation. The love commandment is not a recent addition to the gospel or an advanced teaching for the spiritually mature; it is the apostolic message itself. The false teachers, with their claim to superior knowledge, had quietly moved beyond this basic command. John moves decisively back to it: this is the message, this, and not whatever else is being offered.

That we should love one another. “Love” (agapōmen) is keep loving. This is Jesus’ new commandment (John 13:34–35; 15:12, 17). It is not a supplement to the gospel but a summary of what the gospel produces in those who receive it. Jesus said it would be the badge by which the world would know his disciples. Not their buildings, not their learning, not their size: their love for one another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love only for believers. Christians love all people, even enemies (Matthew 5:44). But love for the family of God is a special mark of belonging to it.

Do I have to like every Christian? No, but you must love every Christian, and the two are not the same. Liking is about natural affinity: shared tastes, easy conversation, a sense of humour that fits yours. You will have that with some believers and not with others, and that is no sin. Love is a settled will for another’s good, shown in action, and it is commanded. You can love a brother you find tiresome by praying for him, helping him, defending his name, welcoming him, and forgiving him. Often, over years, liking follows. Even when it does not, love has done its work.

In a sentence. For this is the message you heard from the beginning: we should love one another.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the believers he has given you to love. Pray for one of them by name today, especially one you find harder to love. Then do something small and practical for him that he will never know came from you.

For worship. The God who commands love is love, and he has never commanded what he has not first done. Before he said love one another, he loved us; before the message was preached, the Son was given. The whole gospel is a message of love from the beginning, and in the church God is making a family that will love one another perfectly for ever, because they have been loved perfectly by him.

verseByVerse.quote: We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother's righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous.

We should not be like Cain, who was of the evil one. Cain is the first example of hatred in Scripture (Genesis 4:1–16), and John uses him as the negative example: not an impulsive crime of passion but the expression of a nature. “Of the evil one” (ek tou ponērou) means from the evil one: he belonged to the devil’s family (v. 10). The first child born in the world became the first murderer. The second child born in the world became the first martyr.

And murdered his brother. “Murdered” (esphaxen) means slaughtered, butchered, cut the throat; it is a word used of slaughtering sacrificial animals. A brutal word for a brutal act. And it is the word used in Revelation of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:6). Abel was slaughtered by hatred; the Lamb was slaughtered by hatred, and for haters.

And why did he murder him? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous. Cain was not provoked by Abel’s wrongdoing, but by his righteousness. God accepted Abel’s offering, which exposed Cain’s evil heart (Genesis 4:4–7; Hebrews 11:4). Evil hates good because good exposes it (John 3:19–20). Righteousness does not have to speak to accuse; its existence is accusation enough to those committed to evil. This explains why the world hates believers (v. 13): the light of a righteous life is experienced as condemnation by those who have chosen darkness, and the natural response is to put out the light.

God’s warning to Cain. Before the murder, God came to Cain and spoke to him, gently. Why are you angry? If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it (Genesis 4:6–7). God saw the hatred while it was still a feeling and offered a way out. Cain went to the field instead. Hatred almost always gets a warning, and the warning almost always comes early.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every conflict between believers is like Cain and Abel. But it warns that hatred begins with envy and resentment, and can end in murder.

Why did God accept Abel’s offering and not Cain’s? Scripture’s own answer is faith: by faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain (Hebrews 11:4). The difference was not first in the gift but in the heart. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and the fat portions, the best, in trust; Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground, and his life showed that his heart was not right with God (Genesis 4:3–5, 7). God looks at the person before the offering. That is why our worship is acceptable only through faith in Christ, the better sacrifice, whose blood speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24).

In a sentence. Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did he murder him? Because his own actions were evil and his brother’s were righteous.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone whose goodness makes you resentful: the colleague who is more conscientious, the sibling who visits your parents more, the Christian whose prayers sound more real? Confess it, and pray for them instead. Then, as Cain should have done, deal with your own heart rather than his.

For worship. Cain asked whether he was his brother’s keeper, with his brother’s blood still on the ground (Genesis 4:9). There is a Brother who never asked it. The firstborn Son of God took his brothers’ keeping on himself at the cost of his life; when they turned on him he did not curse them but died for them. The first brother killed because he hated righteousness; this Brother gives his righteousness away to the unrighteous. In his family hatred is answered with blood that turns enemies into brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you.

Do not be surprised, brothers. “Surprised” (thaumazete) means amazed, astonished, as in 1 Peter 4:12. The pastoral note is precise. The world’s hatred of genuine believers is not a sign of God’s disfavour or Christian failure; it is a consequence of being in the right family. John repeats Jesus’ warning as a defence against the surprise that destabilises.

That the world hates you. “Hates” (misei) is present tense: keeps on hating. As Cain hated Abel, the world hates the righteous. Jesus warned of it: if the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you (John 15:18–20; 17:14). The world’s hatred is evidence that believers belong to Christ, not to it. The appropriate response is not retaliation, which repeats Cain; not assimilation, which surrenders the difference that causes the friction; and not self-pity, which misreads the situation. It is the clear-eyed recognition that the world’s hatred confirms, rather than undermines, our belonging to a Father the world has rejected.

The first centuries. The early Christians knew this verse in their bodies. In the generation after John they were accused of atheism because they would not worship the emperor, of cannibalism because they spoke of eating Christ’s body, and of hatred of the human race because they kept apart from the temples and the games. Tertullian complained that if the Tiber flooded or the Nile failed to rise, the cry went up at once: the Christians to the lion. They were not surprised. They had been told.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every unbeliever hates every believer, or that Christians should be offensive. It means opposition from the world is normal, not strange.

What if the world does not hate me? Does that mean I am compromised? Not necessarily. In many places and seasons God gives his people favour, as Joseph found in Egypt and the early church found with all the people (Acts 2:47). Many unbelievers respect a kind and honest Christian. But ask honestly: do people around me know I follow Christ? Have I ever said something about him that cost me? Is there any point at which my life is clearly different from theirs? If the answer is no, the peace may be the peace of silence. If the answer is yes and they still treat you well, thank God for it and use it for the gospel.

In a sentence. Do not be surprised, my brothers and sisters, if the world hates you.

On a Tuesday. If you meet coldness, mockery or loss for Christ’s sake this week, do not retaliate and do not sulk. Pray for the person who caused it, by name, and look for one way to do him good. And if you meet none, ask whether your faith is visible enough to be noticed.

For worship. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, and he went on loving the world that hated him all the way to the cross. He bore its contempt for the joy set before him, and now he is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. He has overcome the world (John 16:33), and its hatred can reach his people only by passing through his love. The despised one is the exalted one, and those the world despises for his sake will share his throne and his joy.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love abides in death.

We know that we have passed out of death into life. “Passed” (metabebēkamen) means crossed over, moved from one place to another, migrated; and it is perfect tense: have passed and remain. It echoes Jesus: whoever hears and believes has passed from death to life (John 5:24). Conversion is a transfer from spiritual death to spiritual life (Ephesians 2:1–5), a crossing of a frontier from one country to another.

Because we love the brothers. “Because” (hoti): love is the evidence, not the cause. We know we have passed into life because love for fellow believers has appeared in us. Love is the sign of new life, the fingerprint of the new birth. A doctor checks for a pulse not to make the patient alive but to find out whether he is.

Whoever does not love abides in death. “Abides in death” (menei en tō thanatō) means remains in death. Without love, there is no evidence of new life. Such a person is still spiritually dead. Death and life are not merely future destinations but present addresses where a person currently lives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by loving. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9). Love is the fruit and the proof.

I find some Christians hard to love. Does that mean I have not passed into life? No. The question is not whether loving is easy for you but whether love is there at all: a real concern for God’s people, a desire to be with them, a gladness at their good, a grief at their harm. Struggling to love a particular brother is part of the Christian life; refusing to love God’s people as such, despising them and wanting nothing to do with them, would be the alarming sign. Notice that you are troubled by your lack of love. That trouble itself comes from the new life. Ask God to enlarge it.

In a sentence. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love each other. Anyone who does not love remains in death.

On a Tuesday. Look for the evidence of life in yourself this week: who are the Christians you are glad to see, worried for, praying for? Thank God for that love; it is a sign that you have passed from death to life. Then widen it to one more person.

For worship. We were dead. Not sick, not weak, but dead in trespasses and sins, and the God who is rich in mercy made us alive together with Christ. He brought us across the border from the land of death into the country of life, and he did it by going there himself: the Son of God crossed into death for us and came back out with the keys. The love we now have for his people is the first green shoot of resurrection, and it will never die.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.

Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. “Murderer” (anthrōpoktonos) means man-killer. Hatred is murder in the heart, the root from which murder grows. Jesus taught the same: anger and contempt make one liable to judgement (Matthew 5:21–22). God judges the heart, not just the act. Every murder in history was first a hatred somebody did not deal with.

And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him. Eternal life and settled hatred cannot coexist. A heart ruled by hatred shows no evidence of eternal life. This is not a threat against a struggling believer who sometimes feels anger, but a diagnosis of a life marked by settled, unchallenged, unrepented hatred.

The man-killer and the life-giver. John’s word for murderer is the one Jesus used of the devil: he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). Opposite him stands the one who came to give the life that hatred shuts out: the thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly (John 10:10). Hatred makes a man resemble the first; eternal life is the life of the second, for whoever has the Son has life (5:12). To nurse hatred is to keep the devil’s likeness while claiming the Son’s life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a murderer cannot be saved. Paul was complicit in murder (Acts 8:1; 22:20) and was forgiven. It means that a person who lives in unrepented hatred does not have eternal life. Repentance and faith bring forgiveness for any sin.

Is anger always hatred? No. Scripture says, be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger (Ephesians 4:26). There is a righteous anger at injustice and cruelty, which Jesus himself showed (Mark 3:5). Anger becomes hatred when it settles in and turns personal: when you want the other person harmed rather than put right, when you nurse it, rehearse it, and refuse to forgive. Ask: do I want this person restored or destroyed? Would I be glad if God blessed him? The test of the sunset is wise: deal with anger before it has time to harden.

In a sentence. Anyone who hates a brother or sister is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life residing in them.

On a Tuesday. Take hatred seriously: it is murder in the heart. If you harbour it, bring it to the cross today. Name the person to God, confess what you have wished on him, and ask for the grace to wish him good. If you can, do one kind thing for him before the sun goes down.

For worship. Christ was murdered by hatred. The men who shouted for his death were murderers in their hearts long before the nails, and he prayed for them as they did it: Father, forgive them. His blood can wash even hatred out of a heart and put love in its place. There is no murderer so stained, no hater so hardened, that the crucified Lord cannot make him new and give him the eternal life that hatred shuts out.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.

By this we know love. “Know” (egnōkamen) is have come to know. The supreme definition of love is not a feeling or a theory, but an event: the cross. We do not bring our own definition of love to the cross and admire how well it fits; the cross defines love for us and we learn from it. Christ’s self-giving death is what gives the word its content.

That he laid down his life for us. “He” (ekeinos, that one) is Jesus. “Laid down” (ethēken) means placed, set aside, the phrase Jesus used of the Good Shepherd (John 10:11, 15, 17–18). It is voluntary, deliberate self-giving. No one took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord. “For us” (hyper hēmōn) means on our behalf, in our place: substitution. Christ died the death we deserved.
