And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers. “Ought” (opheilomen) means owe, are obligated, are debtors. The love Christ showed is the pattern for our love. The same verb John uses for Christ’s laying down his life is now applied to the believer. Not that our deaths atone, but that we should be willing to sacrifice everything, even life itself, for fellow believers (John 15:12–13). Usually this means daily, practical self-giving (v. 17); sometimes it means literal death, as with martyrs.

The plague in Alexandria. In the third century, when a terrible epidemic struck Alexandria, Bishop Dionysius wrote that while the pagans pushed the sick out of their houses and fled from their dearest, the Christians stayed. They nursed the dying, Christian and pagan alike, washed the bodies of the dead and buried them, and many caught the disease and died themselves. He said they took the sickness of their neighbours on themselves, and he counted those who died that way as martyrs. They had learned what love is from the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our sacrifice has any saving value. Only Christ’s death atones. It means his love, which saved us, now shapes how we love others.

Does laying down my life mean I must never say no, even to someone who mistreats me? No. Christ laid down his life to save, not to enable evil. Love wills the good of the other, and sometimes that means saying no, setting limits, confronting sin, or getting out of danger. Self-sacrifice for a brother in need is commanded; submitting to abuse is not what this verse means, and abuse must never be tolerated in a home or a church. A wife, a child, or anyone being harmed should seek safety and help, and the church should protect them. Laying down your life is a gift freely given in love, not something taken from you by cruelty.

In a sentence. This is how we know what love is: Jesus Christ laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers and sisters.

On a Tuesday. Gaze at the cross today: this is what love is. Then ask God how you can give yourself for someone else this week. It may be an evening given up, a plan set aside, a cost absorbed quietly. Lay down a small piece of your life on purpose, for one particular person.

For worship. He laid his life down, and he took it up again. No one took it from him; he gave it, freely, in our place, and on the third day he took it back by the same authority (John 10:18). So the love that defines all love is not the memory of a dead man’s sacrifice. It is a living Lord who still bears the marks of that day in his hands, and who loves his people now with the same love that carried him to the cross. We have been loved by love itself, and that love is alive and reigning.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone has the world's goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God's love abide in him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him?

But if anyone has the world’s goods. “The world’s goods” (ton bion tou kosmou) is literally the life of the world: livelihood, means of living, possessions. John moves from the dramatic, laying down life, to the everyday, sharing goods. Many will never be asked to die for others, but all are asked to share. He brings the grand truth of verse 16 to its most specific and uncomfortable test: not martyrdom, which may never be asked, but the brother in front of you now, in need you can see, with resources you have.

And sees his brother in need. “Sees” (theōrē) means observes, looks at, contemplates: not a passing glance, but a clear awareness of the need. “In need” (chreian echonta) is having need. He has seen it properly. He knows.

Yet closes his heart against him. “Closes his heart” (kleisē ta splanchna autou ap’ autou) means shuts his inward parts, his compassion, against him. The splanchna are the inner organs, which the ancient world regarded as the seat of the deepest feelings, the place where you feel pity in your stomach. It is the word used of Jesus when he saw the crowds and had compassion on them. The picture is of a man who feels the stirring of pity and deliberately shuts the door on it, like a man closing his front door when he sees a beggar coming up the path.

How does God’s love abide in him? “God’s love” may be love for God, or the love that comes from God. It is a rhetorical question, and devastating: it does not. Love that refuses to help is not God’s love (James 2:15–16). The love defined by the cross is not a feeling that remains private and internal; it must pass through the hands, the wallet, the time, the presence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must give to every request without wisdom (2 Thessalonians 3:10). It means we must not harden our hearts against genuine need when we have the means to help.

How much should I give, and must I help everyone? Scripture does not set a figure for this, but it sets a direction: open-handed, cheerful, proportionate to what God has given you (2 Corinthians 8:12; 9:7). Your first responsibility is to those nearest: your family (1 Timothy 5:8) and the household of faith (Galatians 6:10). You cannot meet every need in the world, and you need not feel guilty for that. But when God puts a particular brother’s need in front of you and you are able to help, do not close your heart. Help wisely, so that it truly helps, and where you cannot help alone, bring the need to the church.

In a sentence. If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person?

On a Tuesday. Is there a fellow believer in need whom you could help this week? Open your heart and your hand. Ask your pastor or deacons quietly whether there is someone in the church facing a bill, a move, a loss, and offer something specific.

For worship. God has never closed his heart against us. He saw us in our need, poor and blind and naked, and his compassion moved him to give, not some of his goods, but his Son. Though he was rich, yet for our sake he became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich. Every gift we give to a needy brother is a small echo of the most extravagant gift ever given.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth.

Little children, let us not love in word or talk. “Word” (logō) and “talk” (glōssē, tongue). Love that is only words: saying I love you or I will pray for you without action. Words alone can deceive the speaker, who confuses saying with doing. John includes himself: let us not.

But in deed and in truth. “Deed” (ergō) is work, action. “Truth” (alētheia) is reality, genuineness. Real love acts, and it is genuine, not hypocritical, not performed for the approval of an audience or the comfort of the giver. This verse is the ethical floor of the entire section: love is verified by what the hands do, not by what the mouth says.

A towel, not a speech. On his last night Jesus did not lecture his disciples about humble love. He rose from supper, tied a towel round his waist, poured water into a basin and washed their feet, Judas’s among them, and then said: if I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:14). John was at that table. When he writes in deed and in truth, he is remembering wet hands on his own feet, and before the next nightfall the same Lord had loved them in the greatest deed of all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean words of love are worthless. Encouraging words are important (1 Thessalonians 5:11). It means words alone are not enough; love must show itself in action.

Is it hypocritical to do loving things when I do not feel love? No; it is obedient. Hypocrisy is pretending to be what you are not in order to be admired. Doing a loving act for someone you do not feel warmly toward, because God commands it, is the opposite: it is love in deed and truth, even when the feelings are absent. Feelings often follow actions. C. S. Lewis observed that when we behave as if we love someone, we soon come to love him. And the act itself is real love, because love is first a will for another’s good. Do the deed, and ask God for the heart.

In a sentence. Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth.

On a Tuesday. Turn one of your words of love into a deed this week: a meal, a gift, help with a task, a visit. If you have promised to pray for someone, pray now, and then send him a message to say you did.

For worship. God did not love us in word only. He said he loved us, through the prophets, many times and in many ways, and then he did it: the Word became flesh, and walked and wept and bled. The love of God has hands, and they are scarred. Everything he has said about his love he has proved, in deed and in truth, on a cross and from an empty tomb.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Assurance, Prayer, and the Mutual Indwelling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After such a demanding call to love, the question follows: what if I have not loved enough? What if my heart condemns me? John answers tenderly: God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. Then comes the freedom of prayer, and a summary of the whole Christian life: believe in the name of God’s Son, and love one another. The Spirit he has given assures us that he lives in us.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Greater than Our Heart

When our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows everything. His commandment is to believe in his Son and to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Assurance rested on love in deed and on the Spirit given to them.

Now: A tender conscience can rest in God’s fuller knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we shall know that we are of the truth and reassure our heart before him; for whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything.

By this we shall know that we are of the truth. “By this” looks back to loving in deed and truth (v. 18). “Of the truth” (ek tēs alētheias) means from the truth, belonging to it. Genuine love is evidence that we belong to God. Practical, genuine love for the brothers is part of the ground on which we settle our hearts.

And reassure our heart before him. “Reassure” (peisomen) means persuade, convince, set at rest. Our hearts sometimes accuse us. In God’s presence, we can quiet them. The conscience accuses; the pattern of genuine love provides counter-evidence, as a lawyer produces the record of a life to answer a charge.

For whenever our heart condemns us. “Condemns” (kataginōskē) means knows something against, accuses. A tender conscience, conscious of failure, may accuse and doubt. John knows his people. He knows there are believers who lie awake rehearsing their failures, who read every warning in Scripture as aimed at them, and who cannot believe that God could be pleased with them.

God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything. “Greater” (meizōn). “Knows everything” (ginōskei panta). There are two readings. In the first, God is greater in mercy: he knows everything, including our genuine love and Christ’s atonement, so we can rest even when our hearts accuse us. In the second, God is greater in judgement: if our hearts condemn us, how much more will God, who knows everything. The context (reassurance, v. 19; confidence, v. 21) supports the first. God’s knowledge is more complete than our self-knowledge. He knows the genuine faith beneath the failures, the love imperfectly expressed but truly intended, the direction of a will still being sanctified. The tender conscience that torments the believer can find rest not in convincing itself but in the greater God, whose verdict about us is more reliable than ours.

Peter on the beach. The best commentary on this verse is a morning by the Sea of Galilee. Peter had denied his Lord three times, with curses. Now the risen Jesus asked him three times, do you love me? and the third time Peter was grieved, and he did the only thing he could. He did not point to his record; his record was a disaster. He appealed to the Lord’s knowledge: Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:17). That is exactly the movement of this verse: from a condemning heart to the God who knows everything. And Jesus did not argue. He said, feed my sheep.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should ignore our conscience when it rightly convicts us of sin. We confess and are forgiven (1:9). It means that when our hearts continue to accuse us after confession, God’s verdict outweighs our feelings.

My conscience keeps accusing me about sins I have long confessed. What do I do? First, distinguish conviction from accusation. The Spirit’s conviction is specific, leads to confession, and ends in peace. Accusation is vague or endlessly repetitive, leads to despair, and never ends; it is the voice of the accuser, or of an anxious mind. Once you have confessed a sin and, where possible, put it right, God has forgiven it (1:9), and to keep punishing yourself is not humility but a refusal of his verdict. Answer your heart with this verse: God is greater. Some believers struggle with an over-scrupulous conscience as a real affliction, and it is wise to talk it through with a pastor, and sometimes a doctor too. Christ does not want you tormented.

In a sentence. This is how we know that we belong to the truth, and how we set our hearts at rest in his presence: if our hearts condemn us, we know that God is greater than our hearts, and he knows everything.

On a Tuesday. If your heart accuses you today, bring it to God. He knows everything, including that you love him, and he is greater than your heart. Write down the accusation, write next to it the verse that answers it (1:9; 2:1–2; Romans 8:1), and read the answer aloud whenever the accusation returns.

For worship. God is greater than our hearts. Our hearts are small, fickle and often wrong; they condemn when God has acquitted, and acquit when God would convict. But he knows everything. He knows every sin we have committed and every sin we will commit, and he chose us and sent his Son for us anyway. Nothing will ever come to light about us that surprises him or changes his mind. There is no safer place to rest a trembling conscience than in the knowledge of the God who knows all and loves us still.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God;

Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us. This is the positive side of verse 20: when our conscience is at rest, clean through confession and Christ’s blood, and our lives show genuine love. Not because of sinless perfection, but because the life is genuinely set toward love, obedience and light.

We have confidence before God. “Confidence” (parrēsian) means boldness, freedom, open-faced freedom of speech, as in 2:28. Not arrogance, but freedom to approach God as a child approaches a loving father (Hebrews 4:16; 10:19). It is the same word used for confidence at Christ’s coming (2:28) and confidence in prayer (5:14). The conscience at rest is a gift; John does not want his people to manufacture false guilt where none is warranted. The one walking in the light, loving in deed and truth, may come to God without cowering, not because he is perfect but because the relationship is real.

The child in the study. Think of a child who walks into his father’s study while he is working. A servant would knock and wait; a stranger would not be admitted. The child pushes the door open, climbs on his knee and starts talking. He is not being presumptuous. He is being a son. That is the confidence of this verse, and it is meant to be the ordinary posture of a Christian at prayer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean confidence rests on our performance. It rests on Christ. But a clear conscience removes the barriers to enjoying that confidence.

Is not confidence before God presumptuous? It would be if it rested on us. Coming to God on the strength of your own goodness would be presumption. But Scripture commands us to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), because our great high priest has gone ahead of us and opened the way with his own blood (Hebrews 10:19–22). Holding back in fear is not humility; it treats his blood as insufficient. True humility says, I have nothing to bring, so I come with Christ. That is the boldest and the humblest thing a sinner can do at the same time.

In a sentence. Dear friends, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God.

On a Tuesday. Come to God today with confidence, as a beloved child, through Christ. Begin your prayer not with an apology for disturbing him but with thanks that you are welcome. If something is on your conscience, confess it first, quickly, and then speak freely.

For worship. The Son has always had confidence before his Father. At the tomb of Lazarus he lifted his eyes and said, Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me (John 11:41–42). That freedom is his by nature, and he has shared it with us. We pray in his name, clothed in his righteousness, brought in by his access, so that the Father who always hears the Son hears his brothers and sisters in him. The Father has never once turned his Son away, and he will not turn away those who come in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and whatever we ask we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him.

And whatever we ask we receive from him. “Whatever” (ho ean). “Receive” (lambanomen) is present tense: keep receiving. A sweeping promise (John 14:13–14; 15:7; 16:23–24), qualified by 5:14: if we ask according to his will.

Because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him. “Because” (hoti): not that obedience earns answered prayer, but that obedient children ask according to their Father’s will, and their prayers align with what pleases him (Psalm 66:18; Proverbs 15:29; James 5:16). A life of obedience and a life of answered prayer go together. This is not a mechanical transaction, obey enough and unlock the answer, but a matter of being in tune: the person who does what pleases God comes to ask for what pleases God, and God is pleased to give it.

The Son who always pleased him. The phrase do what pleases him echoes Jesus’ words about himself: he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). The perfectly obedient Son is the one whose prayers the Father always hears, and Christians pray in his name. Our obedience is never perfect, and our prayers are not heard because of it. But the more our lives are shaped like his, the more our asking is shaped like his, until we find ourselves praying what he prays.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God answers every request exactly as we want if we are obedient enough. God answers according to his wisdom and will (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). It means obedient children pray as their Father desires, and their prayers are heard.

Why are some of my prayers not answered, even when I am trying to obey? They are answered, but not always with yes. Paul, an obedient apostle, asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and the answer was, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus himself, perfectly obedient, prayed in Gethsemane that the cup might pass, and the answer was the cross, which saved the world. God sometimes says no because he has something better, wait because the time is not yet, or yes in a form we do not recognise. A good father does not give a child everything he asks. Keep asking, keep obeying, and trust that your Father hears.

In a sentence. We receive from him anything we ask, because we keep his commands and do what pleases him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your requests to God with confidence today, seeking to please him in everything. Ask yourself whether there is anything you are cherishing that he has forbidden (Psalm 66:18); deal with it first. Then pray specifically, and keep a record so you can see how he answers over time.

For worship. Our Father delights to give. He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, and with him he will graciously give us all things. Every prayer of his children is heard, every request weighed by perfect wisdom and answered by perfect love. He is not a reluctant vending machine but a generous Father, shaping our desires by his word until we ask for what he longs to give, and then giving it.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is his commandment, that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another, just as he has commanded us.

And this is his commandment. “Commandment” (entolē) is singular. The commandments of verse 22 are summed up in one commandment with two parts. These are not two separate obligations to be balanced against each other; they are two aspects of one response to one God. In God’s mind they are one act, because genuine faith in Christ always produces love for the brothers, and genuine love for the brothers is always grounded in faith in Christ.

That we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ. “Believe” (pisteusōmen) is aorist: come to believe, trust. Faith is the first commandment (John 6:29). “In the name” (tō onomati) means in his person and character, all he is. “His Son Jesus Christ” is the full confession the false teachers denied (2:22–23). This is the first mention of believing in 1 John. Everything else John has said, about light, obedience, love and the new birth, rests on this.

And love one another, just as he has commanded us. “Love” (agapōmen) is present tense: keep loving. Faith and love together are the two great tests of the letter. Right belief about Christ and right love for one another are inseparable. Faith looks up and receives; love looks out and gives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith and love are equal grounds of salvation. Faith receives salvation; love flows from it (Galatians 5:6).

How can faith be commanded? Is it not a gift? It is both. God commands everyone to repent and believe the gospel (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30), and the command is real: unbelief is sin, not misfortune (John 3:18; 16:9). Yet no one can believe unless God draws him (John 6:44), and faith is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). The command and the gift meet in the gospel: as Christ is offered and the command is heard, the Spirit gives the faith he commands. Lazarus could not obey the command to come out of the tomb by his own power, but the voice that commanded gave the life to obey. So hear the command, and ask for the gift, and believe.

In a sentence. And this is his command: to believe in the name of his Son, Jesus Christ, and to love one another as he commanded us.

On a Tuesday. Renew your faith in Jesus Christ today, and show it by loving someone. Say to God plainly what you believe about his Son, and then act on it in one relationship: a conversation, an apology, a gift, a visit.

For worship. God has made the whole of his will simple enough for a child: trust my Son, and love one another. Behind that simplicity is the depth of the Trinity: the Father who gives the command, the Son in whose name we believe, the Spirit who pours love into our hearts. The command is not a burden laid on us from outside but the shape of the life God has given us, the life of faith that receives everything from him and the life of love that passes it on.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.

Whoever keeps his commandments abides in God, and God in him. “Abides” (menei) is mutual indwelling. The believer lives in God, and God lives in the believer (John 14:23; 15:4–5). Not alongside, not nearby, not approving from a distance: in. Obedience is the sign of this union. Jesus promised it the night before he died: if anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him (John 14:23). The Lord of glory lodges in the obedient heart.

And by this we know that he abides in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us. “By the Spirit” is the first mention of the Holy Spirit by name in 1 John. The Spirit is the guarantee of God’s presence in us (Romans 8:9, 16; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13–14). How do we know he is in us? By the Spirit’s work: enabling us to confess Christ (4:2), to love (4:13), and to obey. The Spirit gives inner assurance, bearing witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16), and his fruit gives outward evidence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Spirit’s presence is known only by dramatic experiences. The Spirit is known primarily by the fruit he produces: true confession of Christ, love, obedience (Galatians 5:22–23).

Can the Spirit leave me? No. Jesus promised that the Father would give another Helper, to be with you forever (John 14:16). The Spirit is God’s seal on his people for the day of redemption (Ephesians 4:30), and a seal is not broken. You can grieve him by sin (Ephesians 4:30), and you may lose for a time the joy and sense of his nearness, as David feared when he prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Psalm 51:11). But under the new covenant the Spirit is given to remain. If you have him, you will not lose him. Confess what grieves him, and ask him to restore the joy.

In a sentence. The one who keeps God’s commands lives in him, and he in them. And this is how we know that he lives in us: we know it by the Spirit he gave us.

On a Tuesday. Look for the Spirit’s fingerprints this week: a moment when you found yourself trusting Christ, a love for someone that was not natural to you, a temptation refused, a verse that suddenly lit up. Thank God for each one. They are signs that he lives in you.

For worship. God has come to live in us. The Father who dwells in unapproachable light, the Son who sits at his right hand, have made their home in the hearts of ordinary believers by the Spirit. We are temples of the living God. He has not merely forgiven us at a distance or promised to receive us one day; he has moved in, and he will never move out. The Son who once pitched his tent among us now dwells within us, and the Spirit within us cries Abba, Father, in the very voice of the Son (Galatians 4:6).

3.theology:
Adoption and Transformation. The doctrine of adoption is one of the richest in the New Testament, and 3:1–3, with its language of being born of God and called his children, is one of its highest expressions. To be called children of God is not a metaphor of religious devotion; it is a declaration of a new ontological status. We have been brought into the family of God — not as servants, not as subjects, but as children who share in the inheritance of the Son. And adoption in John is both present reality ("so we are," v.1) and future consummation ("what we will be has not yet appeared," v.2). The "not yet" of our glorification does not undermine the "already" of our adoption; the hope of the appearing purifies the life of the one who holds it.

Love Defined by the Cross. John's definition of love in verse 16 is one of the most consequential sentences in the New Testament. He does not say "God is love, therefore love is whatever feels loving." He says love is defined by a specific act: the laying down of the life of the Son. The cross is love's definition, love's measure, and love's demand. Reformed theology has always insisted that the love of God is not sentimentality but holy self-giving at infinite cost. Every theology of love that avoids the cross will eventually become a theology of tolerance — and tolerance is not love. Love is the cross, and the cross makes demands.
3.examples:
Then: The community John writes to had experienced the pain of betrayal — people they had loved had left. The temptation in such a situation is to turn inward, to protect the heart, to love in word only and keep the real self safely guarded. John's word to them is the cross: he laid down his life. Not as an inspiration to imitate from a safe distance, but as the very definition and pattern of what love is. The ones who remained in the fellowship were called to love one another with an openness that made them vulnerable — precisely because that is what love, defined by the cross, requires.

Now: We live in a therapeutic culture that defines love primarily as acceptance and validation. John defines it as sacrifice. The question is not "do I feel warmly toward my brother?" but "am I laying anything down for my brother?" The test of love is not interior but behavioural — not word and talk but deed and truth. A closed hand toward a brother in need, whatever feelings accompany it, is not love in John's sense. The cross makes love costly, specific, and concrete.

4.title: Testing the Spirits and the Love of God
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.<sup>2</sup>By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God,<sup>3</sup>and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.<sup>4</sup>Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.<sup>5</sup>They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.<sup>6</sup>We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.<sup>7</sup>Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.<sup>8</sup>Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.<sup>9</sup>In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.<sup>10</sup>In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.<sup>11</sup>Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.<sup>12</sup>No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.<sup>13</sup>By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.<sup>14</sup>And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.<sup>15</sup>Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.<sup>16</sup>So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.<sup>17</sup>By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.<sup>18</sup>There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.<sup>19</sup>We love because he first loved us.<sup>20</sup>If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.<sup>21</sup>And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 begins with a warning and rises to the fullest teaching on the love of God in the New Testament. The warning: test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. The test is whether a teaching confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Then John says twice, “God is love” (vv. 8, 16). He never lets this become vague. God’s love is defined by its greatest act: he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. That love casts out the fear of punishment, and it flows on through us to one another: “We love because he first loved us.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Testing the Spirits: Discernment in the Last Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits.” Not every teaching that claims to come from God does. False prophets rarely announce themselves; they use Christian words with spiritual intensity. John’s test goes to the heart of the gospel: does the teaching confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? And he ends with confidence: “he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing the Spirits

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: False prophets had gone out into the world.

Now: Ask of any teaching whether it confesses the whole Christ — truly God, truly man, crucified and risen.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, for many false prophets have gone out into the world.

Meaning first. 1 John 4 brings together the two great tests: truth about Christ and love. First, test the spirits (vv. 1–6): every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that denies it is the spirit of antichrist. Believers have overcome the false prophets, because he who is in them is greater than he who is in the world; the world listens to its own, but those who know God listen to the apostles. Second, love (vv. 7–21). God is love, and he showed it by sending his only Son to give us life and to be the propitiation for our sins (vv. 8–10). So we love one another, and the invisible God abides in us by his Spirit (vv. 11–16). Perfect love casts out the fear of judgement (vv. 17–18). We love because he first loved us, and whoever loves God must love his brother (vv. 19–21). The chapter says twice that God is love, and it will not let that sentence float free of the incarnation or the cross.

Beloved, do not believe every spirit. “Spirit” (pneumati) is the spirit behind a prophet or teacher: either the Holy Spirit or a spirit of error (v. 6). The church at that time had many who claimed to speak by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3; 14:29), and not every claim is true. John is neither a sceptic nor credulous. He believes in spirits, which is exactly why he will not believe all of them.

But test the spirits to see whether they are from God. “Test” (dokimazete) is the assayer’s word, used of a coin put in the fire to see whether the silver is real, and the present tense means keep testing. Every teaching, however spiritual it seems, must be tested (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). And the command is plural: discernment is not a gift reserved for leaders but a duty given to every believer.

For many false prophets have gone out into the world. “False prophets” (pseudoprophētai) are the false teachers who had left the church (2:19), claiming to speak for God. Jesus warned of them: beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing (Matthew 7:15; 24:11, 24). Not a future threat but a present reality: they have gone out, and they are travelling the roads between the house churches, teaching. The response is not panic or paralysis but testing.

The true Prophet behind the test. A counterfeit exists only because there is a genuine coin. Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him, and that the people must listen to him (Deuteronomy 18:15); Peter announced that Jesus is that Prophet (Acts 3:22–23). In these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), and every other voice is weighed against his. That is why John’s test, in the very next verse, is a question about Jesus. In all the noise of the world, the church is listening for one voice, and it is his.

The Bereans. Luke gives the model. When Paul preached in Berea, the Jews there received the word with all eagerness, and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). Notice whom they tested: an apostle. They were not rude to him and not suspicious of him; they were eager. But they checked, and Luke calls them more noble for it. A good teacher is never threatened by a congregation with open Bibles.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should be suspicious of all teaching or cynical about every teacher. It means discernment is required, and the standard is apostolic truth about Christ (vv. 2, 6).

How does an ordinary Christian actually test a teacher? You do not need a theology degree. Start with John’s two tests in this chapter: what does he say about Jesus (vv. 2–3), and does he submit to the apostles’ word in Scripture (v. 6)? Then ask: does he handle the Bible honestly, in context? Does his life match his teaching (Matthew 7:16)? Does his message make much of Christ and his cross, or much of himself, money or experience? Does it lead to holiness and love? Read your Bible with him open beside it, and ask your pastor or a mature believer when you are unsure. Testing is not a single event but a habit.

In a sentence. Dear friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world.

On a Tuesday. Test the next sermon, book or online teaching you encounter. What does it say about Jesus? Does it match Scripture? Pick one claim it makes and look up the passage it uses, reading the whole chapter around it.

For worship. God has not left his people defenceless in a world full of voices. He has given us his word, fixed and sure, and his Spirit to open it, and he has promised that his sheep will know the Shepherd’s voice. The Spirit of truth does not compete with the false spirits on equal terms. He is the Spirit of the living God, and every voice that rises against his Christ will fall silent before him.

verseByVerse.quote: By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already.

By this you know the Spirit of God. The test of the Spirit is what is confessed about Christ. John does not tell them to test the spirits by their power, their feelings, their miracles or their success. He tells them to ask one question: who is Jesus?

Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. “Confesses” (homologei) means acknowledges, declares publicly. “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (Iēsoun Christon en sarki elēlythota) is perfect tense: has come and remains in the flesh. The phrasing insists on the permanent reality of the incarnation: not a temporary appearance, but the eternal Son truly and lastingly becoming a real human being, with a real body. The false teachers said the divine Christ only seemed human, or came on the man Jesus for a time (2:22). The Holy Spirit always glorifies Christ and testifies to who he is (John 15:26; 16:14; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

And every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. “Does not confess Jesus” means does not acknowledge Jesus as he truly is, the Christ come in the flesh. Some early manuscripts and church fathers read every spirit that annuls (lyei, dissolves, separates) Jesus, meaning separates the human Jesus from the divine Christ; the best reading is does not confess. And notice the name: Jesus, the man from Nazareth. The spirit of antichrist does not necessarily deny that there is a Christ; it refuses to confess that the Christ is Jesus.

This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you heard was coming and now is in the world already. The antichrist spirit (2:18, 22) is already active, working through false teachers. This is not only a future figure but a present spiritual reality inhabiting false teaching in John’s own time, and in ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who mechanically says “Jesus came in the flesh” is from God. The confession must be genuine, with the full meaning of who Jesus is: God the Son, truly incarnate, the Christ who died and rose. Even demons acknowledged Jesus’ identity (Mark 1:24) without being from God.

Why does it matter so much that Jesus came in the flesh? Because everything he did for us depended on it. Only a real man could stand in the place of men, obey the law we broke, and die the death we deserved (Hebrews 2:14–17). Only a real body could rise from a real grave and guarantee ours. Only one who shares our nature can be our high priest who sympathises with our weakness. And only the eternal Son could make that obedience and death of infinite worth. A Christ who only seemed human could only seem to save. That is why the church has fought hard for this truth in every century: deny it, and the gospel dissolves.

In a sentence. This is how you can recognise the Spirit of God: every spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, but every spirit that does not acknowledge Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and even now is already in the world.

On a Tuesday. Your body matters to God; his Son took one. Thank him today for the flesh he wore: the hands that touched lepers, the feet that walked to Calvary, the side that was pierced. And treat your own body, and others’, as something the Son of God was not ashamed to share.

For worship. The Word became flesh, and he has not stopped being flesh. The Son who sits on the throne of the universe is still a man, with a man’s face and a man’s scarred hands. He took our nature into the life of God and will never lay it down. In him God is not distant from humanity; he has joined himself to it for ever, and in that flesh he lived, died, rose and reigns for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, you are from God and have overcome them, for he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world.

Little children, you are from God. “You” (hymeis) is emphatic, in contrast with the false prophets. “From God” (ek tou theou) means belonging to God, born of him. After the warning about false prophets and the spirit of antichrist, John does not leave the church in anxious alert; he turns at once to comfort.

And have overcome them. “Overcome” (nenikēkate) is perfect tense: have conquered and remain victorious, as in 2:13–14. “Them” is the false prophets: the readers had resisted their teaching and stayed faithful.

For he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world. “He who is in you” is God, by his Spirit (3:24). “He who is in the world” is the devil, the ruler of this world (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11), working through the false prophets. The victory does not rest on the believers’ strength, their theological sophistication or their community, but on the one who is in them, the Spirit of truth, incomparably “greater” (meizōn) than the spirit of error that drives the false prophets. Every believer, however newly converted, however ordinary, however doubting, carries within him a power that has already overcome the spirit driving the false teachers.

The stronger man has already entered the house. The victory John announces was won before his readers ever met a false prophet. Jesus said that no one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and that is what he came to do: the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (3:8). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). The Spirit who lives in believers is the Spirit of this conquering Christ, sent by him from the Father (John 15:26). So when John says you have overcome, he is echoing his Master in the upper room: take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

Elisha’s servant. When the Syrian army surrounded Dothan, Elisha’s servant went out in the morning, saw horses and chariots everywhere, and panicked. Elisha said, do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them. Then he prayed, and the LORD opened the young man’s eyes, and the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). This verse is that prayer answered for every believer. The enemy is real and visible. What is with you is greater, and invisible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will never struggle with false teaching or temptation. It means they will ultimately overcome, because God is with them.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No, not in the sense of being owned or controlled by one. A Christian is indwelt by the Holy Spirit, and the one in him is greater; he has been transferred out of the domain of darkness into the kingdom of God’s Son (Colossians 1:13). The devil can tempt, accuse, deceive and attack believers, and they must resist him (Ephesians 6:11–13; 1 Peter 5:8–9). But he cannot take possession of one who belongs to Christ. If you are troubled by dark thoughts or fears, do not conclude that you are possessed; bring them to Christ, to Scripture, to prayer and to your pastor, and seek medical help where it is needed.

In a sentence. You, dear children, are from God and have overcome them, because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you face today, remember: the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world. Write the verse on a card and put it where you will see it at the moment you usually feel weakest.

For worship. Greater is he. The Spirit who lives in the weakest believer is the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead, and nothing in heaven or earth or hell can stand against him. The ruler of this world has been judged and cast out. He still rages, but he rages on a chain, and the chain is held by the one who lives in us. The hills around every frightened servant are still full of horses and chariots of fire, and the Lord of that host has made his home in a human heart.

verseByVerse.quote: They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.

They are from the world. “They” are the false prophets. “From the world” (ek tou kosmou): their source, values and loyalty are worldly. The world here is the age organised against God, and the origin of the false teachers explains both their message and its reception.

Therefore they speak from the world. Their teaching is shaped by what the world finds intellectually respectable, emotionally satisfying and socially acceptable. In John’s day that meant a spiritual Christ without the embarrassment of a body or a cross; the philosophers of the age would have nodded.

And the world listens to them. The world welcomes teachers who tell it what it wants to hear, because like recognises like (John 15:19). Popularity with the world is no proof of truth; often it is a warning sign. When a message draws enthusiastic reception from those who have no interest in the Christ of the New Testament, the test of verses 2–3 is worth applying.

He who comes from above. John is echoing what he had recorded about Jesus himself: he who is of the earth speaks in an earthly way, but he who comes from heaven is above all (John 3:31). The false teachers speak from below, so they sound like the world. Christ came from above, so he never did, and that is why the world that applauds its own prophets hated him: it hates me, he said, because I testify about it that its works are evil (John 7:7). The crowd that would have nodded at a bodiless Christ shouted for Barabbas.

Itching ears. Paul described the same market: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Timothy 4:3). The ears choose the teachers. A preacher who offers health and wealth without repentance, a Jesus who affirms everything and asks nothing, a spirituality without sin or judgement, will always find a crowd. The crowd is not the test.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everything popular is false, or that faithful teachers will never be heard by unbelievers. Many have come to faith through faithful preaching. It means worldly approval is not the test of truth.

Should churches then avoid being attractive or relevant? Churches should be welcoming, clear and kind, and should speak in language people understand; Paul became all things to all people, that by all means he might save some (1 Corinthians 9:22). There is nothing faithful about being needlessly off-putting. The danger is changing the message to fit the market: softening sin, removing the cross, or promising what Christ never promised. Adapt the packaging freely; never touch the contents. If people are offended by the gospel, that is the gospel’s doing. If they are offended by us, that is ours.

In a sentence. They are from the world and therefore speak from the viewpoint of the world, and the world listens to them.

On a Tuesday. Is a teaching popular because it is true, or because it tells people what they want to hear? Test it by Scripture. And examine your own preferences: what do you like to hear, and what do you avoid? Read a passage of Scripture this week that you usually skip.

For worship. The Word from above never lowered his voice to match the world’s. Fashions rise and fall, and the prophets of each age are forgotten with it, but his word stands, and it has gone on calling men and women out of the world for two thousand years. No market can drown it and no crowd can vote it down. The world listens to its own; but the Son of God speaks, and the dead hear his voice and live.

verseByVerse.quote: We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error.

We are from God. “We” are John and the apostles, the authoritative witnesses (1:1–3). They are God’s spokesmen.

Whoever knows God listens to us. “Listens” (akouei) means hears, heeds. Those who truly know God recognise and accept the apostolic teaching (John 8:47; 10:27; 18:37). The sheep know the Shepherd’s voice: the sheep follow him, for they know his voice; a stranger they will not follow (John 10:4–5). The person shaped by the Spirit of truth recognises truth when he hears it.

Whoever is not from God does not listen to us. Rejecting the apostles’ teaching reveals that one does not belong to God. The church’s response to the apostolic word is itself a diagnostic tool.

The one who hears you hears me. Why should listening to a handful of apostles reveal whether a person knows God? Because Christ put his own voice in their mouths. He told them that the one who hears them hears him (Luke 10:16), and he promised that the Spirit would bring to their remembrance all that he had said and guide them into all the truth (John 14:26; 16:13). The apostolic word is not one religious opinion among many; it is the risen Christ speaking through the men he chose. To receive it is to hear the Shepherd himself.

By this we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error. “Spirit of truth” is the Holy Spirit (John 14:17; 15:26); “spirit of error” (pneuma tēs planēs, spirit of deception) is Satan and his demonic influences. This is the second test of spirits: do they accept the apostolic witness? The criterion is both doctrinal, the content of the confession (vv. 2–3), and receptive, the Spirit-given recognition of the apostolic word. Today that word is preserved in the New Testament, and any teaching that contradicts it comes from the spirit of error.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every church leader today has apostolic authority. “We” refers to the apostles, whose unique authority is now exercised through Scripture. Modern teachers must be tested by the apostolic word, not the other way round.

Is it not arrogant to say whoever knows God listens to us? Could not any group say that? Any group could say it, and many have. The difference is who is speaking. John is an eyewitness apostle, commissioned by Christ, writing what became Scripture. No church, pastor or movement today can claim that for itself; we can only point to what the apostles wrote. So the verse does not make any modern group the judge of truth. It makes the apostolic word the judge of every group, including ours. The humble church is the one that keeps sitting under the New Testament, and lets it correct its traditions.

In a sentence. We are from God, and whoever knows God listens to us; but whoever is not from God does not listen to us. This is how we recognise the Spirit of truth and the spirit of falsehood.

On a Tuesday. Listen to the apostles this week as you would to a living voice. Read one New Testament letter straight through at a sitting, as its first hearers did, and note one place where it corrects you.

For worship. The Spirit of truth is the Spirit of him who is the Truth. Every spirit of error leads away from Christ, and every word of the Spirit of truth leads back to him. On the evening of his resurrection the Lord opened his disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and he has never stopped. By the same Spirit he opens ears across the centuries and the nations, wherever the apostles’ words are read, until the last of those the Father gave him has heard and come home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — God Is Love: The Source, the Measure, and the Goal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “God is love.” John does not mean a warm feeling or a tolerant mood. Love is the life the Father, Son and Spirit have shared from eternity. And this love has been shown: God sent his only Son so that we might live through him, as the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we ought to love one another. And when we do, the invisible God is seen in his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Is Love

Love is from God, and God showed it by sending his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The departing teachers’ knowledge produced schism, not love.

Now: No one has ever seen God; when we love one another, his love is made complete in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God, and whoever loves has been born of God and knows God.

Beloved, let us love one another. “Beloved” (agapētoi) means loved ones. Those who are loved should love. The great theme of the chapter arrives immediately after the testing of verses 1–6, and the order is deliberate: doctrine and love are not alternative emphases for different temperaments but inseparable sides of one life. The church that tests the spirits must also be the church that loves.

For love is from God. “From God” (ek tou theou): love has its source in God. All genuine love flows from him. When we love, we are sharing in a reality that comes from outside ourselves, that does not have its source in our natural generosity or emotional warmth. A river does not make its own water.

And whoever loves has been born of God and knows God. “Loves” (agapōn) is present tense: habitually loves, with agapē, self-giving love. “Has been born of God” (ek tou theou gegennētai) is perfect tense. Love is the fingerprint of the new birth and the evidence of knowing God: not knowledge about him, but the relational knowing that is the fruit of a real meeting with him. Those who love show they know God, because they share his nature.

The commandment from the upper room. When John writes let us love one another, he is repeating what he heard at the Last Supper, on the night Jesus washed his disciples’ feet: a new commandment, that they love one another just as he had loved them (John 13:34). The command came with a measure, and the measure was Christ. The love that is from God did not arrive as an idea; it arrived kneeling with a towel, and a few hours later it was nailed to a cross. To be born of God is to be born into that Son’s family, and the family likeness is his kind of love.

The word the church filled. The Greeks had several words for love. Erōs was desire, the love that wants. Philia was friendship, the love of companions. Storgē was family affection. Agapē was a rather colourless word, little used. The Christians took it and filled it with the cross, until it meant the love that gives itself for the undeserving. They had to, because nothing in the old vocabulary was big enough for what they had seen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who shows any kind of love is born again. John means agape love, the self-giving love defined by the cross (v. 10; 3:16), flowing from faith in Christ (v. 15). Many unbelievers show natural affection and kindness, by God’s common grace, but not the love that comes from new birth.

My unbelieving neighbour is kinder than some Christians I know. How can that be? It can be, and it is humbling. God gives common grace to all people: natural affection, a kind temperament, a good upbringing (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). Some unbelievers are naturally gentle, and some Christians are converted from very hard natures and still have far to go. Compare each person with where he started, not with each other. And notice what John is describing: not niceness, but love that flows from knowing God through Christ, love that includes loving God himself. That said, your neighbour’s kindness should shame the church into greater love, and your Christian brother’s unkindness should be gently confronted.

In a sentence. Dear friends, let us love one another, for love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.

On a Tuesday. Love is from God. Ask him today for more of his love, and show it to someone. When you feel you have no love left for a particular person, do not try to squeeze it out of yourself. Go back to the source, and ask.

For worship. All the love in the universe has one spring. Every mother’s tenderness, every friend’s loyalty, every act of self-giving is a stream that rose in God. And the purest stream of all, the love that loves enemies and lays down its life, flows from him into the hearts of his children by new birth. To love is to drink from God and pass the cup on.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love.

Anyone who does not love does not know God. “Does not know” (ouk egnō) is aorist: never came to know. Lack of love shows that one has never known God. Not merely knows less of him, not has a weaker relationship with him: does not know him. To know the one who is love is to be changed by what he is; to remain unchanged toward love is evidence that the meeting with the living God has not yet happened.

Because God is love. “God is love” (ho theos agapē estin) is the most concentrated sentence in the letter: not merely that God loves, or that love is one attribute among others, but that love is his very nature. Within the Trinity, the Father, Son and Spirit have eternally loved one another (John 17:24). All his actions are loving, including his holiness and justice. As God is light (1:5), so God is love. The two go together: his love is holy, and his holiness is loving.

Why only the Trinity can say this. A god who was a single, solitary person could not be love in himself before creation; there would have been no one to love, and he would need us. The God of the Bible needs nothing. Before the mountains were brought forth, the Father loved the Son and the Son loved the Father in the bond of the Spirit. We were not made because God was lonely, but because his love was so rich he chose to share it.

Where Christians differ: if God is love, can he send anyone to hell? Some argue that a God of love could never punish anyone eternally, and so all will be saved, or the wicked will be annihilated. Verdict: God is love does not mean love is God, or that God’s love overrides his holiness and justice. The same John who wrote that God is love wrote that the wrath of God remains on those who reject the Son (John 3:36) and described the lake of fire (Revelation 20:10–15). John has already said God is light (1:5), holy and just, and he defines love by the cross: God sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). Propitiation means the turning away of wrath, so God’s love does not cancel his justice; it satisfies it at infinite cost. God’s love is seen supremely at the cross, where he satisfied his own justice by bearing his own wrath in his Son. Love that ignores evil would not be true love. God is love, and God is light; his love is holy love. Those who refuse that love remain under the judgement it was given to remove, and face his just and eternal judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is soft, permissive or indulgent. True love seeks the highest good of the beloved, and sometimes that means discipline (Hebrews 12:6) and justice.

Does God love everyone? Yes, in different ways. God loves all people as his creatures: he gives sun and rain to the just and the unjust, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil, and sincerely calls everyone to repent and believe (Matthew 5:44–45; Luke 6:35; Ezekiel 33:11). That love is real, and every unbeliever has received it every day of his life. But Scripture also speaks of a special, saving love God has for his people, chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5; 5:25). You need not solve the mystery to enjoy the love. Anyone who comes to Christ finds that this saving love was set on him from eternity.

In a sentence. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to think God cold, distant or against you, answer with this sentence. Say it slowly: God is love. Then look at your hardest relationship and ask what it would look like for the God who is love to be known there through you.

For worship. God is love. Not a god who sometimes loves, or loves when he is pleased, or loves the lovable, but love itself in three persons, from everlasting to everlasting. That love made us, came after us when we ran, and hung on a cross to bear the judgement it would not ignore. Because it is holy love, it can be trusted: it will never wink at the evil that ruins us, and it will never let go of those it has bought. We have been taken up into the life of a God whose very being is love.

verseByVerse.quote: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him.

In this the love of God was made manifest among us. “Made manifest” (ephanerōthē) means revealed, shown, made visible. God’s love is not just a feeling; it became visible in an event. The claim of verse 8 is grounded in a concrete, historical act. Love is not a philosophical category but a datable, locatable deed: in the reign of Augustus, in the town of Bethlehem.

That God sent his only Son into the world. “Sent” (apestalken) is perfect tense: sent, with continuing effects. “Only Son” (monogenē) means unique, one of a kind, only begotten, as in John 1:14, 18; 3:16. The Son is unique; no other is Son as he is. The word marks the costliness of the giving: not one of many divine representatives, but the unique, irreplaceable Son.

Abraham on the mountain. The phrase reaches back to Moriah. God said to Abraham, take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go up the mountain (Genesis 22:2). Abraham went, and at the last moment God stopped his hand and provided a ram instead. Two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region, God did what he had not allowed Abraham to do. He took his Son, his only Son, whom he loved, and did not hold back his hand. There was no ram for him. He was the Lamb.

So that we might live through him. “Live” (zēsōmen) is eternal life, now and for ever (John 3:16; 10:10). “Through him” (di’ autou): Christ is the means and source of life. We were spiritually dead (3:14; Ephesians 2:1); through him we live. Love does not stay in the divine inner life; it moves outward, descends into the world of the dying, and brings life from the only source that has it.

What it does not mean. “Only Son” does not mean the Son was created or had a beginning. “Only begotten” expresses his unique, eternal relationship with the Father, not a beginning in time.

If believers are also sons of God, why is Jesus called the only Son? Because he is Son in a way no one else can be. He is the eternal Son by nature, sharing the Father’s being from all eternity, God from God. We become children of God by grace: by new birth and adoption, through faith in him (John 1:12–13; Galatians 4:4–7). He is the Son; we are sons in the Son. Jesus kept the difference even after the resurrection: I am ascending to my Father and your Father (John 20:17). Ours is a real sonship, and it is entirely borrowed from his.

In a sentence. This is how God showed his love among us: he sent his one and only Son into the world so that we might live through him.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt that God loves you, do not look first at your circumstances, which change, but at the event, which does not. Write down what it cost the Father to send his Son, and read it back to yourself when the doubt returns.

For worship. He sent his only Son. The Father did not send an angel or a prophet or a message; he sent the one he had loved from eternity, into a world that would reject him, to die. He did not spare him. That is the measure of his love for us, and it is beyond all measuring. If God has given us his Son, there is nothing he will withhold that is good for us, and we live, today and for ever, through the gift of his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.

In this is love. This is the definition of love, and the direction of love is here established once and finally: it runs from God to us, not from us to God. This is the great reversal at the heart of the gospel. The sinner is not at the centre straining upward; God is at the centre, moving downward.

Not that we have loved God. Love did not begin with us. We did not seek God; we were his enemies (Romans 3:11; 5:10). Our love for God is always a response, never the origin. We were the objects of love before we were its agents.

But that he loved us. “He loved” (ēgapēsen) is aorist: a decisive act. God took the initiative, when we were unlovable. God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8; Ephesians 2:4–5). He did not love us because we were lovely; we become lovely because he loved us.

And sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. “Propitiation” (hilasmon), as in 2:2, is the sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath by bearing it in our place. The supreme expression of God’s love is that he himself provided the sacrifice to satisfy his own justice (Romans 3:25–26). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son; it is the loving Father sending his Son to bear the wrath that sin deserves. Love and justice meet at the cross. Penal substitution is the heart of God’s love: by it sinners are received into the family of God without his justice being compromised.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s love is opposed to his wrath. His love is shown precisely in dealing with his wrath against sin by bearing it himself in his Son.

If the Father loved us already, why did he need a propitiation? Because his love is holy. A judge who loved a guilty man and simply let him go would not be loving; he would be corrupt, and the victims of the crime would be betrayed. God’s love does not ignore justice; it pays it. The propitiation is not what made God love us. It is what his love did, at his own cost, so that he could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The cross is not the Father being persuaded to love; it is the Father loving so much that he bore the cost himself, in the person of his Son.

In a sentence. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath from our sins.

On a Tuesday. Meditate on this definition of love today. You did not love him first; he loved you, and sent his Son to bear your punishment. Then measure your love for others by it: not what they deserve, but what you have received.

For worship. In this is love. Not in our devotion, which is cold and fickle, but in his. When we were enemies, he loved us; when we had nothing to give, he gave his Son; when wrath was due, he bore it himself. There has never been a love like this, and there never will be, because there is no one else who could pay what he paid. The cross is God saying, beyond all doubt and for all time, I love you.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

Beloved, if God so loved us. “If” (ei) means since; it is not conditional doubt but logical inference. “So” (houtōs) means in this way, to this extent: in the way just described, sending his Son as a propitiation (v. 10). It echoes John 3:16.

We also ought to love one another. “Ought” (opheilomen) means owe, are obligated, as in 3:16. We owe love to others because of the love God has shown us: not to repay God (we never could), but to pass his love on. That love creates both the obligation and the capacity. Those loved at infinite cost have no ground for withholding love from those who have cost them comparatively nothing; and the love of God poured into our hearts through the Spirit (Romans 5:5) is not merely a standard to imitate but a resource to draw on.

The servant who would not forgive. Jesus told of a servant forgiven a debt so vast it could never have been paid, ten thousand talents, more than a labourer could earn in many lifetimes. He went straight out and seized a fellow servant who owed him a hundred days’ wages and threw him in prison (Matthew 18:23–35). The story is absurd, and that is the point. Once you know what you have been forgiven, every debt owed to you shrinks to its real size.

What the pardon cost. Jesus’ parable does not tell us what it cost the king to cancel the debt. John does: it cost the Father his Son, sent to be the propitiation for our sins (v. 10). That is the force of the little word so. The love we owe one another is measured not by the size of our brother’s offence but by the price of our own pardon, paid in the blood of Christ. Paul draws the same line: walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us (Ephesians 5:2). Only those who have stood at the foot of the cross have the heart to forgive like this.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we love others only out of duty. The love of God poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5) becomes the source and motive of our love.

What if someone has hurt me deeply? Must I love him, and must I trust him again? You must love him, which means forgiving him from the heart, refusing revenge, and wishing and praying for his good (Romans 12:17–21). But forgiveness is not the same as trust, and love is not the same as pretending. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by repentance shown over time. Reconciliation needs both sides. And where someone has been abusive, love does not require you to return to danger; abuse must never be tolerated, and the church should protect the vulnerable. You can forgive a person and still keep a safe distance, report a crime, and let the authorities do their work.

In a sentence. Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

On a Tuesday. Think of the hardest person in your church to love. God loved you when you were hard to love. Love them this week, in one specific way: a greeting, a prayer, an invitation, a kindness they cannot repay.

For worship. Since God so loved us. Everything rests on that so: a Father who did not spare his Son, a Son who did not spare himself. The love that reached us is not a trickle to be rationed against our convenience but an ocean, and it has found its way into hearts that once loved only themselves. We do not love out of our own poverty. We love out of the riches of Christ, and those riches never run dry.

verseByVerse.quote: No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever seen God; if we love one another, God abides in us and his love is perfected in us.

No one has ever seen God. “Seen” (tetheatai) means beheld, gazed upon; it is perfect tense. It is the same statement as John 1:18. God in his essence is invisible (1 Timothy 6:16). The false teachers may have claimed special visions of God. John does not boast of visions; he points to a church.

If we love one another, God abides in us. Though God is invisible, his presence becomes evident in his people’s love. This is the most astonishing claim about the church in the letter: when believers love one another across the boundaries of preference, history and difference, God himself is made perceptible in the world in a way that no private vision, no treatise and no programme can achieve.

And his love is perfected in us. “Perfected” (teteleiōmenē) means completed, brought to its goal, perfect tense, as in 2:5. God’s love for us reaches its intended goal when it produces love in us for others. The love that began in the eternal Trinity, was shown in the incarnation and reached its depth on the cross, reaches its goal when it flows through us to one another.

So that the world may believe. On the night before he died, Jesus told his disciples that all people would know they were his disciples by their love for one another (John 13:35), and he prayed that they would be one, so that the world may believe that the Father had sent him (John 17:21). The love John describes is Christ’s own love, reproduced in people he has redeemed. When the world looks at a church that loves, it does not see God’s essence, but it sees the shape of the cross: proud people serving, enemies reconciled, the strong carrying the weak.

What the pagans saw. In the second century the pagan satirist Lucian mocked the Christians for their gullibility, but even he noticed how they rushed to care for any brother in prison, sending food and money and visitors. Tertullian reported the pagans saying of them, see how they love one another. The world could not see God. It could see that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God abides in us only because we love. God abides in us by his Spirit, given at new birth (v. 13). Our love is the evidence of his presence.

If no one has seen God, what about Moses, Isaiah and others who saw him? They saw real appearances of God, his glory shown in a form they could bear: the burning bush, the cloud, the throne high and lifted up. Moses was told plainly, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Exodus 33:20), and he saw only the back of his glory. Many think the appearances of the LORD in the Old Testament were the Son before his incarnation. No one has seen God in his essence. The only God, who is at the Father’s side, has made him known (John 1:18). To see Jesus is to see the Father (John 14:9).

In a sentence. No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to make his invisible love visible through you today. Look around your church on Sunday for one person on the edge, and make sure he leaves having been seen and loved.

For worship. The invisible God has chosen to be seen. He showed his glory once in his Son, full of grace and truth, and he is painting that likeness now in forgiven sinners who love one another. The portrait is unfinished and the brush strokes are clumsy, but the face is unmistakably his. And the portrait is not the end. The day is coming when his servants will see his face (Revelation 22:4), and the God no one has ever seen will be the light of every eye.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Abiding in Love: Confidence, Fear Cast Out, and the Visible Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Assurance rests on the Spirit God has given (v. 13) and the confession of his Son (v. 15). From that union comes confidence even for the day of judgment, because “as he is so also are we in this world.” Perfect love casts out the fear of punishment. And love for the invisible God is tested by love for the brother we can see.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear Cast Out

Those who abide in love have confidence for the day of judgement. Perfect love casts out fear, and we love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Confidence rested on union with the Son, not on claimed knowledge.

Now: The brother we can see tests our love for the God we cannot see.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.
