By this we know that we abide in him and he in us. This is mutual indwelling, as in 3:24. We do not deduce that we abide in God from moral achievement or sustained feeling. We know it.

Because he has given us of his Spirit. “Of his Spirit” (ek tou pneumatos autou) means from his Spirit. Every believer has received the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), God’s pledge that we belong to him (2 Corinthians 1:22). His presence is known by his work: enabling us to confess Christ (v. 2), to love (vv. 7, 12), and to cry out to God as Abba, Father (Romans 8:15–16). This is not private mysticism but the common possession of every believer, and it is the reason we can say we know rather than we hope or we feel.

Poured out by the exalted Son. The Spirit by whom we know is not a gift that floats free of Christ. John had recorded that the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified (John 7:39); the gift had to wait for the cross, the resurrection and the ascension. At Pentecost Peter explained the sound and the fire: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God, had received the promised Holy Spirit from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33). Every believer who knows that he abides in God knows it by a gift bought at Calvary and given from the throne.

The deposit. Paul calls the Spirit the guarantee of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14), using the word for a deposit paid on a purchase, or an engagement ring. A merchant who paid a deposit was bound to complete the sale. The Spirit in us now is the first instalment of heaven, God’s pledge that the rest is coming. He is not a sample that might be withdrawn but a down payment that commits the buyer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we receive only part of the Spirit. “Of his Spirit” means we share in the Spirit God gives. He is a person, not a substance divided up.

How can I tell the Spirit’s witness from my own wishful thinking? Look at what he produces. The Spirit’s witness is not a voice that says you are saved while leaving your life unchanged. It always comes with his fruit: a heart that confesses Jesus as Lord and Son of God (v. 15), a love for his people (v. 12), a hatred of sin, a desire to obey, and a turning to God as Father (Romans 8:15). Wishful thinking can produce a feeling; it cannot produce a new love for holiness and for Christ. If you see these, however weak, the Spirit is at work, and you may trust his witness.

In a sentence. This is how we know that we live in him and he in us: he has given us of his Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for his Spirit within you, the pledge that you belong to him for ever. And live today as one who has been sealed: you are not your own; you carry the presence of God into every room you enter.

For worship. God has given us himself. Not only gifts, not only promises, but his own Spirit to live in us, the same Spirit who moved over the waters and raised Christ from the dead. He is the deposit of glory, the seal of ownership, the voice within that cries Abba. The God who is love has not loved us from a distance. He has come in.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world.

And we have seen and testify. “We” are the apostles, eyewitnesses (1:1–3). “Seen” (tetheametha) means beheld, and it is perfect tense. The proclamation rests on eyewitness observation, not spiritual intuition. Though no one has seen God (v. 12), the apostles saw the Son, who reveals the Father (John 1:18; 14:9). The same verb is used of both: no one has beheld God; we have beheld the Son. That is the whole gospel in two verbs.

That the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world. “Saviour of the world” (sōtēra tou kosmou) is the title the Samaritans gave Jesus (John 4:42), and it is rare in the New Testament. It carries the widest scope: not the Saviour of one tribe or nation, but of people from every nation, culture and century who come to him in faith. In the Roman world the emperor was hailed as saviour of the world on coins and inscriptions; John gives the title to its true owner.

The Samaritan village. It is worth remembering who first said it. Not the apostles, not the rabbis, but a town of despised half-breeds in Samaria, brought to Jesus by a woman with five husbands behind her. After two days with him they said to her, we no longer believe because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world. The first people to see how wide his salvation was were the people everyone else thought were outside it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every person in the world will be saved. Jesus is the Saviour of the world in that he is the only Saviour for all peoples, and he saves people from every nation (Revelation 5:9). Those who reject him are not saved (John 3:18, 36).

What does he actually save me from? From sin in every dimension. From its guilt: he bore the penalty, so there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). From God’s wrath, which we deserved (1 Thessalonians 1:10). From sin’s power: he breaks its rule and gives us the Spirit to fight it (Romans 6:14). From the devil, who held us captive (Hebrews 2:14–15). From death, which he defeated by rising (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). And one day from sin’s very presence, when we see him and are made like him (3:2). He saves us not only from all that, but for himself: for fellowship with God, which is eternal life.

In a sentence. And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent his Son to be the Saviour of the world.

On a Tuesday. Praise Jesus, the Saviour of the world. Pray for a nation or people group that needs to hear of him. Find out the name of one unreached people, learn three facts about them, and pray for them by name each day this week.

For worship. The Father sent the Son. Out of the love of the Trinity a Saviour came into a world that had no claim on him, and he came not for one tribe but for the world. Emperors claimed the title and died. He took it and rose. From Samaritan villages and Roman garrisons, from every century and continent, a people is being gathered who will say with one voice, this is indeed the Saviour of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.

Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God. “Confesses” (homologēsē) means acknowledges, declares. This is the true confession, which the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). Not merely words, but genuine faith that Jesus, the man, is the eternal Son of God. It is the outer confirmation of abiding, corresponding to the inner confirmation of the Spirit in verse 13. To confess him is to entrust oneself to him and to say, with full personal weight: this Jesus is the Son of God.

God abides in him, and he in God. Confession of Christ is evidence of union with God; faith, love and the Spirit all bear witness together. Confession is not a condition for abiding in the sense of a work that earns it; it is the open hand of faith that receives the gift of union with God.

Peter at Caesarea Philippi. When Peter said, you are the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus told him that flesh and blood had not revealed it to him, but his Father in heaven (Matthew 16:16–17). That is the confession of this verse, and it is always a gift. No one says it truly by his own insight. Every time a person confesses Jesus as the Son of God from the heart, heaven has been at work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that merely reciting a creed brings union with God. The confession must come from genuine faith (Romans 10:9–10), and it will be accompanied by love (v. 16).

Is confession a one-time act, and must it be public? It begins at a point and continues for life. The New Testament expects the first confession to be made openly, and baptism is the appointed way: a believer is baptised on his profession of faith, publicly declaring that he belongs to Christ (Acts 2:41; 8:36–38; Romans 10:9–10). But confession does not stop at the water. It continues in worship, in speaking of Christ to others, and in standing for him when it costs. Jesus said that whoever acknowledges him before men, he will acknowledge before his Father (Matthew 10:32). A secret faith that never confesses is in danger.

In a sentence. If anyone acknowledges that Jesus is the Son of God, God lives in them and they in God.

On a Tuesday. Confess today, aloud: Jesus is the Son of God. Say it to God in prayer, and look for one opportunity to say it to someone else, simply and without embarrassment. And if you believe but have never been baptised, speak to your pastor this week.

For worship. Jesus is the Son of God. The baby in the manger, the man on the cross, the body in the tomb, the Lord on the throne: one person, the eternal Son. To confess him is to be joined to God himself. There is no higher dignity a human tongue can have than to speak that truth, and no deeper safety a human soul can know than to be found in him.

verseByVerse.quote: So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him.

So we have come to know and to believe the love that God has for us. “Come to know” (egnōkamen) and “believe” (pepisteukamen) are both perfect tense: we have known and believed, and continue to. To know is the relational knowing that has accumulated over time; to believe is committed trust, placed and continuing. We know his love because he has shown it (vv. 9–10); we rely on it by faith, and the two go together. “Has for us” (echei en hēmin) means has in us, among us.

The same two verbs. John had heard these two verbs together before. When many disciples walked away from Jesus, Peter answered for the Twelve: we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God (John 6:69). Now, at the end of a long life, John uses the same pair, in reverse order, and the object has become the love God has for us. The love of God is not known apart from the Son; it is known in him. To believe in God’s love is to put your weight on Christ, and to know it is to have spent a lifetime in his company and found him true.

God is love. This is repeated from verse 8 for emphasis. Now the second declaration frames the mutual indwelling: to abide in love is to abide in God, because God and love cannot finally be separated.

And whoever abides in love abides in God, and God abides in him. “Abides in love” (menōn en tē agapē) means lives continually in God’s love, receiving it and showing it. To live in love is to live in God, because God is love. Love is not a virtue we add to our relationship with God; love is the atmosphere in which God himself dwells, and where his love is received and passed on, there God is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who loves anything is in God. The love in view is God’s love revealed in Christ, received by faith (v. 15).

How do I come to know and believe God’s love when I do not feel loved? By looking where John looks: not inward first, but at the cross. Feelings of being loved are affected by temperament, illness, upbringing and circumstances, and they can lie. The fact of God’s love was settled in history, when he sent his Son (v. 10). Read the accounts of the crucifixion slowly and say: this was for me. Rely on it the way you rely on a bridge, by putting your weight on it, not by first feeling confident. Speak it back to God in prayer. And let other believers love you; God often makes his love felt through his people.

In a sentence. And so we know and rely on the love God has for us. God is love. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God in them.

On a Tuesday. Rest in God’s love for you today. Know it, believe it, and live in it. When you catch yourself acting from fear, of failure, of people, of the future, stop and say: I am loved by God. Then act from there.

For worship. We have come to know and believe the love God has for us. It took us years, and we are still learning it. But it was there before we knew it, there before we were born, there before the world began. It does not grow or shrink with our understanding. God is love, and to live in his love is to live in him, in the safest and widest and warmest place in all creation.

verseByVerse.quote: By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment, because as he is so also are we in this world.

By this is love perfected with us. “By this” refers to abiding in love (v. 16). “Perfected” (teteleiōtai) means brought to completion. Love reaching its goal has a purpose that looks to the end of history.

So that we may have confidence for the day of judgment. “Confidence” (parrēsian) is boldness, as in 2:28 and 3:21. “Day of judgment” (tē hēmera tēs kriseōs) is the final judgement at Christ’s return. Believers can face it without fear.

Because as he is so also are we in this world. “As he is”: Christ, now exalted, perfectly loved by the Father and righteous. Not as he was, but as he is: the vindicated, glorified Son, in whom the believer is hidden (Colossians 3:3). “So also are we”: we share his standing before the Father, loved as he is loved (John 17:23), accepted and righteous in him, and being made like him in love. The judgement we deserved has been borne by him, and the verdict that belongs to him is shared with those united to him by faith (Romans 8:1). The confidence of the last day is not a reward for the most sanctified; it is the gift of union with the one who has already received the Father’s declaration.

The judgement already passed. The day of judgement is the day God declares his verdict on every human life. But for the believer, that verdict has already been given, and given publicly. It was given when God raised Jesus from the dead, declaring his substitute righteous and his sacrifice accepted. The one who will sit on the throne on that day is the one who died for us. We will be judged by our Saviour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are as perfect as Christ in character now. It means they share his acceptance and standing with the Father, and are growing in his likeness.

Will believers be judged at all? Yes, but not to determine whether they are saved. Everyone will stand before the judgement seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), and the lives of believers will be opened: what was done for him will be acknowledged and rewarded, and some work that was worthless will be burned up, though the believer himself is saved (1 Corinthians 3:12–15). Our works will be shown as the evidence of our faith (Matthew 25:31–40). But the question of condemnation is closed: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). It will be a Father’s welcome, not a court deciding our fate.

In a sentence. This is how love is made complete among us, so that we will have confidence on the day of judgement: in this world we are like Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Thank God that because you are in Christ, you can face the day of judgement with confidence. Then live today in a way that you will be glad to see opened on that day: one kindness done for Christ that no one else will ever notice.

For worship. As he is, so are we. The Son sits at the right hand of the Father, crowned, beloved, beyond the reach of any accusation, and those who are in him share his place. When the books are opened and the dead stand before the throne, the believer will look up and see on the throne the face of the one who loved him and gave himself for him. The Judge is our Brother, and his verdict was spoken on Easter morning.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love.

There is no fear in love. “Fear” (phobos) here means terror, dread of punishment. Not the reverent fear of God that Scripture commends (Proverbs 1:7; 1 Peter 1:17), but the terrified dread of a criminal before a judge, the cringing of a slave before a master who knows a penalty is owed.

But perfect love casts out fear. “Perfect love” (hē teleia agapē) is complete, mature love. “Casts out” (exō ballei) means throws out, drives away, the word used of Jesus casting out demons and driving out the money changers. As we grow in knowing God’s love for us, terror is driven out. Love that has taken in the propitiation of verse 10 and the union of verse 17 displaces this dread.

For fear has to do with punishment. “Punishment” (kolasin) is penalty. Fear expects punishment. But for believers, Christ has borne the punishment (v. 10). There is nothing left to fear. The bill has been paid; the creditor has sent the receipt.

And whoever fears has not been perfected in love. Fear of judgement shows that God’s love has not yet fully reached the heart: the love that paid the penalty has not yet been fully believed. The cure is not greater willpower but a deeper knowing and believing of his love (v. 16).

Two kinds of fear. The Puritans distinguished a slavish fear from a filial fear. A slave fears his master’s whip; a son fears grieving his father. The slave wants to get away; the son wants to come close. Love casts out the first and deepens the second. The more you know that God will never punish you, the more you will hate to wound him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should never feel any fear, or that reverent fear of God is wrong. It means terror of condemnation has no place in those who know God’s love in Christ (Romans 8:15).

I still fear death and judgement. Does that mean I am not a Christian? No. It means you are not yet perfected in love, which is true of every believer this side of glory. John is describing what love does as it grows, not setting an exam you must pass first. Fear of death is natural, and even Christ was troubled at its approach (John 12:27). The cure is not to scold yourself but to feed on the gospel: Christ died to deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Hebrews 2:15). Each time the fear comes, take it to the cross and say, the punishment has been borne. Love is still casting the fear out, and it will finish the job.

In a sentence. There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear, because fear has to do with punishment. The one who fears is not made perfect in love.

On a Tuesday. If you fear God’s judgement, look again at the cross: your punishment has been borne. Let his love drive out your fear. Notice where else fear rules you, the fear of people, of failure, of the future, and ask whether God’s love for you might cast that out too.

For worship. The punishment that brought us peace was upon him. All the terror that should have been ours fell on the Son in the darkness of Calvary, and he cried out because he was forsaken, so that we never will be. Now the Father’s house is open, and his children come in not cringing but running. Perfect love has entered the world in Christ, and wherever it goes, it throws fear out of the door.

verseByVerse.quote: We love because he first loved us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We love because he first loved us.

We love because he first loved us. This is one of the most compact statements of the gospel’s logic in Scripture: six words in English, containing everything. “We love” (hēmeis agapōmen) is probably a statement rather than an exhortation (let us love). “First” (prōtos): God’s love came before we loved him or anyone (v. 10). Some manuscripts add him (we love him), others God; most likely the original simply says we love, covering love for God and for others. God’s love is the source, cause and pattern of all our love.

The echo. Our love for God and for one another is not self-generated virtue or accumulated moral character; it is the echo of a love that reached us first. Augustine said the heart is restless until it rests in God (Confessions 1.1); John adds that a heart at rest in God’s love begins at last to love.

Simon, do you love me? John had watched this verse happen. By a charcoal fire Peter had denied Jesus three times (John 18:18, 25–27); by another charcoal fire on the shore the risen Lord cooked him breakfast and asked him three times, do you love me (John 21:9, 15–17). Peter’s love had failed completely, and Christ came first: he lit the fire, fed the man who had denied him, and restored him. Every Christian’s story has the same order: the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me (Galatians 2:20), and only then did I love him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we loved God before he drew us. Our love is entirely his gift and work in us (Romans 5:5). This is grace: God loves first, and his love produces ours.

Did I choose God, or did he choose me? Both are true, but not in the same way. You really did turn to God and trust Christ; you were not dragged against your will. But your choosing was the fruit of his. You did not choose me, but I chose you, Jesus said (John 15:16), and God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), not because of anything he foresaw in us but because of his own love (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). When you came to him, you found he had been coming to you all along. That is not a cause for confusion but for worship, and it means your salvation rests on something stronger than your grip.

In a sentence. We love because he first loved us.

On a Tuesday. Memorise this verse. Let it humble you and fill you with gratitude: he loved you first. The next time you are proud of how much you love God, or discouraged by how little, remember that your love was never the starting point. His was.

For worship. He loved us first. Before we were born, before we sinned, before the world was made, he set his love on us. When we were running from him, he came after us; when we were dead, he made us alive. Every flicker of love we now have for him is the reflection of a fire that has been burning toward us from eternity. We love, because he first loved us, and he will go on loving us first for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone says, 'I love God,' and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.

If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. Another false claim, as in 1:6, 8, 10; 2:4, 6, 9. A claim to love God while hating a fellow believer is not merely inconsistent but impossible.

For he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen. “Has seen” (heōraken). The argument moves from easier to harder: if you cannot love a visible person, how can you love the invisible God? Love for God is tested by love for his children, who bear his image and are his family. It is easy to love a God you have imagined. It is much harder to love the man who sits in front of you at church, with his irritating habits and disappointing failures, and that is the point. If the love of God has truly been received, it will flow toward his other children too.

The brother Christ is not ashamed of. The brother you have seen is not only God’s child; he is Christ’s brother. The Son is not ashamed to call his people brothers (Hebrews 2:11), and he said that whatever is done to the least of his brothers is done to him (Matthew 25:40). The difficult man in the next pew is a brother for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11). Hatred of him cannot sit beside love for God, because it despises the one the Son was glad to call family and bought with his own blood.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for God depends on love for people. Love for God comes first. But the two are so connected that the absence of one exposes the absence of the other.

Can I love God and still struggle to forgive a brother? Yes, for a time; struggling is not the same as hating. Forgiving a deep wound is often a process, not a moment, and believers can be genuinely fighting to forgive while still feeling the pain. What John condemns is settled hatred that refuses to forgive and does not want to. If you are praying for the grace to forgive, asking God to bless the one who hurt you even through gritted teeth, and refusing to take revenge, you are not the liar of this verse. You are a Christian doing one of the hardest things a Christian is asked to do. Keep going.

In a sentence. Whoever claims to love God yet hates a brother or sister is a liar. For whoever does not love their brother and sister, whom they have seen, cannot love God, whom they have not seen.

On a Tuesday. Your love for God will show in how you treat his people this week. Love them practically. Choose one believer you see regularly and find it hard to love, and ask God to let you see him as one of his own children, which he is.

For worship. God has put his children in front of us so that our love for him would have somewhere to go. Every brother is a gift, even the difficult ones, because each one is a place where the invisible God can be loved in visible ways. And the God whom we have not seen has seen us: all our ugliness, all our hatred, all our failure to love. He loved us anyway, and he did not stay unseen. He came near enough to be looked at and touched, and he wore a brother’s face for us.

verseByVerse.quote: And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this commandment we have from him: whoever loves God must also love his brother.

And this commandment we have from him. “From him” is from Christ, or God. The inseparability argued in verse 20 is now grounded in the commandment itself.

Whoever loves God must also love his brother. “Must also” (kai): also. The two great commandments, love for God and love for neighbour, are inseparable. To love God genuinely is to love what God loves, and God loves his children. The chapter began with the command to test the spirits; it ends with the command to love the brothers. The two are not unrelated: the Spirit of truth always produces love, and the spirit of error always, eventually, produces division.

Both loves in one act. The commandment came from Christ, who summed up the whole law as love for God and love for neighbour (Mark 12:29–31), and he did more than command it. On his way out to Gethsemane he said, I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father (John 14:31); and having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1). At the cross his love for the Father and his love for his brothers were one act of obedience. The commandment we have from him is the shape of his own life, now being written into ours.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for others is equal to love for God. God is to be loved with all our heart; neighbours as ourselves. But love for God always overflows in love for others.

What if loving a brother seems to conflict with loving God? Then love God first, and you will find that this is the truest love for your brother too. If a brother asks you to sin, to lie for him, to join in his wrongdoing, or to approve what God forbids, love for God says no, and so does real love for him, because it seeks his good, not his comfort (Acts 5:29; Matthew 10:37). Loving a brother never requires disobeying God. Usually there is no conflict at all: the God you love commands you to love, and the brother you love is best served by your obedience to God.

In a sentence. And he has given us this command: anyone who loves God must also love their brother and sister.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to deepen your love for him today, and to let it overflow to the people around you. Before you pray tomorrow morning, think of one brother or sister you will see during the day, and pray for them first.

For worship. The God who commands both loves is gathering a family in which both will one day be perfect. Here our love for him is faint and our love for one another is patchy, and we fail at the very point where the command presses hardest. But the Son who kept the commandment for us is making us like himself. A day is coming when no brother will be hard to love and no heart will be cold toward the Father, and the whole household of God will fill heaven with a love that never grows cold.

4.theology:
God is Love. The statement "God is love" (vv. 8, 16) is one of the most misused sentences in Scripture. It is taken to mean that love is God — that whatever we call love must be divine, that God must approve of whatever we name as love. John means the opposite: God defines love, not the other way around. And he defines it immediately by a specific act: the sending of the Son to be the propitiation. To say "God is love" in John's sense is to say that God, in his innermost being, is the kind of God who sends his only Son into the world to die for sinners who could not save themselves. That is the love John is talking about. It is not soft; it is costly. It is not tolerant; it is propitiatory. It is not vague; it has flesh and blood and a cross and an empty tomb.

The Expulsion of Fear. The pastoral application of the doctrine of propitiation in verses 17–18 is one of the most comforting passages in the New Testament. The believer who is tortured by fear of God's judgment has not yet fully grasped what the propitiation means: that the very wrath they fear has been exhausted, absorbed, satisfied in the beloved Son. Perfect love casts out fear not by denying the reality of judgment but by pointing to the one who bore it. Reformed theology speaks of the "double jeopardy" of the cross: it would be unjust for God to punish twice what Christ has already borne. The blood of Jesus is the answer to every accusing conscience, every fear of condemnation, every midnight terror of a soul that wonders whether it is safe with God.
4.examples:
Then: The community had been shaken by teachers who claimed spiritual authority and offered a more sophisticated understanding of God. The test John gives is arrestingly simple: do they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Not "do they seem spiritual?" Not "do they have impressive experiences?" But: do they hold to the incarnation? This is always the fault line. Every theological error that has ever devastated a church has at some point compromised either the full deity or the full humanity of Christ. John's readers are given a test simple enough for a child and decisive enough to unmask every false spirit.

Now: "We love because he first loved us" is the answer to every form of Christian guilt and striving. The Christian life is not a performance of love in order to earn God's approval; it is a response of love to a love already given, already completed, already victorious at the cross. When love runs dry — as it will — the answer is not to try harder but to go back to the source: "In this is love, not that we have loved God..." The spring of all Christian love is the love of God in the cross of his Son. Drink there again, and love will flow.

5.title: Faith that Overcomes, Life that is Sure
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.<sup>2</sup>By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.<sup>3</sup>For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.<sup>4</sup>For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.<sup>5</sup>Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?<sup>6</sup>This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.<sup>7</sup>For there are three that testify:<sup>8</sup>the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.<sup>9</sup>If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.<sup>10</sup>Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.<sup>11</sup>And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.<sup>12</sup>Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.<sup>13</sup>I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.<sup>14</sup>And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.<sup>15</sup>And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.<sup>16</sup>If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that.<sup>17</sup>All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.<sup>18</sup>We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.<sup>19</sup>We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.<sup>20</sup>And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.<sup>21</sup>Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
5.overview:
The last chapter draws the letter’s threads together. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, loves God’s children and overcomes the world, and the victory is faith. God has testified about his Son, and his testimony is this: eternal life is in the Son. “Whoever has the Son has life.”

Then John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Not hope or feel, but know. Those who know may pray with confidence and intercede for a sinning brother. The letter ends with Jesus Christ declared “the true God and eternal life”, and one last command: keep yourselves from idols.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Faith, Love, and the World-Overcoming Victory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John ties faith, new birth and love together as a single reality. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Messiah has been born of God, and anyone who loves the Father loves his children too. We know we love God’s children when we love God and keep his commands, and his commands are not a crushing weight. For everyone born of God overcomes the world, and the victory that overcomes the world is our faith. Who overcomes the world? Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as the Victory

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children. Faith in the Son of God overcomes the world.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Ordinary faith in Jesus was being called insufficient.

Now: The faith that overcomes is not heroic; it is trust in the Son of God who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him.

Meaning first. 1 John 5 draws the letter together around faith in the Son of God and the assurance it brings. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God and loves God’s children; his commands are not burdensome, because faith overcomes the world (vv. 1–5). Jesus came by water and blood, his baptism and his death, and the Spirit, the water and the blood all testify to him: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son (vv. 6–12). John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life (v. 13). They can pray with confidence, and should pray for a brother who sins, though there is a sin that leads to death (vv. 14–17). The letter closes with three certainties: Christ keeps those born of God; we are from God, while the world lies in the power of the evil one; and the Son of God has come, so that we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ, the true God and eternal life (vv. 18–20). Last word: little children, keep yourselves from idols (v. 21). The letter that began with hands touching the Word of life ends by naming him the true God.

Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ. “Believes” (pisteuōn) is present tense: keeps believing. “That Jesus is the Christ” is the confession the false teachers denied (2:22). It is faith in the person of Christ. The three great themes of the letter, faith, new birth and love, are bound together in this single verse, which is the hinge between chapters 4 and 5.

Has been born of God. “Has been born” (gegennētai) is perfect tense: has been born and remains so. Notice the order: the present tense believes is the evidence of the perfect tense has been born. New birth comes first; faith follows as its result and sign. As in 2:29, 3:9 and 4:7, the new birth produces righteousness, love, and here, faith. Regeneration precedes faith.

Lazarus in the tomb. Jesus stood at the grave and called, Lazarus, come out (John 11:43). Lazarus came. But nobody imagines that he first decided to come out and then was made alive. He could not hear until he was alive, and the voice that called him gave him the life to answer. That is the order of this verse. A dead man does not cooperate in his own resurrection; he walks out because he has been raised.

And everyone who loves the Father loves whoever has been born of him. “The Father” is literally the one who begot (ton gennēsanta). A family principle: if you love a father, you love his children. Family love is not optional for those who genuinely love the head of the family; it reaches all who bear the family likeness.

Where Christians differ: does faith cause new birth, or does new birth cause faith? Arminians generally hold that a person believes and is then born again, with faith coming from the person’s free choice enabled by prevenient grace. Verdict: The grammar of this verse, and John’s pattern throughout (2:29; 3:9; 4:7), shows that being born of God comes first and produces faith, righteousness and love. Jesus taught that one must be born again to see the kingdom (John 3:3), and that those who believe were born of God (John 1:12–13). Dead sinners cannot believe until God gives them life (Ephesians 2:1–5). This is effectual calling: God regenerates, and the regenerate believe. Faith is truly ours, but it is the fruit of God’s prior work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is unnecessary or passive. Those born of God truly and actively believe. Nor does it mean a person can be born again and never believe; faith always follows.

If new birth comes before faith, should an unbeliever just wait to be born again? No. The command to everyone is to repent and believe now (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30), and no one has to wait. God gives new birth through the hearing of the gospel (1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18), so the place to be is under the word, and the thing to do is to come to Christ. If you find that you want him, that wanting is itself a sign that God is at work. Do not try to look behind the curtain to see whether you have been born again before you believe. Believe, and you will find that you were.

In a sentence. Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and everyone who loves the father loves his child as well.

On a Tuesday. If you believe that Jesus is the Christ, thank God: it is evidence that he has given you new birth. Then look around your church this Sunday and say to yourself of each person: born of the same Father. Greet one you have never spoken to.

For worship. God does not wait for the dead to make the first move. He speaks into the grave, and the dead live. Every believer in every age is a walking resurrection, a sinner who could not come until God made him alive and then came running. Our faith is real, but it is his gift, and the Father who begot us into his family will never disown one child he has made.

verseByVerse.quote: By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments.

By this we know that we love the children of God. Earlier, love for others proved love for God (4:20). Now, the reverse: love for God proves love for others is genuine. The two tests are complementary: there is no God-centred obedience that excludes love for his people, and no genuine love for his people that excludes obedience to God.

When we love God and obey his commandments. True love for others is rooted in love for God and expressed in obedience. Love for people that ignores God’s commands is not genuine love. Sometimes love requires saying no, correcting, or refusing to approve sin, because God commands it. Love for God expresses itself in obedience to his commandments, which include the command to love the brothers.

As I have kept my Father’s commandments. John learned this order from Jesus. In the upper room the Lord said, if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15), and then gave himself as the pattern: if you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love (John 15:10). The Son’s whole life was love for the Father expressed in obedience, and that obedience was love for us, for the Father’s charge was that he lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:17–18). In Christ, loving God, obeying him and loving his children were never apart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love for others is merely obedience to rules. It means genuine love for others flows from love for God and follows his ways.

What if a fellow Christian says I am unloving because I will not approve of his sin? Then examine yourself honestly, and then stand firm gently. Ask: have I been harsh, proud or careless in how I spoke? If so, apologise for that. But love does not mean celebrating what God forbids. A doctor who tells a patient that a tumour is harmless is not kind. True love keeps the friendship open, speaks the truth with tears rather than contempt, does practical good, and prays. Jesus was the most loving man who ever lived, and he told the woman caught in adultery both that he did not condemn her and that she must go and sin no more (John 8:11).

In a sentence. This is how we know that we love the children of God: by loving God and carrying out his commands.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to deepen your love for him, so that your love for others becomes truer. Think of one relationship where you have been choosing comfort over truth, or truth without kindness, and ask God for the balance.

For worship. The love that flows between the Father and the Son has found its way into a family. The Son obeyed the Father, and out of that obedience came the cross, where children were bought for the Father’s house. Now the same love runs through them: they love the Father, they keep his word, and they love one another, clumsily but truly. God is not collecting private devotees. He is raising a household in which every child bears the likeness of the eldest Brother.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome.

For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. “The love of God” here means our love for God. “Keep” (tērōmen). Love for God is not merely emotion; it is obedience (John 14:15, 21, 23). This is a thoroughly biblical equation, as old as Moses, who joined loving the LORD to keeping his charge, his statutes, his rules and his commandments always (Deuteronomy 11:1).

And his commandments are not burdensome. “Burdensome” (bareiai) means heavy, oppressive, crushing. Contrast the heavy burdens the Pharisees laid on people (Matthew 23:4). Jesus said, “My yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). God’s commands are not crushing, because they are good, they come from a loving Father, and he gives the new heart and Spirit to keep them (v. 4; Ezekiel 36:26–27). For the one born of God and indwelt by the Spirit, the new birth creates the capacity to delight in what God commands (Psalm 119:35; Romans 7:22).

Why his yoke is easy. The commandments are not burdensome because Christ has carried the crushing part of them. The law’s curse fell on him: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). What he lays on his people now is not the law as a ladder up to God but his own yoke, and he calls the weary to take it as one who is gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:28–29). The commandments are no smaller in content. They are lighter because the one who gives them has already borne their penalty, and gives the Spirit to keep them.

The wings of a bird. An old preacher’s image: wings add weight to a bird, and yet they are not a burden; they are what lift it. Take them off to lighten the load, and the bird can no longer fly. God’s commandments are like that for his children. They feel like weight only to those who do not yet know what they are for. To a heart that loves God they are the very means of rising toward him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean obedience is always easy or painless. Sometimes it is costly. But it is not a crushing weight, because love makes it light.

Then why does obedience sometimes feel so hard? Because sin still lives in us, and the old nature pulls against the new (Galatians 5:17). The command is not heavy; our resistance makes it feel heavy. Some obedience is hard because it costs: forgiving a deep wrong, giving up a relationship, telling the truth at a price. Jesus himself sweated in Gethsemane. Not burdensome does not mean effortless. It means the command is good, the Father who gives it is kind, and the strength to obey comes with it. When obedience feels like grinding burden, the question is not first how do I try harder, but is the love of God real and growing in me? Go back to his love, and the load will lighten.

In a sentence. In fact, this is love for God: to keep his commands. And his commands are not burdensome,

On a Tuesday. Does obedience feel like a burden? Ask God to renew your love for him; love makes his commands a delight. Choose one command you find heavy, and before you obey it today, thank God for what it shows you about his goodness.

For worship. The God who commands is the God who loves, and he never asks his children to carry what he has not first lifted. His commandments are the shape of the life his Son lived, and they are written now on hearts he has made new. What once came as tablets of stone and a sentence of guilt has become, in Christ, the delight of a child who wants to please his Father. The law that once condemned us has become the road we walk with him, and every step of it leads home.

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith.

For everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. “Everyone” (pan) is neuter: everything that has been born of God, stressing the birth more than the person. “Overcomes” (nika) means conquers, wins victory, present tense. “The world” is the system opposed to God (2:15–17). God’s children are not crushed by the world but triumph over it, and this is why his commands are not burdensome.

And this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith. “Victory” (nikē) is the only use of this word in the New Testament, and the name of the Greek goddess of victory, whose statues were familiar across the cities of Asia. “Has overcome” (nikēsasa) is aorist: a decisive victory. The decisive victory was won when Christ overcame the world (John 16:33) and when we first believed. “Our faith”: faith is the means by which we share Christ’s victory. Not our strength, but trust in the victorious Christ: faith is the hand that reaches out and holds the one who has already won.

The old man in the arena. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, had been a disciple of John himself. In about AD 155, as an old man, he was brought into the stadium and the proconsul urged him to swear by the emperor and curse Christ, and he would be released. He answered that for eighty-six years he had served Christ, and Christ had never done him wrong; how could he blaspheme his King who saved him? He was burnt. The crowd thought they had watched the world defeat an old man. They had watched faith overcome the world.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never struggle or lose battles. It means the war is won, and faith keeps winning.

I feel defeated by the world, not overcoming it. How is this true of me? Overcoming the world does not mean winning every skirmish or feeling triumphant. It means the world cannot finally have you. It cannot make you stop trusting Christ for good, cannot take your eternal life, cannot separate you from his love (Romans 8:35–39). Every time you turn back to Christ after failing, refuse a temptation, keep believing through grief, or choose obedience over the world’s approval, you are overcoming. Victory is often quiet and looks like perseverance. And your victory rests on his, which was complete when he rose from the dead.

In a sentence. for everyone born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world, even our faith.

On a Tuesday. Thank Christ for his victory over the world. Trust him today, and share in it. Name one way the world is pressing you this week: to fear, to envy, to conform, to despair. Answer it with one act of trust in Christ.

For worship. Christ has overcome the world. He said it in the upper room the night before the world crucified him, and three days later he walked out of the grave to prove it. Every power that set itself against him is broken. Every believer who trusts him, however weak, is joined to that victory. The world may still roar, but it roars at a people whom it cannot defeat, because their faith rests on one who has already won.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?

Who is it that overcomes the world. A rhetorical question, and it has exactly one answer.

Except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? Only those who believe that Jesus, the man, is the divine Son of God overcome the world. Not faith in general, but faith in Jesus as the Son of God. This is precisely what the false teachers denied (2:22–23; 4:2–3). Without true faith in the true Christ, there is no victory. Not a generic spirituality, not trust in a divine principle, not confidence in one’s own spiritual resources, but faith in this person, with this identity, doing this work. The question is exclusive by design and inclusive by invitation: anyone who believes this overcomes; no one who refuses it does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith in itself, as a psychological force, overcomes. The object of faith is what matters: Jesus, the Son of God.

What if my faith is weak? Does it still overcome? Yes, because it is not the strength of your faith that wins but the strength of the one you trust. A child holding his father’s hand across a busy road is safe not because his grip is strong but because his father’s is. A weak faith in a strong Christ overcomes; a strong faith in a false Christ does not. Jesus spoke of faith like a grain of mustard seed (Matthew 17:20), and a man once cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and Jesus helped him. Bring the faith you have, and ask him to grow it.

In a sentence. Who is it that overcomes the world? Only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Confess today that Jesus is the Son of God, and stand in his victory over the world. When you feel overwhelmed, do not first measure your faith. Look at its object, and say his name.

For worship. Jesus is the Son of God. The eternal Son took flesh, fought the world on its own ground, and won. To believe in him is to stand on the winning side of history before the battle is over. No empire, no ideology, no persecution, no temptation has ever conquered one who truly trusted him, and none ever will. The victory belongs to the Son, and he shares it with all who believe.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Three Witnesses and the Life That Is in the Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Jewish law a matter was settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides three: the Spirit, the water and the blood. The water and blood mark the beginning and end of Jesus’ ministry, his baptism and his death. God’s own testimony is greater than any human testimony, and it is this: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. There is no middle ground: whoever has the Son has life.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Witnesses

The Spirit, the water and the blood agree: the one who was baptised is the one who died. God has given eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The false teaching separated the Christ of the baptism from the Jesus of the cross.

Now: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is he who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ; not by the water only but by the water and the blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.

This is he who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. This is the most debated verse in the chapter. “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death, the public events that mark the beginning and end of his ministry and together declare who he is. At his baptism, the Father declared him Son and the Spirit descended (Mark 1:9–11). At his death, he shed his blood for sins (1:7). Some see a reference to the water and blood that flowed from his side (John 19:34), or to baptism and the Lord’s Supper, but the baptism-and-death reading fits the context best.

Not by the water only but by the water and the blood. The false teachers, like Cerinthus, apparently taught that the divine Christ came on Jesus at his baptism (water) but left before his death (blood), so that only the man Jesus died. John insists: Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came through both. The Son of God himself died on the cross. The false teaching would happily keep a heavenly Christ who descended on the river bank and spoke beautiful words; it could not bear a Christ who bled. John will not let the blood be taken away, because the blood is where the salvation is.

And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth. “Testifies” (martyroun) means bears witness. The Holy Spirit bears witness to Christ: at his baptism, through the apostles’ preaching, through Scripture, and in believers’ hearts (John 15:26; 16:14). The Spirit is the truth: the Spirit of truth (John 14:17). And the Spirit, who is truth itself, bears witness not to a divided Christ but to the one Jesus Christ who is both God and man.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the water of baptism saves. John speaks of Christ’s historical baptism and death as the events that testify to who he is.

Why does it matter that the Son of God himself died, and not only the man Jesus? Because a mere man’s death could pay for, at most, one man’s sins, and not even his own if he were a sinner. The worth of the sacrifice depends on who offers it. Because the one who died was the eternal Son, truly man and truly God in one person, his death has infinite value, enough for all his people of every age (Hebrews 9:14; Acts 20:28). Scripture can even say that they crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). God did not send someone else to suffer while he stayed safe. He came himself.

In a sentence. This is the one who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ. He did not come by water only, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies, because the Spirit is the truth.

On a Tuesday. When you hear Christianity described as a set of fine teachings, remember the blood. The heart of the faith is not Jesus’ advice but his death. Read one of the Gospel accounts of the crucifixion this week and say at each step: this was the Son of God.

For worship. He came by water and blood. The one on whom the Spirit descended like a dove at the Jordan is the one who hung on the cross at Golgotha; the voice from heaven that said this is my beloved Son spoke of the man who would cry, it is finished. God did not hand our salvation to a substitute while keeping his distance. The eternal Son was baptised into our condition and bled to end it, and the Spirit of truth will not let us forget it.
verseByVerse.note: “Water and blood” probably refer to Jesus’ baptism and his death — against teachers who said the divine Christ left Jesus before the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there are three that testify: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.

For there are three that testify. “Three”: the Old Testament required two or three witnesses to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). The legal background is a court. God provides three, and they agree.

The Spirit and the water and the blood. The Spirit testifies to Christ; the water (his baptism) and the blood (his death) testify by what happened at them. The Spirit’s testimony is the inward, ongoing witness given to believers (v. 10; 4:13); the water and the blood are the historical events that publicly declared his identity at the beginning of his ministry and at its completion.

And these three agree. “Agree” (eis to hen eisin) means are toward the one thing, converge. All three bear one consistent witness: Jesus is the Son of God who came in the flesh and died for sins. The convergence of these witnesses is not accidental but providential: God has ensured that the testimony to his Son is abundant, consistent and legally sufficient. Those who deny it are not lacking evidence; they are refusing it.

Textual note. Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven, known as the Johannine Comma: “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth.” These words appear in the King James Version, but they are not found in any Greek manuscript before the fourteenth century (and then only in a handful), are absent from the early church fathers who debated the Trinity and would surely have quoted them, and appear to have originated as a marginal comment in some Latin manuscripts that later crept into the text. Erasmus left them out of the first two editions of his printed Greek New Testament and added them in the third, after a single late Greek manuscript containing them was produced; from that line of printed texts they passed into the King James Version. However true the statement is in itself, it is almost certainly not part of what John wrote. The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on them; it is taught clearly throughout Scripture (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14; John 1:1; 14:16–17). And the three witnesses John actually gave, Spirit, water and blood, supply all the testimony his argument needs.

What it does not mean. Removing the late addition does not weaken the doctrine of the Trinity. It simply means we rest the doctrine on what Scripture actually says.

Does this mean the Bible has errors, or that I should not use the King James Version? Neither. The Bible as God gave it is without error. God has preserved his word through thousands of manuscripts, more than for any other ancient book, and comparing them lets us see almost exactly what the apostles wrote; the places where manuscripts differ are few, mostly tiny, and none of them changes any doctrine. Noticing a later addition is part of honouring the original. The King James Version is a noble translation that has fed believers for four centuries, and you can read it with profit, simply knowing that this one sentence was added later. Modern translations mark such places in a footnote.

In a sentence. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water and the blood; and the three are in agreement.

On a Tuesday. If someone tells you that the Bible has been changed beyond recognition, you can answer calmly: we know where the few doubtful places are precisely because we have so many manuscripts, and none of them touches the gospel. Thank God for that, and keep reading the word he has kept.

For worship. God is not silent about his Son, and he is not vague. He has spoken at the river and at the cross, and he speaks by his Spirit in every heart that believes. Three witnesses, one testimony, all agreeing: this is my Son. The God who cannot lie has made sure that no one who wants to know who Jesus is need be left without evidence, and he has preserved that testimony through every century for us.
verseByVerse.note: Some late manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in heaven (known from the King James Version). They are not in the early Greek manuscripts and the ESV omits them.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we receive the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater, for this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son.

If we receive the testimony of men. “Receive” (lambanomen) means accept. We accept human testimony every day: in courts, history, science, ordinary life. We trust the doctor’s diagnosis, the map, the history book, the friend who tells us the road is closed.

The testimony of God is greater. “Greater” (meizōn) means more reliable, more authoritative. God cannot lie (Titus 1:2). If we trust human witnesses, how much more God. God is the one who is truth itself, who cannot be deceived and cannot deceive.

For this is the testimony of God that he has borne concerning his Son. “Has borne” (memartyrēken) is perfect tense: has testified and the testimony stands. God the Father has testified about his Son: at his baptism, the transfiguration, his miracles, his resurrection, through the Spirit and the Scriptures (John 5:31–39; 8:18). At the Jordan and on the mountain the Father’s own voice was heard: this is my beloved Son (Matthew 3:17; 17:5). And in raising him from the dead, God declared him to be the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean human testimony is worthless. The apostles’ eyewitness testimony is God’s means of testifying (1:1–3). But behind their testimony is God’s own.

Where do I hear God’s testimony today? In Scripture, above all. The Father’s voice at the Jordan, the miracles, the empty tomb and the apostles’ witness are all recorded there, and the Bible is God’s own testimony in written form (2 Timothy 3:16). You hear it whenever the word is read and preached. And the Spirit who inspired it confirms it in your heart as you read and hear (v. 10). You do not need a private voice or a vision. Open the Gospels, and God himself is testifying to you about his Son.

In a sentence. We accept human testimony, but God’s testimony is greater, because it is the testimony of God, which he has given about his Son.

On a Tuesday. Trust God’s testimony about his Son today, more than any human opinion. Notice how readily you believe the news, the forecast or a friend’s report, and then ask why you hesitate over what God has said. Read Matthew 3:13–17 and hear the Father speak.

For worship. The Father has never been neutral about his Son. Men weighed Jesus and found him wanting: the priests called him a blasphemer, Pilate washed his hands, the crowd chose Barabbas. Then God gave his verdict, and he gave it from an empty tomb. Every human testimony against the Son has been overturned by the testimony that is greater, and the God who cannot lie invites us to rest our whole weight on his word about Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son.

Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony in himself. “Believes in” (pisteuōn eis) is literally trusts into, puts faith in. “Has the testimony in himself”: God’s outward testimony becomes an inward witness in the believer, by the Spirit (Romans 8:16; Galatians 4:6). Faith receives and takes in God’s witness. This is not private subjectivism; it is the objective testimony of God, confirmed by the Spirit within the believer’s own experience of new life.

Whoever does not believe God has made him a liar. Unbelief is not neutral or merely intellectual; it calls God a liar (1:10). To receive a witness’s testimony, hear it clearly, and then refuse it is not a neutral act of caution; it is an attack on the witness’s truthfulness.

Because he has not believed in the testimony that God has borne concerning his Son. Unbelief in the gospel is not merely a spiritual problem; it is a slander against the God who testified.

Honouring the Son. Why is unbelief so grave? Because God’s testimony is about the one he loves most. Jesus said that whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him (John 5:23), and John had written that whoever receives Christ’s testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true (John 3:33). To refuse Jesus is not to decline one religious option among many; it is to tell the Father that his word about his beloved Son is false. To believe in him is the reverse: it is to say amen to God about Jesus.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every doubt is calling God a liar. Honest struggles with doubt are different from settled unbelief (Mark 9:24; Jude 22).

What if I do not sense any inner witness? The inner witness is usually quieter than people expect. It is not normally a voice or a feeling of certainty, but the simple fact that, when you hear the gospel, you find it true and cannot let it go; that Christ is precious to you; that you call God Father; that you want to obey him. That is the Spirit at work (Romans 8:15–16). And the inner witness always rests on the outer one: God’s testimony in Scripture. If your sense of assurance is faint, do not go looking inside yourself for it. Go back to the testimony, read it, and believe it. The inner witness grows as you feed on the outer.

In a sentence. Whoever believes in the Son of God accepts this testimony. Whoever does not believe God has made him out to be a liar, because they have not believed the testimony God has given about his Son.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the inner witness of his Spirit, confirming that his testimony about Jesus is true. If you have a friend who does not believe, pray that he will hear the testimony with new ears, and ask God for an opening to share why you believe it.

For worship. God does not leave his testimony outside us, like a notice on a board. He writes it on the heart. The Spirit who spoke through the prophets and apostles now speaks within the believer, saying amen to every word about the Son. We have the testimony in ourselves because God has come to live in us. His truth has become our conviction, and our conviction is his gift.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.

And this is the testimony, that God gave us eternal life. Here is the content of God’s testimony, stated with the economy of a creed. “Gave” (edōken) is aorist: a completed gift. Eternal life is a gift, already given to believers (John 3:16; 10:28; Romans 6:23). Already accomplished, already given, requiring only to be received.

And this life is in his Son. “In his Son” (en tō huiō autou). Eternal life is not a thing separate from Christ, but found in him, in union with him (John 1:4; 11:25; 14:6). Eternal life is not a commodity distributed apart from Christ; it is located in a person, which is why having the Son (v. 12) and having life are the same thing. No formula, ritual, spiritual discipline or religious achievement can transfer the life apart from the Son in whom it lives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eternal life is only future. It is a present possession (v. 13).

Were Old Testament believers saved through the Son too? Yes. There has only ever been one way of salvation: by grace, through faith, in Christ. Old Testament believers looked forward to the promised Redeemer through the promises and sacrifices God gave, as we look back to him (Romans 4:1–8; Hebrews 11:13, 26; John 8:56). Abraham rejoiced to see Christ’s day; Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures. The life they received was the same life, and it was in the same Son, whose sacrifice covered the sins of his people before his coming as well as after (Romans 3:25).

In a sentence. And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the gift of eternal life, which is yours in his Son. When you are tempted to look for life elsewhere, in success, in a relationship, in an experience, remind yourself where it is kept: in the Son, and nowhere else.

For worship. God gave us eternal life, and he wrapped it in his Son. He did not hand us a thing and send us away; he gave us a person, and the life is in him. To have him is to have everything: the life of God himself, unending, unspoilable, beginning now and opening out for ever. The Father could give no greater gift, because he has nothing greater than his Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.

Whoever has the Son has life. “Has” (echōn) means possesses, holds: in a personal relationship through faith. To have Christ is to have life: the starkest contrast in the letter. Not more or less life depending on spiritual development; not life of a different quality depending on doctrinal precision: has or does not have.

Whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life. No Christ, no life. There is no other way (John 3:36; 14:6; Acts 4:12). This is Christian exclusivism, stated with utter clarity. It is both the most inclusive possible invitation, since anyone from any background may have the Son by faith, and the most exclusive possible statement, since no other means of possessing life exists. To soften this is not pastoral generosity but a failure of love: it leaves people comfortable in a condition John has just described as the absence of life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean those without Christ have no biological life. They lack eternal life, the life of God.

What about someone I loved who died without professing faith? This is one of the hardest questions a Christian carries, and Scripture does not give us a different way of salvation to ease the pain. But it does give you some things to hold. You do not know what happened in that person’s heart, perhaps in the last hours, and God is not bound by what we saw. The Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25), and he is kinder and wiser than we are. You may grieve and leave them in his hands. And let the grief make you urgent for the living: tell those still with you about the Son, while there is time.

In a sentence. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.

On a Tuesday. Do you have the Son? If so, you have life. Who do you know who does not have him yet? Pray for them and tell them. Write down three names, pray for them each day this week, and ask God for one opportunity to speak.

For worship. Life has a name, and the name is Jesus. All the life in the universe flows from him; all the life of God dwells in him; and he gives himself freely to everyone who will receive him. Whoever has the Son has life, and the Son gives himself to beggars, to children, to the dying thief, to anyone who comes. There is no one so dead that he cannot make alive, and no one who has him will ever die.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — Knowing What We Have in Christ: Assurance, Prayer, and the True God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John states his purpose: “that you may know that you have eternal life.” Those who know may pray boldly, intercede for a brother who sins, and rest in three great certainties: the one born of God is kept from the evil one; we belong to God while the world lies in the power of the evil one; and the Son of God has come and given us understanding to know the true God. He is “the true God and eternal life”. So keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.theology:
That You May Know

John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life. They may pray with confidence, intercede for a sinning brother, and rest in what they know.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The letter closes on Jesus Christ as the true God and eternal life.

Now: Having the true God, refuse every substitute.

verseByVerse.quote: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life.

I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God. “These things” are the whole letter. Here is the stated purpose of the entire letter. John writes not to evangelise but to assure: his audience already believes, and what they need is confidence in what believing gives them.

That you may know that you have eternal life. “Know” (eidēte) means know with settled certainty: not hope, not feel, not reasonably expect, but know. “Have” (echete) is present tense: eternal life is a present possession. The tests of the letter (truth about Christ, obedience, love) are not meant to make believers anxious but to give them assurance. The knowledge John offers is not the hidden knowledge of the false teachers; it is the plain, testable, Spirit-confirmed knowledge that comes from believing in the name of the Son of God. Assurance is not presumption; it is the right response to the reliability of God’s word about his Son.

Two letters, one purpose. The Gospel says (John 20:31): these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name. The letter says: I write these things to you who believe, that you may know that you have eternal life. The Gospel brings people to the door; the letter tells them they are inside. An old apostle spent his last years making sure that the children of God did not live like orphans.

In the name of the Son. John’s assurance hangs on one phrase: you who believe in the name of the Son of God. Believers can know they have eternal life because the life does not depend on the strength of their believing but on the one they believe in, and he has spoken plainly about his sheep: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John had heard those words. The certainty he offers is not confidence in ourselves; it is confidence in Christ’s promise, Christ’s blood and Christ’s grip.

Where Christians differ: can a believer be sure of salvation? Roman Catholic teaching has generally held that, apart from special revelation, no one can be certain of final salvation; some Protestants hold that assurance belongs only to a few mature believers. Verdict: John wrote so that ordinary believers may know they have eternal life. Assurance rests first on God’s promise in Christ (vv. 11–12), is confirmed by the Spirit’s inward witness (v. 10; Romans 8:16), and is supported by the fruit of faith, love and obedience. It is the normal privilege of every Christian, though it may be weak or clouded at times, and it grows as faith grows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean assurance comes from our own performance. It comes from trusting God’s testimony about his Son.

If assurance is normal, why do I lack it? There are several common reasons, and each has a remedy. Some look only at themselves, not at Christ; look first at the promise (vv. 11–12). Some are holding on to a known sin, which clouds the sense of God’s favour; confess it and turn (1:9). Some are going through suffering, depression or exhaustion, which darkens everything; be patient with yourself, and lean on others. Some were taught that doubt is proof of being lost; it is not. The Westminster Confession says that a true believer may wait long and struggle before he has assurance, and may have it shaken, but is never utterly without the seed of faith (Westminster 18.3–4). Keep coming to Christ. Assurance is the fruit of faith, not its root.

In a sentence. I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God so that you may know that you have eternal life.
