On a Tuesday. If you believe in the Son of God, you have eternal life. Say it to yourself in the first person: I believe in the Son of God, and I have eternal life. Then live today as someone whose future is settled: generous, unafraid, free to serve.

For worship. God wants his children to know. He is not a Father who keeps his sons in suspense about whether they will be thrown out. He has written it down, sealed it with his Son’s blood, and put his Spirit in our hearts to say it to us. The life he has given is eternal, which means it cannot end, and he has told us so plainly that the weakest believer may say, with the old apostle, we know.
verseByVerse.note: John’s Gospel was written that readers might believe; this letter that believers might know they have eternal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us.

And this is the confidence that we have toward him. “Confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, as in 2:28; 3:21; 4:17. Assurance of eternal life leads to boldness in prayer. The assured believer of verse 13 immediately has a posture toward God: bold, open, unashamed.

That if we ask anything according to his will he hears us. “According to his will” (kata to thelēma autou) is the governing condition of prayer (Matthew 6:10). Prayer is not bending God to our will but aligning ourselves with his. “Hears” (akouei) means hears favourably, listens with intent to grant. We learn his will through Scripture, and the Spirit helps us pray (Romans 8:26–27). The condition does not lower expectations; it clarifies them. The question shifts from will God hear me? to what is God’s will? The person who knows God through his word can pray with confidence, because he is asking in the direction God is already moving.

Asking in his name. The boldness John describes was given in the upper room. Jesus told his disciples that whatever they asked in his name he would do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son (John 14:13–14). To pray in his name is not to add a formula at the end; it is to come on his merit and ask what he would ask. At Lazarus’s tomb he said, Father, I thank you that you have heard me; I knew that you always hear me (John 11:41–42). Our prayers are heard because we come in the name of the Son who is always heard.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must know God’s will in every detail before praying. We bring our requests honestly, submitting them to his wiser will, as Jesus did in Gethsemane.

Should I add if it be your will to every prayer? Is that a lack of faith? It is not a lack of faith when the matter is one Scripture leaves open, such as healing, a job or a particular outcome; it is humble trust, and Jesus prayed that way in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39). James says we should say, if the Lord wills (James 4:15). But where God has plainly revealed his will, there is no need to hedge: pray boldly that he will forgive, make you holy, give you wisdom (James 1:5), spread the gospel, and keep his people. The phrase should never be a way of expecting nothing. It is the trust of a child who asks freely and lets his Father decide.

In a sentence. This is the confidence we have in approaching God: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for something you know is God’s will from Scripture, such as growth in holiness or the spread of the gospel, with confidence. Find one promise in the Bible this week and pray it back to God word for word.

For worship. The God of heaven listens. He who holds the galaxies bends to hear the whisper of a child, and he hears with the intention of giving. His will is not a wall against our prayers but a channel for them, and it is good, pleasing and perfect. We do not come to him as strangers hammering on a locked gate. We come as children already welcomed, through a torn curtain, and the Father who delights in his Son delights to hear those who come in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of him.

And if we know that he hears us in whatever we ask. Being heard by God is the same as receiving. The logic of verse 14 is pressed to its conclusion.

We know that we have the requests that we have asked of him. “Have” (echomen) is present tense: the answer is as good as given, even before we see it. If God hears a prayer according to his will, it is granted, in his time and way (Mark 11:24). Not we will have but we have. God’s hearing is itself the act of granting. It is not a blank cheque for any desire labelled prayer; it is the confident posture of the person whose asking has been shaped by the God he knows.

Every promise is Yes in him. How can John say we already have what we have asked? Because the answer is anchored in Christ, not in the strength of the asking. All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20), and he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all will graciously give us all things with him (Romans 8:32). The Father who has already given his best will not withhold anything good that is asked according to his will. The cross is the pledge behind every answered prayer.

Daniel’s three weeks. Daniel prayed and fasted for three weeks, and when the answer finally came, the messenger told him: from the first day that you set your heart to understand, your words have been heard, and I have come because of your words (Daniel 10:12). For twenty-one days Daniel saw nothing. But he had been heard on the first day. Delay is not refusal, and silence is not deafness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the answer always comes immediately or in the form we expect. It means God’s favourable hearing is itself the guarantee.

If God has already heard, why keep praying about the same thing? Because Jesus told us to. He told the parable of the widow who kept coming to the judge, to show that we ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1–8), and he taught us to ask, seek and knock, all continuous (Matthew 7:7). Persistent prayer is not nagging an unwilling God but trusting a willing one, and it changes us as we wait: it deepens our desire, purifies our motives, and keeps us dependent on him. Keep praying until God answers or shows you that his answer is different from what you asked.

In a sentence. And if we know that he hears us, whatever we ask, we know that we have what we asked of him.

On a Tuesday. Thank God in advance for prayers prayed according to his will. He has heard, and he will answer. Keep a simple list of what you have asked, and come back to it in a month to note what he has done.

For worship. Our prayers do not vanish into an empty sky. They arrive at a throne, before a Father who has promised to hear, through a Son who lives to intercede for us. Not one prayer prayed according to his will has ever been lost. He keeps them, the book of Revelation says, like incense in golden bowls before the throne, and in his perfect time he answers every one.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life—to those who commit sins that do not lead to death. There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death.

If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death. This is the most contested passage in the letter. The confident intercession of verses 14–15 is immediately applied to one of the most painful pastoral situations: a sinning brother. It is an example of praying according to God’s will. “Brother” means a fellow member of the church. “Not leading to death” (mē pros thanaton) is sin that does not end in spiritual death: most likely the ordinary failures and sins of genuine believers, for which repentance and forgiveness remain available (1:9).

He shall ask, and God will give him life. “Ask” (aitēsei) is pray. God answers intercession by restoring and sustaining the sinning believer’s spiritual life. God gives life through the prayers of his people.

There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that. The sin that leads to death is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by the false teachers who left the church (2:19, 22): a deliberate, persistent denial of the Son despite knowing the truth, akin to the blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:29) and the apostasy of Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26. John does not forbid praying for such people; he simply does not command it, since they have rejected the only means of life. His refusal to command prayer for that is not a ban on interceding; it is pastoral honesty, for a prayer for restoration assumes the person can still be restored.

All wrongdoing is sin, but there is sin that does not lead to death. “Wrongdoing” (adikia) is unrighteousness. John does not make light of any sin; all of it is serious. But the sins of believers who remain in Christ do not lead to spiritual death, because his blood cleanses them (1:7).

I have prayed for you. The church’s prayer for a stumbling brother copies something Christ does. On the night Peter would deny him, Jesus said, Simon, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:31–32). Peter fell, but his faith did not die. John has already told his readers that if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (2:1). When believers pray for a sinning brother and God gives life, they are praying in step with the Advocate, who always lives to make intercession for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

Where Christians differ: what is the sin that leads to death? Roman Catholic teaching distinguishes mortal sins (which destroy grace and lead to death unless confessed) from venial sins. Others think John means a sin punished by physical death under God’s hand of discipline (Acts 5:1–11, Ananias and Sapphira; 1 Corinthians 11:30), or the unpardonable sin of blaspheming the Spirit (Matthew 12:31–32); and the honest truth is that we cannot be dogmatic about every detail. Verdict: In context, the sin leading to death is not a category of especially bad acts that a believer may commit and so lose salvation, but the settled apostasy of those who deny Jesus is the Christ, as the false teachers did. True believers, born of God, are kept from it (v. 18). There is no list of mortal sins that sends a genuine believer to hell; all their sins are covered by Christ’s propitiation (2:1–2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we can know with certainty that someone has committed the sin that leads to death, so that we should give up on them. That judgement belongs to God.

Could I have committed the sin that leads to death? If you are worried that you have, that worry is strong evidence that you have not. The sin John means is a settled, hardened rejection of Christ by people who no longer care, who have walked away and want nothing more to do with him. A person who fears he has sinned beyond forgiveness and still wants Christ is not that person. The very desire to be forgiven is the work of the Spirit, who does not work in the hearts of the finally hardened. Come to Christ now. He has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37), and that promise has no exception clause.

In a sentence. If you see any brother or sister commit a sin that does not lead to death, you should pray and God will give them life. I refer to those whose sin does not lead to death. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying that you should pray about that. All wrongdoing is sin, and there is sin that does not lead to death.

On a Tuesday. Is a fellow believer struggling with sin? Pray for them specifically today, and ask God to restore them. Do not gossip about him; pray for him. And if the Lord gives you the opportunity, go to him gently, as one who could fall the same way (Galatians 6:1).

For worship. The Father hears his children pleading for one another, and he answers with life. When a brother stumbles, the Father does not wait for him to find his own way back; he stirs up the prayers of the church and answers them with life. No sin of a believer is too dark for the blood that cleanses from all sin, and no wandering child is beyond the reach of a Father who runs to meet him on the road. The church on its knees for the fallen is a picture of the mercy that once came running for each of us.
verseByVerse.note: The “sin that leads to death” is probably the settled rejection of Christ shown by those who left the church.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning, but he who was born of God protects him, and the evil one does not touch him.

We know. This is the first of three closing certainties (vv. 18, 19, 20), three hammer blows of assurance at the end of the letter.

That everyone who has been born of God does not keep on sinning. As in 3:6, 9: the present tense means habitual, settled sin. The habitual orientation of the regenerate life is away from sin, not settled into it.

But he who was born of God protects him. “He who was born of God” (ho gennētheis ek tou theou, aorist) is Christ, the eternally begotten Son (some manuscripts read protects himself, referring to the believer, but the better reading points to Christ). “Protects” (tērei) means keeps, guards. The believer does not keep himself safe by his own strength; Christ keeps him (John 10:28; 17:12, 15; Jude 24). Jesus said it in his prayer on the last night: while I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost (John 17:12).

And the evil one does not touch him. “Touch” (haptetai) means lay hold of, grasp so as to harm, seize. Satan may tempt and attack, but he cannot seize the believer and drag him back into his power. This is the perseverance of the saints: kept by Christ. Not a promise of immunity from temptation or spiritual attack, but of final security: the evil one cannot finally own or destroy the one Christ is keeping. The believer is not unassailed; he is undefeatable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin or never suffer spiritual attack. It means Satan cannot finally claim them.

Does this mean Satan cannot harm me at all, through illness or persecution? Not quite. Job was afflicted in body, family and possessions with God’s permission, and Paul received a messenger of Satan to harass him (2 Corinthians 12:7). Believers are tested, persecuted and sometimes killed (Revelation 2:10). But Satan works only within the limits God sets, and he cannot touch the life that is in Christ. He could take Job’s health but not his God; he could kill the martyrs but not separate them from Christ’s love (Romans 8:38–39). The worst he can do to the body becomes, in God’s hands, the means of bringing his child home.

In a sentence. We know that anyone born of God does not continue to sin; the One who was born of God keeps them safe, and the evil one cannot harm them.

On a Tuesday. Thank Jesus that he keeps you, and that the evil one cannot lay hold of you. When you are afraid of falling away, pray not first, help me hold on, but, Lord, you are holding me; keep me. Then do the next obedient thing.

For worship. The Son keeps his own. He who was born of the Father before all ages stands guard over every one of his people, and he has never lost one. The evil one prowls and roars, but he cannot lay a finger on the life that is hidden with Christ in God. We are kept by the power of God through faith, for a salvation ready to be revealed, and the hand that holds us bears the marks of the nails.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one.

We know that we are from God. The second certainty. “From God” (ek tou theou) means born of him, belonging to him.

And the whole world lies in the power of the evil one. “Lies” (keitai) suggests passive lying, like someone asleep in another’s arms. “In the power of the evil one” (en tō ponērō) is literally in the evil one. The world in its rebellion against God is under Satan’s influence (John 12:31; 2 Corinthians 4:4; Ephesians 2:2), not actively fighting him but resting in his embrace, unaware and unresisting. There are only two realms, and no neutral ground between them.

Lifted up to draw. The verse that names the world’s captor goes straight on to name its rescuer. Now will the ruler of this world be cast out, Jesus said, and I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself (John 12:31–32); and John adds that he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die. The world lies passive in the evil one’s grip and cannot climb out. But the Son lifted up on the cross is drawing people out of every nation, and those who are from God are the ones he has drawn. To be from God is to have been pulled out by a crucified hand.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Satan is equal to God or has ultimate control. God is sovereign; Satan’s power is limited and already broken by Christ (3:8; Colossians 2:15).

How should I treat a world that lies in the evil one? Should I withdraw? No. Jesus prayed not that the Father would take us out of the world, but that he would keep us from the evil one (John 17:15), and he sent us into it (John 17:18). The world is not to be feared, despised or imitated, but loved and reached. Your unbelieving neighbours are not the enemy; they are captives of the enemy, asleep in his arms, and the gospel is the voice that wakes them. So be in the world as a light, not a mirror: work well, love well, speak of Christ, and refuse its idols. Separation from sin, yes; separation from sinners, no.

In a sentence. We know that we are children of God, and that the whole world is under the control of the evil one.

On a Tuesday. Thank God that you belong to him, and pray for those still lying in the power of the evil one. Think of one person at work or on your street who seems far from God, and pray that God will wake him, and that you might be part of the waking.

For worship. We were once asleep in the same arms. The whole world lies in the evil one, and so did we, unaware and unresisting, until a voice broke the sleep. The Son of God entered the strong man’s house, bound him, and carried us off as his plunder, and now we are from God. Nothing in us began the rescue, and nothing in the evil one can undo it. The same grace is still reaching into the world, waking the sleepers one by one and bringing them home.

verseByVerse.quote: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true; and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.

And we know that the Son of God has come. The third and culminating certainty. “Has come” (hēkei) means has arrived and is present. The incarnation, the great fact with which the letter opened (1:1–2), is restated as the ground of everything.

And has given us understanding. “Understanding” (dianoian) is mind, insight, the capacity to grasp. Not secret knowledge for an elite, as the false teachers claimed, but a renewed mind given to all believers. Not merely information but the spiritual capacity to know the true God.

So that we may know him who is true. “Him who is true” (ton alēthinon) is the genuine one, the real one: God the Father, in contrast with false gods (John 17:3).

And we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. Union with the Father is union with the Son.

He is the true God and eternal life. “He” (houtos, this one) most naturally refers to Jesus Christ, the nearest antecedent. One of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, alongside John 1:1 and 20:28. Jesus is the true God and is himself eternal life (1:2). The circle from the prologue is now complete: the eternal life that was with the Father and was made manifest (1:2) is now declared to be the true God himself.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called the true God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some scholars, take he to refer to the Father. Verdict: Grammatically, this one most naturally refers to the nearest person, Jesus Christ. John has just called Jesus eternal life (1:2), and his Gospel calls Jesus God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28). The letter that opens with the eternal life made visible closes by naming him the true God. Jesus is fully God, one with the Father, as the church confesses.

Thomas’s confession. John’s Gospel reaches its height when Thomas, faced with the risen Jesus and his wounds, says, my Lord and my God! (John 20:28). Jesus did not correct him. The letter reaches its height in the same place. The man whom John heard and saw and touched is the true God. The apostle who leaned on his chest at supper ends his letter on his knees.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Jesus is the Father, as if the two were one person under two names. They are distinct persons, both fully God.

How can Jesus be the true God when he prayed to the Father? Because God is one being in three persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet one God (Matthew 28:19). The Son praying to the Father is not one God praying to another, nor God praying to himself, but one divine person speaking to another within the one life of God. And as man, the Son truly prayed, depended and obeyed, as our representative. The incarnation did not make him less God; it made him also man. Scripture holds both together: I and the Father are one (John 10:30), and the Father is greater than I (John 14:28), the second spoken of his humble state as man.

In a sentence. We know also that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true. And we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Worship Jesus Christ today as the true God and eternal life. When you pray, speak to him directly, as Thomas did: my Lord and my God. And when someone tells you Jesus was only a good teacher, answer gently with this verse.

For worship. He is the true God. The baby who was laid in a manger, the man who wept and slept and bled, is the living and true God, Creator of all, before whom angels veil their faces. And he is eternal life, not merely its giver but its very self. We are in him: hidden in the true God, joined to eternal life, held by the one who made the stars and bore our sins. There is nothing higher to know, nothing deeper to have, nothing truer to worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Little children, keep yourselves from idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Little children, keep yourselves from idols.

Little children, keep yourselves from idols. “Keep” (phylaxate) means guard, protect yourselves. “Idols” (eidōlōn) are images, false gods. It is one of the most abrupt closings in the New Testament, and exactly right: after declaring Jesus to be the true God (v. 20), John warns against every false god. In Ephesus, where John probably wrote, the temple of Artemis and emperor worship meant literal idols were everywhere. The word also covers the false Christ of the false teachers, a god made in their own image, and anything we put in God’s place: money, pleasure, status, self (Colossians 3:5). Christ keeps us (v. 18), and we are to keep ourselves; both are true. The best protection is the deep knowledge of the one who is true. You cannot treasure the real and be satisfied with the counterfeit.

The last word of an old man. Fathers who know they are dying say the thing that matters most. John has written of light and love, of the Son and the Spirit, of new birth and eternal life, and he ends not with a blessing but with a warning, spoken with the tenderest name he has: little children. He knew how easily the heart drifts to substitutes. Calvin said the human mind is a perpetual forge of idols. The old apostle’s final act of love was to stand at the door of the forge.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers keep themselves saved by their own effort. It means they actively guard their hearts as those whom Christ keeps.

How do I recognise an idol in my own life? An idol is anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, meaning, comfort, approval. Ask some searching questions. What do I worry about losing most? What do I daydream about? Where does my money go first? What makes me angry when it is threatened? What do I turn to when I am anxious or sad? Whose approval do I most crave? An idol is usually a good thing made into a god thing: a child, a career, a body, a reputation, a cause. The answer is not merely to smash the idol but to love Christ more, so that it shrinks back to its proper size.

In a sentence. Dear children, keep yourselves from idols.

On a Tuesday. What is competing with Christ for first place in your heart? Name it, and put it down today. Then replace it: spend the time, money or attention you would have given it on something that honours Christ, and tell him that he is better.

For worship. There is one true God, and he is enough. Every idol promises what only he can give and gives nothing back but emptiness. He alone made us, redeemed us, keeps us and will bring us home. The Son who is the true God has come, and in him we have found the real thing. Little children, keep yourselves from idols, because you have been given the living God, and nothing else deserves your heart.

5.theology:
Faith as Victory. The declaration of 5:4 — "this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith" — is one of the most important statements about the nature of faith in Scripture. Faith is not a spiritual achievement, a heightened state of consciousness, or a moral virtue we cultivate. It is a hand that receives, a trust that rests, a confidence that looks away from itself to the Son of God who has already overcome. "Has overcome" — this points to the finished work of Christ at the cross as the source and ground of the believer's victory. We do not overcome the world by spiritual heroism; we overcome it by trusting the one who already has.

Assurance as Gift. The stated purpose of the letter — "that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13) — stands as a rebuke to every theology that treats Christian assurance as presumption or spiritual pride. John writes to produce certainty. Reformed theology has always distinguished between assurance and presumption: presumption claims safety without evidence; assurance rests on the testimony of the Spirit, the evidence of new birth, and the promises of God. The three tests of the letter are not meant to produce anxiety but confirmation — the gentle hand of a faithful pastor showing the believer where the signs of life are visible. To know that you have eternal life is not arrogance; it is the appropriate response to the faithfulness of the God who cannot lie.
5.examples:
Then: The community, battered by false teaching and painful departure, needed to know one thing above all: that they had not missed it, that they were in the Son, that the life they had received was real and was eternal. John writes to give them that certainty — not a new experience, not a higher spirituality, but the settled confidence of those who have the Son and therefore have life. The simplicity of the final verdict — "whoever has the Son has life" — is both the most inclusive and most exclusive statement possible: inclusive, because anyone may have the Son; exclusive, because there is no life outside of him.

Now: In an age of therapeutic Christianity, where the goal is often feeling good about ourselves, John's letter is a corrective and a comfort. Assurance in John is not a feeling to be cultivated; it is a knowledge to be received — grounded in the testimony of God himself (5:9–10), confirmed by the evidence of new birth, and resting ultimately on the person of the Son. "This is the true God and eternal life" — Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, today, and forever. Whatever else may be uncertain in a Christian life, this is not: whoever has the Son has life, and the Son cannot be taken away.
